spec.topic: Should schools replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You want schools to drop report cards altogether. Why?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Schools should replace report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences, because parents often misread a single letter grade.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How do you mean, misread?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: A letter grade squeezes a whole term of work into one symbol, which is the reason parents misread it. I taught for fourteen years myself.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying a grade hides what the child actually did.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Yes. Working parents often cannot attend a daytime conference, though, and that is the real weakness of my proposal.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Can that be fixed?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Schools can offer evening and video conference slots, which means working parents can still take part.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, conferences can fit around parents' work schedules.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Schools can staff those extra slots because two conferences a year is few enough to cover. My sister teaches third grade, I should add.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Is that realistic?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: It is realistic, since most schools already hold two parent evenings a year.

spec.topic: Should households keep a shared emergency cash fund for unexpected expenses?

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether households should keep a shared emergency cash fund. Ayesha, could you start us off?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Households often face unexpected expenses while many households receive income irregularly.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Because those pressures can disrupt a household budget, households should keep a shared emergency cash fund.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Unexpected expenses can require payment immediately, so a shared emergency cash fund gives households immediate access to money for urgent bills.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Because income may arrive irregularly, a shared emergency cash fund can help households save through flexible contributions.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: The difficulty is that regular contributions to a shared emergency cash fund can be impractical for households with irregular income.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: In other words, a shared emergency cash fund can help households build emergency savings through flexible contributions even when income is irregular. That directly challenges the concern about irregular income.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: The meeting minutes will be circulated on Friday.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Clement keeps a list of local repair services on his phone.

utterances.speaker: Harriet

utterances.text: We should prohibit them, since they emit pollutants that worsen local air quality.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: I support proportional representation for national elections because it gives parties seats that more closely match their shares of the vote. That closer match is the central reason to replace single-member constituencies.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Single-member constituencies give each district a named representative. Each district elects one person whom residents can identify as their representative, which explains that direct link.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: As a personal note, I have never worked for a political party.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Proportional representation gives voters fewer wasted votes. I offer that reduction in wasted votes as another reason national elections should use proportional representation.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Coalition bargaining can blur responsibility for government decisions. Proportional representation tends to produce coalition governments, and that is why coalition bargaining can blur responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Residents have someone specific to contact when their district elects one representative; that is a further reason single-member constituencies give each district a named representative. I voted in the last national election.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Tariq's proposal, in other words, is that national elections should use proportional representation instead of single-member constituencies.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: No: national elections should retain single-member constituencies instead of adopting proportional representation. The reason is that single-member constituencies give voters a direct way to remove an unpopular local representative.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Proportional representation gives smaller parties a realistic chance of winning seats. That is also a reason national elections should use proportional representation.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So you are saying that smaller parties would have a realistic chance of winning seats under proportional representation.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Proportional representation lowers the threshold for smaller parties to win seats, which is why it gives smaller parties a realistic chance of winning seats.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Proportional representation makes fewer votes ineffective. That is why I think it should replace single-member constituencies.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: To sum up, national elections should use proportional representation rather than single-member constituencies.

spec.topic: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Item two is the jury rules paper. Rafael, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: My view is that criminal trials should require unanimous verdicts in every serious offence. The reason is that unanimity forces jurors to keep deliberating until every doubt has been aired.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: That matters, since a verdict reached after every doubt has been aired is more reliable.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Wrongful convictions of serious offenders are intolerable. Also, the state's power to imprison someone for years demands the highest standard of proof, which is another reason for unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Unanimity makes it harder for the prosecution to win a conviction.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: But a single stubborn juror can block a conviction that eleven others consider justified.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So you are saying Rafael's proposal would let one holdout juror override the rest of the jury.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Yes, and retrials after hung juries cost the court service a great deal of money.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Quick aside: the heating in this room has been broken all week.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Hung juries are rare, occurring in only a small share of trials, which is why the retrial cost is a small problem next to one wrongful conviction.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Put another way, a single juror's doubt can legitimately prevent a conviction for fairness, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Unanimity is the safest guard against unjust imprisonment. Also, I must leave at four.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: In other words, unanimity should stay for every serious offence, and I want the committee to recommend that.

spec.topic: Should youth football leagues prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Our agenda item is whether youth football leagues should prohibit heading until players reach sixteen. Annelise, would you like to begin?

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: I recommend prohibiting heading until players reach sixteen because repeated heading can increase young players' risk of concussion.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: A further reason for that policy is that younger players may not reliably use safe heading technique.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Youth leagues already have trained coaches who can supervise technical drills, which is another reason to adopt the prohibition.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Because repeated heading carries that risk, a sixteen-year age cutoff would also be easy for leagues to administer.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Since younger players may not reliably use safe technique, they need gradual instruction before they attempt heading.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed rule would be straightforward for leagues to apply by age.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Put another way, younger players should receive step-by-step preparation before heading.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: A total ban until sixteen would remove a useful chance for coaches to teach safe decision-making through controlled exercises. The presence of trained coaches makes that concern concrete.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: In other words, a total ban until sixteen would take away controlled opportunities for coaches to teach safe decision-making, and that is why I object to the proposed prohibition.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Separately, the league's annual safeguarding meeting is scheduled for June.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: The registration deadline for next season is 1 August.

spec.topic: Should publicly funded research be required to publish all results, including failed experiments?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Our question is whether publicly funded research should be required to publish all results, including failed experiments. Camille, you support that requirement.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: I do. Publicly funded research should be required to publish all results, including failed experiments, because unpublished failed experiments distort the evidence available to the public.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Unreported failures make successful findings appear more reliable than they are, which is why the evidence becomes distorted.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: I oppose a blanket rule. Failed experiments often produce noisy results, so journals should not be compelled to publish every failed experiment.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: A public register can label null results as preliminary. Clear labels can prevent readers from treating every failed experiment as decisive evidence.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Small research teams may struggle to meet detailed reporting requirements. A simpler disclosure route would reduce the reporting burden.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Camille, you mean that a simpler disclosure route would reduce the reporting burden on small research teams.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: There is also a privacy problem: a searchable archive could expose sensitive information about research participants. Strong anonymization is essential before failed experiments enter such an archive.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Since clear labels can prevent readers from misreading null results, you are saying that the obligation should cover a public register rather than a journal article for every failed trial.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: For context, my laboratory has tested the same recruitment method three times.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Because a simpler disclosure route would reduce the reporting burden, the rule should require a public record while allowing delayed release for privacy and patent reasons.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed rule would require a public record while allowing delayed release for privacy and patent reasons.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should public hospitals offer free genetic testing to patients with a strong family history of inherited disease?

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The public hospital serves patients from three counties. I support making this testing free, but the practical question is whether the service can handle it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What makes you think the hospital could assess these patients properly?

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The hospital's genetics clinic has two counsellors on duty.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Because two counsellors can review family histories promptly, the clinic can assess patients who may need testing.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Since prompt family-history reviews can identify likely mutation carriers, patients can be offered testing before their illness becomes apparent.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: That early identification matters because it lets patients learn about their inherited-disease risks before symptoms appear.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Because patients who know their risks early can begin surveillance sooner, they have a better chance of avoiding severe complications.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: That is why public hospitals should offer genetic testing free of charge to patients with a strong family history of inherited disease.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that public hospitals should provide no-cost genetic testing to patients with a strong family history of inherited disease?

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, the proposal would remove the price barrier for those high-risk patients.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal is to remove the price barrier for patients at inherited-disease risk.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Exactly: high-risk patients would not have to pay for genetic testing.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The concern is that free genetic testing could overwhelm public genetics clinics and lengthen waits for every patient.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: That risk is real, but it can be managed with appointment limits and additional funding.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: I have worked in the hospital's genetics service for eight years.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should every secondary school student have to pass a financial-literacy course to graduate? Laleh, you start.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Yes, every student should complete one before graduating, because young adults take on debt with no preparation at all.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: And the reason they are unprepared is that most borrowers cannot explain how the interest on their loans works.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: But the school timetable has no room for another mandatory course. I taught economics for ten years, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, Yusuf, a new required course would have to push out an existing subject.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: A requirement makes sense, since financial literacy can be taught inside maths lessons.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: So you are saying, Sunita, that the requirement would not need an extra class.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: My daughter's school already runs a budgeting club, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take a vote from the studio audience after the break.

spec.topic: Should pharmacies be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor’s appointment?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for clearly diagnosed minor infections without a doctor's appointment. The reason is that this would make treatment more accessible to patients who cannot quickly see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, this policy could encourage inappropriate antibiotic use, which is a serious objection to unrestricted pharmacy prescribing.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, I support giving pharmacies limited authority to provide antibiotics for straightforward minor infections.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Pharmacists can use a short clinical checklist to identify symptoms that require medical referral.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because pharmacists can use that checklist, it would help them screen patients consistently.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The same checklist would reduce the risk of treating infections that need a doctor's assessment, because it would direct those patients to medical care.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many pharmacies already provide vaccination and medication-advice services.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, pharmacies should be permitted to prescribe routine antibiotics for clearly diagnosed minor infections without a doctor's appointment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because pharmacies would have that permission, patients would gain a practical route to prompt treatment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Patients should also receive clear instructions to complete any antibiotic course that a pharmacist prescribes.

spec.topic: Should gene editing be permitted to prevent inherited diseases in human embryos?

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I think gene editing should be permitted to prevent inherited diseases in embryos, because severe conditions like Tay-Sachs bring enormous suffering to children and families.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Another reason is that editing the embryo is the only way to stop the mutation being passed down to every later generation.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Off-target edits could add new mutations that nobody can detect before birth.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: That is why embryo editing is unsafe at present, but you want it allowed anyway.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Side note: Fiona's brother-in-law works at a fertility clinic, if anyone wants a practical view.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Preimplantation testing already lets couples pick embryos free of the mutation. In other words, selection makes editing unnecessary for most families.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Selection fails when both partners carry two copies of the faulty gene, since every embryo is affected, so editing is needed in those rare cases.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Unrelated, but the first licensed gene-editing trial in Britain was announced last spring.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: I would limit permission to serious diseases that have no alternative.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: So you are saying editing should be allowed only for severe conditions where selection cannot work.

spec.topic: Should governments cap the fees charged by payment-processing companies to small businesses?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether governments should cap the fees that payment-processing companies charge small businesses. Eamon, why support a cap?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Small businesses usually have less bargaining power than large retailers when negotiating payment-processing fees. Because of that imbalance, a government fee cap would reduce the transaction costs paid by small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Astrid, what wider benefit would you expect?

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Since small businesses usually have less bargaining power than large retailers, a government fee cap would give them a fairer chance to compete with large retailers.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: The same bargaining imbalance is why a government fee cap would make payment costs easier for small businesses to budget.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: The national merchants' association will hold its annual conference in June.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Would a cap affect what firms can do with the money they save?

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Because small businesses usually have less bargaining power than large retailers, a government fee cap would leave small businesses with more cash for wages and stock.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: That bargaining disadvantage is also why a government fee cap would encourage small businesses to invest in new services.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Jasper, does the proposal offer any certainty beyond lowering the bill?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Yes. Since small businesses usually have less bargaining power than large retailers, a government fee cap would make processing costs more predictable for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: However, that prediction is wrong: a government fee cap would not make processing costs more predictable for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Astrid, are you saying the immediate effect would be lower charges rather than merely better negotiating conditions?

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: So you are saying that a government fee cap would directly lower what small businesses pay per transaction.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: In other words, Astrid's point is that a government fee cap would narrow the competitive gap between small businesses and large retailers.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: The parliamentary committee has scheduled a vote on the proposal for Thursday.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to the question of predictability after the break.

spec.topic: Should councils allow residents to vote directly on how a fixed portion of the annual budget is spent?

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether councils should let residents decide directly how a fixed portion of the annual budget is spent. Anika, you support the proposal; please begin.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: A six-month pilot in three wards recorded strong resident participation. Residents in that pilot selected projects that reflected their local priorities, because the pilot gave them a direct say.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Direct budget votes may exclude residents who have little spare time. The town library roof was repaired last spring, although that is a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: However, direct budget votes need not exclude residents who have little spare time when councils offer several ways to take part.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: A fixed share of the annual budget can be administered with a simple public ballot.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: So you are saying that the reserved budget share could be managed through a simple public ballot. In other words, the three-ward pilot recorded strong resident participation; that evidence supports your point about inclusion.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: The pilot showed that residents can identify worthwhile local projects. That is why councils should let residents vote directly on a fixed portion of the annual budget.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Thank you both. We will return to the question of accountability after the break; the next televised debate is scheduled for October.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should voting be compulsory, with a modest penalty for those who abstain without justification? Bilal, you start.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Voting should be compulsory, with a modest penalty for abstaining without a justification. Turnout at the last local election was only thirty-one percent, so a small minority made the decision for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jasper, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: But forcing people to the polls infringes their freedom, since the right to vote includes the right to stay home.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Australia has compulsory voting and turnout there is above ninety percent, which is another reason to adopt it. I lived in Melbourne for six years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Lorenzo, you look unconvinced.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Forced votes are often uninformed votes, because people with no interest in politics will tick boxes at random.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Lorenzo, you are saying compulsion lowers the quality of election results?

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Put another way, Lorenzo thinks a small informed turnout beats a large indifferent one.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Nadia, why do you back the fine?

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Voting is a civic duty like jury service, and that is why compulsion is right.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: In other words, Nadia, voting is a duty we owe, not an optional extra.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: A fine is not modest for a low-paid worker, since it can equal a day's wages.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Lorenzo, last word.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: A fine does nothing about distrust of politicians, because distrust is why most non-voters stay home.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Lorenzo, is that a fine cannot repair trust in politicians. My own polling station is in a primary school, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether local authorities should replace some on-street parking with secure bicycle storage. Wilhelmina, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Bicycle theft is widespread in the area, and secure storage reduces bicycle theft. That is why local authorities should replace some on-street parking with secure bicycle storage.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Short-stay parking supports local retailers. Because of that, local authorities should not replace parking spaces.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Alejandro, what would the replacement provide?

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: One car parking space can hold twelve securely stored bicycles. Since that capacity would make cycling more practical, local authorities can replace ten percent of their on-street parking spaces.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Femi, does the scale of the change affect your objection?

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Demand for on-street parking already exceeds the available supply. Therefore, removing some on-street parking would not solve traffic congestion.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: To clarify, the proposal is a limited conversion of ten percent of parking spaces rather than wholesale parking removal.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So you are saying that Femi's objection is that removing some parking would not solve traffic congestion?

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: Retailers need loading bays to receive deliveries, but the proposed bicycle storage can be installed without removing loading bays.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: Because preserving loading bays protects shop access, it supports replacing selected parking spaces; that is another reason for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Femi

utterances.speaker: Alejandro

spec.topic: Should supermarkets stop offering plastic produce bags?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Supermarkets should stop offering plastic produce bags. These thin bags are used for a few minutes and then thrown away, which is reason enough.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Single-use plastic bags break into fragments that persist in soil and water for decades, and that is why discarded produce bags are a lasting source of pollution. That in turn is a strong case for removing them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Besides, most fruit and vegetables have their own skin and do not need a bag.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Shoppers do need some way to carry loose items such as green beans and mushrooms.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But reusable mesh bags and paper bags can carry loose items, and they cost only a few cents.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I keep three mesh bags in my coat pocket.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Removing the bags would make shoppers carry produce loose or bring their own containers, which changes habits.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: People adapt quickly once a free convenience disappears, since carrier bag charges introduced in several countries cut bag use sharply within a year.

utterances.speaker: Author

spec.topic: Should schools abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students?

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether schools should abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition. Anika, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Class rankings create unhealthy competition among students because they make students compare their positions constantly.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Gideon, you support keeping the current system. Why?

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Class rankings give teachers a quick benchmark for comparing academic performance. Because that benchmark is visible, students can identify academic gaps sooner.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Noor, what is your response to that benefit?

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Schools should keep class rankings because they provide useful performance information.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: I disagree: schools should abolish class rankings. Anika's younger brother prefers studying science to studying history.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: So Gideon is saying that schools should keep class rankings because rankings provide useful performance information.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: In other words, class rankings turn classmates into rivals.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Private progress reports can give students useful feedback without publishing a class order.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Abolishing class rankings would reduce the pressure that students feel to outperform their classmates.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The audience will receive printed voting cards after the closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Because of the unhealthy competition created by rankings, and because private reports preserve useful feedback while reducing pressure, schools should abolish class rankings and adopt private progress reports instead.

spec.topic: Should people be expected to return online purchases to physical shops?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Online shopping has made returns a big business. Should people be expected to take their returns back to a physical shop?

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Yes, people should return online purchases to a shop where they can. Return collection vans add traffic and emissions.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Collection vans stop at dozens of doors to pick up only a handful of parcels, which is why the emissions add up. I live two streets from a retail park myself.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But rural and disabled customers cannot easily get to a shop.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: That is why I would apply the expectation only to people living near a shop.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the duty falls only on people with a shop nearby.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Right. And people should do it because shops gain: one retailers' group found that a third of people returning items buy something else.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does it not cost shoppers time?

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: A typical in-store return takes about twenty minutes in total. Retailers should also share drop-off points for returns.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why would sharing help?

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Shared drop-off points make in-store returns convenient, which is why retailers should share them.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying returns can be made convenient.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Yes. Put another way, van collections of returns worsen congestion and pollution, and we can avoid that.

spec.topic: Should cashless businesses be required to accept physical money?

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether businesses that currently take only digital payments should be required to accept physical money. Isaac, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Cashless businesses should be required to accept physical money because the requirement would protect customers who cannot use cards or payment apps.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: The requirement would also ensure that customers are not excluded from ordinary purchases.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Cash remains important during power cuts and network failures, which is another reason for the rule.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: But requiring cash acceptance would impose handling and security costs on small businesses. For the record, I paid for my breakfast with coins that morning.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Physical money is a practical fallback for customers without reliable digital access, and small shops can comply with a cash requirement by using a simple till procedure.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: So you are saying that physical money remains a practical fallback for customers without reliable digital access.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: In other words, physical money gives customers a workable alternative to digital payment. Small shops would not need elaborate systems to comply with the requirement because a simple till procedure would be enough.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: To put Lucia's point another way, the fallback role of physical money is especially important for people who lack reliable digital access.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: A national cash-acceptance rule would create one clear standard for businesses, which would make it easier for customers to know where they can pay with cash.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: A clear national standard should therefore be mandatory.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Before we close, Isaac, I am told you have a strong preference about the drinks supplied in this studio.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: I prefer tea to coffee during televised debates.

utterances.speaker: Gideon

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: And that entitlement is real, since unequal access to injury information lets insiders profit unfairly from betting markets.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Matteo, you had a concern?

utterances.speaker: Gideon

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Noted. Separately, the league office is moving to a new building next season.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: In other words, teams could disclose only availability status and not the diagnosis, which meets the original requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: We will pick this up later. The committee meets again on the fourteenth.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Peak-hour traffic on the busiest town-centre streets is routinely crawling. That is why local governments should charge drivers entering those streets during peak hours.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: To put Jelena's point another way, peak-hour traffic on the busiest town-centre streets routinely crawls. Because that congestion delays buses, a peak-hour entry charge would improve bus reliability.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal is a peak-hour entry charge for the busiest town-centre streets. Because the proposal would deter some car journeys, the proposed charge would reduce the number of cars entering those streets.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed fee would make buses more reliable. That shows that more reliable buses would make public transport more attractive.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: What Yusuf means is that the proposed charge would reduce car volume in the busiest streets. That is why reducing car volume there would make crossing those streets safer.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The market's new awning is green.

utterances.speaker: Amara

utterances.text: The council can protect low-income workers with targeted exemptions from the charge.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Targeted exemptions can prevent the charge from becoming regressive; that is why the council can protect low-income workers with targeted exemptions.

utterances.speaker: Kieran

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Funny aside: my daughter still writes her shopping lists by hand.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: But handwriting lessons take time from subjects pupils need more later, because adults rarely write more than a few lines by hand.

utterances.speaker: Kieran

utterances.speaker: Kieran

utterances.speaker: Babajide

utterances.speaker: Meera

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether police should be required to livestream all custodial interrogations. Agnieszka, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Police should be required to livestream every custodial interrogation because livestreaming would deter officers from using coercive tactics.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: But a universal livestreaming requirement could expose informants and victims, so I oppose the proposal. Separately, I spent eight years working as a criminal-defence solicitor.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Arjun, what practical benefit would the recordings provide?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: A recording would give courts an independent account of what happened during questioning; that is why I support mandatory livestreaming.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: So, Agnieszka, you are saying that every custodial interrogation should be livestreamed.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal under discussion is to livestream every custodial interrogation rather than only selected interviews.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Put another way, Agnieszka's proposal is a live video record of every custodial interrogation.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: What is the strongest evidence for making the requirement universal?

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: A neutral recording would let courts review disputed questioning, which is another reason to require livestreaming.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: Livestreaming would deter officers from using threats during interrogations; that is why I accept that it could improve some interviews, though not enough to justify a universal rule.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Police departments could keep footage restricted while active cases were continuing, and that is another reason to require livestreaming.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Most interrogation rooms already have secure cameras, which is another reason to require the livestreaming rule.

utterances.speaker: Meera

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Item two: whether terminally ill patients should have a legal right to request assisted dying. Milos, would you start?

utterances.text: I think they should have that right, because forcing a dying person to endure severe suffering against their will violates their autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: That is also my view, since palliative care cannot relieve every kind of suffering at the end of life.

utterances.speaker: Harriet

utterances.speaker: Milos

utterances.speaker: Helga

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: A law with strict safeguards protects patients while respecting their choices, and that is why I back it.

spec.topic: Should amateur boxing replace winning by knockout with points-only scoring?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You want amateur boxing to drop the knockout as a way of winning. Why?

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Amateur boxing should move to points-only scoring, because a knockout is a sign that a boxer has suffered serious brain trauma.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Doesn't removing the knockout take away what the crowds come to see?

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Amateur boxing exists to develop young people, not to provide a spectacle. I have coached juniors for fifteen years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the purpose of the sport is development rather than entertainment.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Yes, and that is why points-only scoring suits it: judges would then reward clean technique rather than damage. Our club gym floods every spring, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Head guards already make amateur boxing reasonably safe, though.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: But head guards do not stop the brain moving inside the skull, since the damage comes from the rotation of the head, which padding cannot prevent.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, a head guard protects the skin, not the brain.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Exactly. Points-only scoring also removes the incentive to hit harder than necessary, because a boxer who cannot win by stoppage gains nothing from a heavier punch.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would you say to coaches who worry that points scoring is too subjective?

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Subjective judging is a fair worry, but electronic scoring would make results more consistent.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How would that work in a small club hall?

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: That is possible because the sensors register every clean hit.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So, to put it plainly, you would give up the knockout for the sake of safety.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Yara, you are close to this one.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Priya, can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Put another way, trucks pay a much smaller fee than restaurants, which is unfair to restaurants, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Alejandro, where does that leave you?

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: I think daily trading should be limited to a few days a week, because limiting trucks that way would protect restaurants while keeping most of the benefit.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Yara, what else worries you?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Daily trading by food trucks leaves litter in the squares.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: So you are saying trucks leave rubbish behind in public squares.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: One more fact before we close.

utterances.speaker: Priya

spec.topic: Should sixteen-year-olds be allowed to vote in local elections?

utterances.text: Vikram, should sixteen-year-olds be allowed to vote in local elections?

utterances.text: Yes, they should, because councils decide on buses, schools and youth services that sixteen-year-olds use every day.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say they are too young to judge.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: People say sixteen-year-olds lack the maturity to vote, but many of them already work and pay tax.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about turnout?

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Sixteen-year-olds who vote with parents and teachers nearby keep voting as adults, since voting is a habit that forms early.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that an early first vote creates lifelong voters.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Yes, and that is another reason to lower the age: in Scotland's 2014 referendum, sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds turned out at higher rates than those aged eighteen to twenty-four.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Isn't there a risk that parents will tell them how to vote?

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Parents influence adult voters too. Put another way, nobody votes free of outside influence.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, adult voters are swayed by family and friends as well.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Schools can teach how the council works before pupils turn sixteen, which is one more reason to lower the age. I am a former councillor, so I have seen the gap first hand.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And the cost?

utterances.speaker: Vikram

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Vikram

spec.topic: Should parents give children a fixed weekly allowance or pay for completed chores?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Parents should give children a fixed weekly allowance rather than pay them for completed chores.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A predictable weekly amount teaches children to budget. That is why a fixed allowance is preferable to payment for every task.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Children can plan their spending more effectively when they know exactly how much money they will receive, because certainty makes budgeting possible.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A fixed allowance can make children treat household chores as optional; that is the strongest objection to my recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some children refuse to do chores unless a payment is offered. Because of that pattern, the objection deserves to be taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A small family survey found that children completed more chores when each task had a stated price. This evidence supports the claim that some children refuse unpaid chores.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Children also need opportunities to make mistakes with small amounts of money.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Parents can keep a fixed allowance while paying separately for occasional jobs outside normal family responsibilities. This arrangement works because it preserves both regularity and choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A hybrid system can distinguish ordinary family duties from exceptional paid work.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Separating ordinary duties from occasional jobs clarifies what parents expect.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Children are more likely to understand which tasks are expected and which tasks are optional when expectations are clearly separated, which shows the value of defining the two categories.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My first allowance was kept in a glass jar on my bedroom shelf.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, my recommendation is a regular payment rather than a price list for family life.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the main concern is that a fixed allowance may weaken children's motivation to do chores.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In essence, a hybrid arrangement leaves routine duties unpaid while allowing occasional jobs to be paid.

spec.topic: Should election day become a public holiday?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Election day should become a public holiday. Many people simply cannot leave work easily to vote on a weekday.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Hourly workers often lose pay or risk their shifts if they take time off to vote, which is to say that many people are in effect shut out of voting by their work schedules.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A public holiday would give nearly everyone a free day to vote.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Turnout in the last general election was only about sixty percent.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Turnout would rise with a holiday, because a free day removes the main obstacle, and countries that vote on a rest day or holiday often record higher turnout than ours.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say a holiday would cost the economy a day of lost output.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that loss would be small next to the benefit of a stronger democracy, since a working democracy is worth far more than one day of output.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Others object that a holiday would not by itself bring people to the polls.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: They add that polling stations could simply stay open late and so serve people who work.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, a holiday alone is not enough, and longer hours alone do not fix the problem for people on long or split shifts.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Weekday voting is a habit inherited from the nineteenth century, when farmers needed time to travel to town.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Voting is a civic duty that belongs among the shared occasions of national life.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I have voted at the same school hall for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, election day should be moved off the working calendar, because the case for a holiday is strong.

spec.topic: Should schools let students choose their own start times within a daily attendance window?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You head a school that has tried letting students pick their own arrival time. Should schools do this generally?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Yes, schools should let students choose their start times within a daily window. Teenagers' body clocks run later, so early starts leave many of them sleep-deprived.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why does that matter for school?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Because sleep-deprived students learn less in morning lessons, so the early start defeats its own purpose.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But teachers say flexible starts make it harder to plan lessons that need the whole class there.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Core lessons can simply be timetabled in the middle of the window, when everyone is present, and that is why it is workable in practice.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Do you have evidence it works?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: We ran a pilot last year, and late arrivals fell by a third, which shows it is workable.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Is there anything else in its favour?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Yes, students who choose their start time feel more responsible for their own attendance.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying flexible starts give students a sense of responsibility for their own attendance.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Exactly. Personally my own commute takes forty minutes, so I would have loved it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You have worked with young offenders for years. What is your position on conferences versus court?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying only minor offences should go to a conference.

spec.topic: Should mandatory minimum sentences for drug offences be abolished?

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Mandatory minimum sentences for drug offences should be abolished, because they prevent judges from imposing proportionate punishments.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Mandatory minimum sentences can require the same lengthy punishment for low-level couriers and major suppliers. That is why they block proportionate sentencing.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: I reviewed the latest sentencing table over coffee.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: But mandatory minimum sentences give courts a consistent baseline. That baseline matters because it prevents unjustified differences between similar cases.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: So you are saying that abolition would remove fixed minimum terms for all drug offences?

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Yes, because treatment programmes reduce repeat offending more effectively than long prison terms.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: In other words, your reason for abolition is that treatment reduces repeat offending more effectively than long prison terms.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Another reason is that mandatory minimum sentences pressure defendants to plead guilty before they can properly assess their cases; that is another reason to abolish them.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: The public gallery was unusually quiet that morning.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: A carefully designed sentencing guideline can preserve consistency without fixed minimum sentences. It can direct judges while allowing limited adjustments; that is why guidelines are a better tool.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: In other words, you want guidelines rather than fixed minimum terms to provide consistency.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: The ability to adjust a sentence is essential because drug cases differ greatly in culpability.

utterances.speaker: Author

spec.topic: Should local authorities merge neighbouring refuse-collection services to reduce administrative costs?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether neighbouring local authorities should merge their refuse-collection services to reduce administrative costs. Constance supports the proposal; why?

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: The neighbouring councils should merge their refuse-collection services because they currently maintain separate administrative teams that duplicate work.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Rosalind, what is the strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: If the councils merge their refuse-collection services, annual administrative overhead will fall. Shared procurement would reduce contract prices and deepen the administrative savings; that is another reason to merge.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: So you are saying that Constance wants the neighbouring councils to operate one refuse-collection service?

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed merger would interrupt refuse collections while the new system was being established.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: The councils use different colours on their collection calendars.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Residents would keep the same collection frequency under the proposed merger; that is why the service change is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal promises lower spending on refuse-collection administration. The merged authorities could share one scheduling platform, which is another practical reason to approve the merger.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Because the authorities could share one scheduling platform, duplicate licence fees would disappear.

spec.topic: Should restaurants automatically add service charges to every bill?

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Restaurants should add a service charge to every bill, because it gives staff a predictable income instead of leaving them to gamble on tips.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But an automatic charge takes away the customer's power to reward good service, and that is why waiters would stop trying hard.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: So you are saying tips are what keep waiters motivated.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Exactly. I waited tables for two summers in Leeds, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: But motivation comes from decent pay and good management, since studies of hospitality turnover name low wages as the main reason people quit.

utterances.speaker: Xavier

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: So you are saying restaurants skim the charge. A law sending every penny to staff would stop that, which is one more reason to adopt the charge.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Such a law would be hard to enforce, because inspectors rarely audit restaurant payrolls.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Put another way, you think the law would not be enforced in practice. Incidentally, I had dinner last Friday at a restaurant that adds a service charge.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: In other words, the law would be a dead letter, and that is why diners should be allowed to opt out.

utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether governments should automatically register every citizen who is eligible to vote. Laleh, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Many eligible citizens fail to register before voting deadlines. Automatic registration would make voting easier by removing a paperwork hurdle, because people would not have to begin the process themselves.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Some identity databases contain duplicate or outdated citizen records.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: I support automatically registering eligible citizens to vote. Countries with automatic registration report fewer registration-related barriers, which supports my claim that many eligible citizens fail to register.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Joaquin, is inaccurate data your main objection?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: But because some identity databases contain duplicate or outdated records, automatic registration could place inaccurate entries on voter rolls. That is an objection to adopting Laleh's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Automatic registration would make voting more accessible to people who move frequently. Since accessibility is a democratic benefit, governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying that governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Data checks can remove duplicate entries before election day. Separately, the next national election is scheduled for a Thursday.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: In other words, automatic registration would remove the need for eligible citizens to complete a separate voting application.

utterances.text: What Laleh means is that automatic registration would help citizens who move frequently.

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: The disagreement is now clear: the proposal promises easier access, while the concern is whether the records can be kept accurate.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Because automatic registration removes paperwork barriers and data risks are manageable, automatic registration is responsible.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

spec.topic: Should ports impose emissions limits on visiting cruise ships?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ports should impose emissions limits on visiting cruise ships. I grew up in a harbour town where ferries sat at the quay.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason is that cruise ships keep their engines running at berth for hours.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Residents near the cruise terminal suffer more asthma, which the figures show: hospital admissions for breathing problems rose in the district after the terminal opened.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Limits will not drive cruise lines away, since they already comply with strict limits in the Norwegian fjords.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a rival port without limits would lure the ships away. I should add that my cousin works at the pier office.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Retrofitting is affordable, because a shore-power adapter costs under one percent of a ship's price.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Voluntary pledges by cruise lines are not enough, because they carry no penalty for breaking them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a promise without a fine is only advertising.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Major ports should therefore require ships to connect to shore power. A ship plugged in produces no exhaust at the quay.

utterances.text: Bilal, do you agree?

utterances.text: Participation grades also reward effort that exams miss, which is another reason to allow them. I taught for twelve years before going into politics.

utterances.text: Businesses should replace fixed allowances with unlimited paid leave, because staff who are trusted take ownership of their work.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How does a leave policy create trust?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: The reason is that unlimited leave is a clear signal that people are trusted. My company has run it for three years now.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Many employees take less leave under these schemes than they did before.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: On the contrary, at my company staff now take two more days a year than before. Burnout resignations have also halved, which gives you a second ground for the change.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying staff take more leave when nobody counts their days.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Exactly. One practical worry is that small firms may struggle to arrange cover.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How should a firm begin?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Managers must take leave themselves, which is why a firm should begin with a pilot in one team.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, start small and test it before rolling it out.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Yes, and the reason managers matter is that staff copy what their leaders do.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, leaders have to take their own leave.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some firms now offer unlimited paid leave instead of a fixed number of days. Where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Businesses should not make that switch, because employees under unlimited leave tend to take fewer days off than they did under a fixed allowance.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why would people take less when they are allowed more?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Since there is no stated number, nobody can tell what a normal amount is. They look to colleagues and managers to judge it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And does it matter if they rest less?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Yes. Employees who take fewer days off become more exhausted, and exhausted employees make more mistakes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But supporters say unlimited leave gives people freedom to rest whenever they need it.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: It is a freedom on paper only, since people fear looking uncommitted.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the freedom is not real.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Exactly, employees under unlimited leave do not truly have the freedom to rest.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What was your own experience?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: My first job was in a bakery with a fixed allowance of twenty days.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could a company fix the problem by setting a minimum number of days?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Unlimited leave can work if the company sets a minimum number of days that staff must take.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So, put another way, a mandatory minimum is just a fixed allowance under a new label.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Right. Also, I have been interviewed on this subject several times before, and fixed allowances are easier for payroll to account for when staff leave.

spec.topic: Should governments ban the release of genetically modified mosquitoes to control disease?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should ban releasing genetically modified mosquitoes. Javier, you open.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: No ban. The reason is that trials have cut local dengue-carrying mosquito populations by over eighty percent.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Noor, does that persuade you?

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Partly. Fewer dengue-carrying mosquitoes means fewer people infected, which is why those trial numbers matter.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: But released mosquitoes could have unforeseen effects on the ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: So, Joaquin, what you mean is that there is a risk nobody can yet rule out?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Yes. I should say I grew up somewhere dengue was common, so I take it seriously.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Since only a few species feed on mosquitoes, and they have other prey, I would say the ecological worry is overstated.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Noor, your view on the alternative?

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: A ban would push communities back to insecticide spraying, and spraying harms the ecosystem more than modified mosquitoes do, so I oppose a ban.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: We are over time, so we will stop there.

spec.topic: Should livestock producers pay a methane tax based on herd emissions?

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: I think livestock producers should pay a methane tax based on their herd emissions. The reason is that livestock methane emissions impose climate costs that producers do not currently pay for.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: But a methane tax based on herd emissions would punish producers who have few affordable mitigation options. My cooperative sells cheese at weekend markets.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Revenue from a methane tax could fund digesters on livestock farms. The reason that revenue would help is that public funding would make methane digesters affordable for more livestock producers.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Affordable digesters would give livestock farms a practical way to reduce their taxable emissions, which is why a small-farm exemption should be included.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: A methane tax should include an exemption for small farms. An emissions threshold for small farms can be administered only with reliable herd records.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: So you are saying that a methane tax should exempt small farms.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Since an emissions threshold depends on reliable herd records, those records would let officials compare emissions fairly across farms.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Because reliable records allow fair comparisons, the methane tax should use measured emissions rather than simply counting animals. A tax based on measured emissions would require reliable monitoring.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Because reliable monitoring is required, farms could share monitoring equipment to reduce its expense. Shared monitoring equipment would lower compliance costs for livestock producers.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed methane tax would be tied to recorded herd emissions instead of head count.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: A methane tax should offer credits for verified emissions reductions, because those credits would encourage producers to invest in mitigation.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Those investment incentives are why a methane tax with credits for verified reductions would be politically workable.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: In other words, a politically workable methane tax would use credits tied to verified emissions reductions, because that condition would encourage producers to invest in mitigation.

spec.topic: Should clinical trials be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups?

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are debating whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nadia, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Clinical trials should be required to enroll equal numbers from all major demographic groups. Equal demographic representation would make the findings more applicable to the whole population, which is why I support the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: I think a universal equal-number rule is too rigid for some studies. For context, I have advised investigators in three rare-disease trials.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Including all major demographic groups in trials is scientifically valuable because treatment effects can differ across demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The disagreement seems to concern whether equal participation is always feasible, not whether representation matters.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: My research team opened a new research office last month.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Recruitment quotas can delay a clinical trial.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Equal numbers are not appropriate for every clinical trial, because a trial for ovarian cancer may need to recruit mainly women.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But, in other words, a universal equal-number rule is too rigid for some studies.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: So you are saying that every major demographic group should have the same enrollment number in every trial.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: The policy should require equal demographic numbers only when the disease and eligible population make that scientifically appropriate, because that flexibility would protect scientific validity.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Put another way, equal demographic numbers should be required only when the disease and eligible population make that scientifically appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Equal representation is not identical to fair representation, because a trial may need to recruit more participants from a smaller eligible group to estimate treatment effects reliably.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Since treatment effects can differ across demographic groups, and since a universal equal-number rule is too rigid for some studies, clinical trials should report their demographic coverage and justify departures from equal representation. In other words, they should disclose their coverage and explain any departure from equal representation.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: That gives us a possible compromise: representation is expected, but researchers must explain scientifically justified exceptions. Tariq, your final response?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Recruitment quotas can postpone the completion of a clinical trial, so any requirement should allow a documented exception process.

utterances.text: Should scientists be allowed to create embryos solely for laboratory research?

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Early-stage embryos can reveal how inherited diseases begin. Because of that, studying early-stage embryos can help scientists develop treatments for inherited diseases.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that studying early-stage embryos can help develop treatments for inherited diseases. For that reason, and because that knowledge could improve treatment, scientists should be allowed to create embryos solely for laboratory research when strict safeguards are in place.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: There is a serious objection, however: creating embryos solely for research risks treating potential human life merely as a means.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Another reason for permission is that independent review boards can enforce strict consent, storage, and destruction safeguards for research embryos.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, Dolores supports allowing research embryos only under strict safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Dolores

spec.topic: Should mobile operating systems be required to allow alternative app stores?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Damien, should mobile operating systems be required to allow alternative app stores?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Yes, mobile operating systems should be required to allow alternative app stores. Alternative stores would give users more choice about where to obtain applications.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: They would also give developers another way to distribute applications, and that could preserve competition between distribution platforms.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: I usually download applications from the store that comes preinstalled on my phone, so this policy would not force me to change my habits.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Alternative stores could be required to meet clear security standards, although some critics say they would create unacceptable security risks for ordinary users.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The requirement would not mean that alternative stores received the same prominence as the default store. A mobile operating system could allow them while warning users before installation.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: In practical terms, the proposal concerns access to alternative stores rather than equal promotion of every store. Independent developers would benefit from having more than one distribution channel.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You are saying that the security objection assumes every alternative store would be completely unregulated.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And to clarify the competition point, alternative stores would preserve the default store while preventing it from being the only legal option.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that allowing alternative stores would expand consumer choice without requiring users to leave the default store?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, security standards and installation warnings could address the main risks associated with alternative stores.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Finally, the argument is that alternative distribution channels would make it harder for one company to control access to mobile applications.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Exactly. I also think the policy is worth considering even if most people continue using the default store.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Separately, I prefer phones with long battery life.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: To put Pradeep's objection plainly, the claim is that insurance coverage would fund appearance goals instead of genuine health care.

utterances.speaker: Kai

utterances.text: In other words, these medications provide a medically meaningful treatment for adults without diabetes. They should not be excluded simply because diabetes is absent.
