spec.topic: Should local governments convert vacant municipal buildings into affordable workspaces for small businesses?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Deirdre, you want councils to turn their empty buildings into workspaces. Why?

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Councils should convert vacant buildings into affordable workspaces for small businesses, because empty buildings cost money to heat and secure every year.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Isn't the worry that councils make poor landlords?

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Councils have certainly run property badly before, but a managed-workspace operator can run these buildings on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the council owns the building and a specialist handles the day-to-day running.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Exactly. Rents for small firms in my town have doubled in ten years, which is why many have closed, and that is the reason to act.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Doesn't it distort the property market?

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: It does not distort the market, since private landlords have left these buildings empty for years, which is another reason to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some argue the money should go to schools instead.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: That ignores that conversion costs are repaid from rents within eight years, which is another reason to convert, since tenants' rents cover the running costs.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the scheme pays for itself.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Yes. The first pilot in the north end filled all twenty desks within a month, which shows demand is real.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: I visited that pilot last week and it smelled of fresh paint.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Did you try the sandwich shop on the ground floor? My cousin runs it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, empty buildings become a starting place for local firms.

spec.topic: Should routine antibiotic use in livestock be prohibited entirely?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: I think routine antibiotic use in livestock should be prohibited entirely. Routine dosing of healthy livestock should be classified as preventive antibiotic use.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: I support banning routine preventive dosing, but not treatment prescribed for a diagnosed infection.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: In other words, routine dosing of healthy livestock is preventive antibiotic use; because of that distinction, a prohibition should target preventive dosing rather than medically necessary treatment.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Resistance can move from livestock farms into human communities, and that risk should not be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Exactly; that is why routine antibiotic use in livestock threatens the effectiveness of important human medicines.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: To put the mechanism plainly, antibiotic-resistant bacteria can spread from livestock farms to people.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Routine antibiotic use on many farms creates widespread exposure to antibiotics, which makes that spread more likely.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: That is not enough to establish necessity: widespread routine antibiotic use does not prove that every herd needs antibiotics.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Some livestock farmers already keep detailed treatment records.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: I would like veterinary perspectives to be included in future farming-policy discussions.

spec.topic: Should governments build desalination plants despite their high energy use and marine impacts?

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Governments should build desalination plants despite their high energy use and marine impacts because prolonged droughts are making reliable freshwater supplies less secure.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: As a side note, I collect old maps of coastlines.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: I disagree with the proposal. Desalination plants can damage marine ecosystems through concentrated brine and disrupted intakes.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Renewable electricity can power desalination plants. That is increasingly practical because renewable electricity is becoming cheaper in many coastal regions, and that is why I still support building them.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: So you are saying that renewable electricity can power desalination plants. I also plan to post photographs from a desalination plant tour next month.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: I understand the ecological objection, but modern intake systems can reduce the marine harm caused by desalination, which is another reason to build carefully regulated plants.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: In other words, governments should add desalination to their water-supply options.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Expanding reservoirs is expensive in regions where suitable valleys are scarce; that is another reason governments should consider desalination.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Desalination plants can provide water during prolonged droughts, which is why governments should not reject them solely because they consume energy.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: To put Florin's point another way, safer intake systems reduce the marine harm caused by desalination.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: A desalination plant can publish daily data on salinity and marine impacts.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: In other words, a desalination plant can report its environmental effects every day.

utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether banks should be allowed to use facial recognition instead of passwords for customer authentication. Maeve, you support the change.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Banks should be allowed to use facial recognition instead of passwords for customer authentication. The reason is that customers frequently reuse passwords across banking websites.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But banks should not use facial recognition without a password fallback, because customers must not be locked out when a facial scan fails.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: So you are saying that banks should be permitted to replace passwords with facial scans for authentication. For context, I have used a banking application for six years.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: I support that point because banks should provide a non-biometric fallback for customer authentication. Facial scans can fail in poor lighting, which is why the fallback matters.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: As a separate point, my local bank branch has installed new security cameras.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel therefore agrees that any permission for facial authentication must include a reliable alternative. Yara, does that safeguard change your objection?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: No, it does not remove the privacy concerns, but we can return to those after the break.

spec.topic: Should neighbours be allowed to reserve public parking spaces outside their homes?

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Residents often circle for a long time before finding parking near their homes because evening demand exceeds the available parking supply.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: The public library closes at six on Thursdays.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Neighbours should be allowed to reserve public parking spaces outside their homes. If neighbours are allowed to reserve spaces, late-returning residents would have dependable parking.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: So you are saying that neighbours should be allowed to reserve public parking spaces outside their homes.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Exactly. Dependable parking would reduce the time late-returning residents spend circling for a space.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: The lift in my building has been unreliable this month.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But public parking bays should remain available to everyone rather than being controlled by individual households.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Public parking bays serve visitors and residents alike, which is why I question giving them to particular households.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: In other words, keeping public parking bays available to everyone means that no household gets exclusive control of them.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Since the bays must remain available to everyone, a reservation system for public parking bays would require costly enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Put another way, a reservation system would need officials to police who may use each space.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: That enforcement burden would be wasteful when the spaces already serve the whole street.

utterances.text: Transport authorities should use facial recognition on fare evaders, because evasion costs the network millions every year.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: I ride the tram every day myself. But facial recognition would put every passenger under surveillance just to catch a few evaders.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: So you are saying that catching a few evaders would cost every passenger their privacy.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Pilot cameras in Lyon cut evasion by a third, which is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Put another way, cameras should do the ticket inspectors' job of spotting evaders.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: The city council votes on this next month. We will take a short break.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should wedding guests be expected to contribute toward the couple's honeymoon?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: I do not think wedding guests should be expected to contribute toward the couple's honeymoon, because a wedding invitation should not create a financial obligation.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What makes that financial obligation particularly unfair?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Wedding guests already pay for travel and suitable clothing; that existing expense is why a wedding invitation should not create a financial obligation.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Can those expenses really make such a difference?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: For example, travel and clothing costs can exceed five hundred pounds for some wedding guests, which is why I regard those existing expenses as significant.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: The couple plans to spend two weeks travelling during its honeymoon.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does the purpose of the honeymoon affect your view?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Yes. A honeymoon is an optional luxury rather than a necessary wedding expense, so that is another reason wedding guests should not be expected to fund it.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: The couple has chosen a small seaside hotel for the honeymoon.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some couples say a honeymoon fund is simply a modern form of a wedding gift.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: However, couples can reasonably expect guests to contribute when they request honeymoon money instead of ordinary gifts, because cash contributions toward a honeymoon can replace gifts from a wedding registry.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So is the problem the request itself or the pressure behind it?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: A honeymoon fund can make guests feel pressured to give money; consequently, wedding guests should be free to decline a request for honeymoon money. That pressure is also why I disagree with treating contributions as an expectation.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, your position is that wedding guests should not be expected to contribute toward the honeymoon.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Exactly. Voluntary contributions toward a honeymoon are acceptable, because guests may genuinely want to give the couple money for their honeymoon.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, you accept voluntary honeymoon contributions but reject making them an expectation.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Yes. Couples should offer guests a clear no-gift option when mentioning a honeymoon fund, and offering that option keeps a honeymoon contribution request respectful.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Guests feel respected when they can decline a honeymoon contribution without embarrassment, which is why offering a no-gift option keeps the request respectful.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: To sum up, your position is that offering a no-gift option keeps a honeymoon contribution request respectful.

spec.topic: Should students be permitted to retake failed exams without their original grades counting?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should students be allowed to retake failed exams without the original grade counting? Sunita, you start.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Yes. Students should be allowed to retake failed exams without the original grade counting.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: But that ignores fairness: a retaker gets a second attempt that nobody else gets.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Florin, you are saying retakers get two chances while everyone else gets one.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Can I say something personal? I resat a chemistry paper myself in my first year.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: One bad exam day should not define a student's whole record, since a single result often reflects illness or stress rather than ability.

utterances.speaker: Host

spec.format: opinion essay by a single author
spec.topic: Should secondary schools make community service a graduation requirement?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Community service already occupies a small part of many teenagers' lives. That fact alone does not settle whether schools should require it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A graduation requirement would give every student a clear opportunity to contribute to the community.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Requiring service would expose every student to civic responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Community organizations often need dependable help with routine tasks.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a universal service requirement would ensure that every student encounters civic responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, compulsory service can burden students who have jobs or caring responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Schools can reduce that burden by offering several types of placement and flexible schedules.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, schools can make service flexible enough to accommodate different students.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Schools can make the requirement more equitable by providing placements during school hours.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Reflection sessions can help students understand what they learned from serving.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Reflection sessions connect practical service with broader civic lessons.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, reflection turns practical work into civic learning.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Allowing students to choose among approved placements would make the requirement more meaningful.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author completed a community clean-up during secondary school.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I therefore conclude that secondary schools should make community service a graduation requirement, because it gives every student an opportunity to contribute, exposes students to civic responsibility, supports organizations that need dependable help, and can be made equitable, reflective, and meaningful.

spec.topic: Should pregnant patients be offered paid time off for every antenatal appointment?

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Our agenda item is whether pregnant patients should receive paid time off for every antenatal appointment. Arjun, please start us off.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Pregnant patients often have to use annual leave for antenatal appointments. Because of that, paid time off would prevent pregnant patients from using annual leave for those appointments.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Before we begin, the meeting room projector needs a new bulb.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Since paid time off would prevent patients from using annual leave, I propose that employers offer pregnant patients paid time off for every antenatal appointment.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: A second reason to adopt this policy is that offering paid time off would reduce the risk that pregnant patients postpone antenatal care.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: However, that proposal could leave small teams short-staffed when several appointments occur in the same week.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposed policy could create staffing gaps for small teams.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal is that every pregnant patient would receive paid time off for each antenatal appointment.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Each antenatal appointment can be documented with its date and duration. Because of that straightforward record, a standard paid-leave rule would be easy for employers to administer.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: One unrelated practical note: the staff kitchen closes at four o'clock. Let us return to the decision.

spec.topic: Should employees receive company shares instead of part of their annual bonuses?

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether employees should take company shares instead of part of their annual bonus. Leilani, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Yes, part of the bonus should be paid in shares, because shares give employees a lasting stake in how the company performs.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: But that is a bad deal for staff, since their wages and their savings would then depend on the same employer.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Isaac, where do you come down?

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Cash motivates better than shares, because share prices move for reasons no employee controls.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: So you are saying cash is the better motivator.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: I read a survey on this last week, though I cannot recall who ran it.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Share awards also help firms keep skilled people, since unvested shares are forfeited when someone resigns.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Most private firms could not offer shares at all, the reason being that there is no market where staff could sell them.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: So you are saying shares are simply not an option for most private firms.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Which is also why a share award is worth less to staff than the same sum in cash.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Isaac, is there another objection?

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Yes: issuing shares to staff dilutes existing shareholders, since each new share shrinks the percentage held by everyone else.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Leilani, you have the last word.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: In other words, staff should be paid partly in ownership of the firm, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: For the record, I hold a few shares in my own employer, as it happens.

spec.topic: Should online voting be introduced for national elections?

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Online voting should be introduced for national elections, because turnout among people under thirty is far lower than among older voters and voting from a phone would make it easier for them to take part.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: It would also let voters abroad and voters with disabilities take part without having to travel.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: I'm against it. It can't be made secure enough, since a single successful attack on the system could change a national result. I work in network security, so I do not say that lightly.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Estonia has run online voting for years without a proven case of fraud.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: That tells us little about a large country, since Estonia has only about 1.3 million people, far fewer than most states.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Fine, but online voting is at least as safe as national elections need it to be.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Sorry for the short reply, I'm typing this on a train.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: My worry is different: voting at home removes the privacy a polling booth guarantees, which is why vote buying and family pressure would be harder to detect.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: So you are saying that voting at home removes the privacy a polling booth guarantees.

spec.topic: Should offshore wind developers compensate fishing communities for lost access to traditional grounds?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether offshore wind developers should compensate fishing communities for lost access to traditional grounds. Selin, you support compensation; make your case.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Offshore wind construction exclusion zones block fishing communities from their traditional grounds. Because of that loss of access, fishing communities' incomes fall.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Alejandro, you oppose the proposal. Before we come to your objection, Selin, what should developers do?

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: For both of those reasons, offshore wind developers should compensate fishing communities for lost access to traditional grounds.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: The proposed turbines would be visible from the harbour on clear days.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: Offshore wind developers earn revenue from the electricity their projects sell; that commercial gain is another reason fishing communities deserve compensation for lost access.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: But compensation is unnecessary for fishing communities.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: So you are saying that offshore wind developers should compensate fishing communities for the access they lose.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: In other words, Alejandro's position is that compensation is unnecessary for fishing communities.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: As an aside, the harbour's spring regatta is scheduled for the first Saturday in May.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether hospitals should replace paper consent forms with recorded video explanations. Samir, you support the change?

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Yes. Hospitals should replace paper consent forms with recorded video explanations because patients can replay recorded explanations before making a decision.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: But a recorded video cannot respond to a patient's individual questions. That limitation makes a complete replacement risky.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Paper consent forms are often signed before patients understand the risks. That means some patients sign consent forms without understanding what they are agreeing to.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Patients should receive a clear explanation before they sign consent, because people need understandable information before agreeing to treatment.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Rohan raises the concern about personal questions, while the other panellists are focusing on clarity and access. Samir, what would the practical benefit be?

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: A recorded explanation gives every patient the same core information, because that makes the core information more consistent across clinicians.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: My clinic opens at seven o'clock each morning. Still, I think staff could answer questions after patients watch the recording.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Recorded explanations can include captions and several languages, which means more patients can access the core explanation.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Clinicians can answer individual questions after patients watch the recording; therefore, patients can receive individual clarification even when a recording is used first.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Hospitals can securely store recordings with a patient's consent record. In other words, captions and several languages allow more patients to access the core explanation.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: So you are saying that the recorded explanation would make the core information consistent across clinicians?

utterances.text: Tonight we are debating whether professional tennis tournaments should shorten every match to best-of-three. Maeve, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Maeve

utterances.speaker: Aurelio

utterances.speaker: Nadia

utterances.speaker: Maeve

utterances.speaker: Nadia

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Orla, you work with the grounds crews.

utterances.text: But a ban ignores that battery blowers cannot shift wet leaves off paths fast enough. I pass the council depot every morning on my way to work.

utterances.text: Battery blowers are now powerful enough for council grounds work, since Brompton's battery-only crews cleared every park last autumn.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: In other words, battery blowers have caught up with petrol ones on power. I once had a summer job clearing school playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Karima, what about the people who live next to the parks?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Residents beside parks complain constantly about blower noise, because petrol blowers are far louder than battery ones.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi

spec.format: opinion essay by a single author
spec.topic: Should governments guarantee enough funding to keep public-defender caseloads below a fixed maximum?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Governments should guarantee enough funding to keep public-defender caseloads below a fixed maximum.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The first reason is simple: a defender carrying hundreds of open cases cannot give any client more than a few minutes of preparation.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That matters because rushed preparation makes wrongful convictions and unnecessary guilty pleas more likely.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second reason is that a fixed cap gives defenders a legal basis to refuse new cases they cannot handle.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But caps are rigid, and they ignore the fact that some cases take far longer than others.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That objection fails, since a cap can be set as a weighted measure in which serious felonies count for more than minor offences.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a weighted cap is not a crude count of files.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once watched a defender meet a client for the first time in a courthouse corridor.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Guaranteed funding is also cheaper in the long run, because each wrongful conviction costs the state years of prison expenses.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My own city adopted its public-defender office in the 1960s.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put differently, governments should treat caseload limits as a basic part of the right to counsel.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Businesses that use contractors should pay higher taxes. The rule would make companies account for the wider effects of their staffing choices.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Carmen, what is the strongest case for that proposal?

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Contractor arrangements often remove employer contributions to pensions and paid leave. That is why businesses using contractors should face a higher tax.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Shifting security costs onto workers can leave them less financially secure. This is why the transfer of costs is not merely an accounting change.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: The gap between permanent employees' protections and contractors' protections creates a public cost. That is why the insecurity caused by the gap deserves a policy response.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: A higher business tax could recover part of that public cost. For that reason, the protection gap supports taxing the business rather than leaving workers to absorb it.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: A higher tax would make replacing permanent staff with contractors less attractive. That is why taxing the protection gap could change staffing decisions.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Keeping permanent roles preserves employer contributions and workplace continuity. This shows why making replacement less attractive could protect more than individual benefits.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: The tax should apply when contractors replace permanent staff. That is why the policy should be tied to replacement rather than to contracting in the abstract.

utterances.speaker: Imogen

utterances.text: The measure should focus on replacement rather than on every use of contractors. In other words, firms adding capacity would not automatically face the tax.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: The measure should distinguish substitution from an expansion of a workforce. Put another way, the relevant question is whether contractors have taken the place of employees.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: The tax should target contractor substitution rather than all contractor use. utterances.speaker: Imogen

utterances.speaker: Matteo

utterances.speaker: Imogen

spec.format: opinion essay by a single author
spec.topic: Should parents be able to opt their children out of lessons about evolution?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Parents should not be able to opt their children out of lessons about evolution, since evolution is the central organising idea of modern biology.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is because a child who skips it cannot follow the rest of the syllabus. In other words, pupils who miss these lessons will be unprepared for later science courses.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some will reply that parents have a right to decide what their children are taught about matters of belief, but that ignores how the subject is actually taught.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Schools present evolution as a scientific theory and do not ask anyone to give up a religious belief, which is a reason to refuse opt-outs.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Allowing opt-outs would let each family carve its own gaps into the curriculum. Put another way, the curriculum would become uneven from one classroom to the next.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My own biology teacher once ran a lesson on finches using a shoebox of dried seeds.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Children should be able to question what they are taught, and that is easier when they know the evidence. Put differently, knowing the evidence for evolution lets them judge the theory for themselves.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The exam boards already test evolution in the final school examinations, which shows how much pupils would lose by missing it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: It may be that opt-outs will become more common in the next decade.

spec.format: opinion essay by a single author
spec.topic: Should mining companies provide larger financial bonds for cleaning up abandoned mines?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Mining companies should post much larger financial bonds for cleaning up their sites. The bonds held today cover only a fraction of real reclamation costs, and that alone justifies the change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: When a mining company goes bankrupt, taxpayers inherit the cleanup, and that is why bonds should match the true cost. In other words, an undersized bond is a hidden public subsidy to the industry.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Industry groups reply that larger bonds will make small mines unviable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But in the states that already demand full-cost bonding, small operators still open new mines every year.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Abandoned mines also leak acid water into rivers for centuries, which is a further reason not to leave the funding to chance.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I grew up near a former copper mine, and I still remember the orange stream behind the school.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Reclamation costs do change as a pit grows, of course.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A firm that cannot fund its own cleanup should not hold a mining permit, which is why full bonds are only fair. In other words, a company with no money for restoration has no business digging.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Larger bonds give firms a reason to restore land early, and that is another reason to demand them, since the money comes back once the land is certified as restored.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To put it simply, mining firms should fund their cleanup in full before they dig.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should councils publish what their highest-paid contractors earn? Josefa, you start.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Councils should publish the salaries of their highest-paid contractors, because that pay comes out of public money.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Publication would let taxpayers spot overpriced contracts, which is another reason to do it.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: But the pay of a contractor's staff is a private matter between the firm and its employees, since those staff are not public employees.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: So, Leopold, you are saying a contractor's staff pay is simply not the public's business.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Exactly. And my own firm was audited last year, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Taxpayers have a right to know where the money from council invoices ends up, and that is a further reason for publishing.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: In Bergen, publication cut top contractor fees by eleven percent in two years, which shows that taxpayers do spot overpriced contracts.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Publication would drive firms away from bidding for council work, because they will not accept having their pay disclosed.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: So you are saying disclosure would shrink the pool of bidders.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Only people paid more than the council leader would be named, so publication is workable without exposing ordinary staff, which is why councils should go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: I have followed this issue for ten years as a councillor.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

spec.topic: Should public contracts require companies to disclose their full supply chains?

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether public contracts should require companies to disclose their full supply chains. Matteo, you support the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Yes, public contracts should require companies to disclose their full supply chains, because public oversight needs visibility of all the companies performing work under those contracts.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: I oppose that requirement, because requiring full supply-chain disclosure would impose a costly administrative burden on companies.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Esther, does that burden outweigh the transparency benefit?

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Before Esther answers, I should mention that my office moved to a new building in April.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: So you are saying that public contracts should require companies to disclose their full supply chains?

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: My company employs 240 people. My alternative is that public contracts should require companies to report their direct suppliers rather than their full supply chains.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Full disclosure is necessary because hidden subcontractors can conceal labor abuses from public buyers.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: In other words, Adrian is saying that reporting direct suppliers would be sufficient instead of disclosing the entire supply chain.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: That is why full disclosure matters: procurement officers cannot properly verify companies that do not identify suppliers beyond the first tier.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Public buyers can phase in supply-chain reporting and provide standard reporting templates.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: That would keep compliance manageable for small companies because the reporting could be introduced gradually with a common format.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Put another way, Esther is proposing a gradual reporting system with standard templates for companies.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Matteo, give us your final position.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Both earlier reasons support my conclusion: public buyers should make full supply-chain disclosure a condition of receiving public contracts.

utterances.text: Parents should be allowed to choose embryos with increased resistance to disease. It would spare children a lot of suffering.

utterances.text: But it would start a slide toward designer babies, because the line between disease resistance and enhancement is blurry.

utterances.text: Mostly, yes. By the way, I volunteer at a children's ward on Saturdays.

utterances.speaker: Hamza

utterances.speaker: Odette

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Besides, repairing corroded bridges costs councils far more than the extra price of alternative de-icers.

utterances.speaker: Leopold

spec.topic: Should companies be allowed to charge different prices according to customers’ purchasing histories?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should companies be allowed to set prices according to a customer's purchase history?

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: No, they should not. It turns loyalty into a penalty, because the people who buy the most are the ones quoted the highest prices.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How does that actually happen?

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Firms learn from your history that you will not shop around, which is why loyal customers end up paying more than newcomers.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, you want a ban on pricing by purchase history.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Yes, and here is another reason to stop it: nobody can see what other customers are being charged.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Is there no upside at all?

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Though, to be fair, targeted discounts do help budget shoppers. I buy most of my food at a local grocer, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Anything to add before we finish?

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: I read last month that two airlines already use loyalty-scheme data when setting fares.

utterances.text: Historical arrest data reflect where officers have already chosen to look. That is why the software can amplify existing enforcement bias.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: I have worked with patrol officers for twelve years. A further reason for prohibition is that predictive-policing software can make biased patrol patterns appear objective.

utterances.text: Human officers must retain final authority over patrol assignments, because predictive-policing software should not influence patrol assignments. In other words, predictive-policing software should not influence patrol assignments.

spec.topic: Should governments guarantee a minimum price for small farmers’ essential crops?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments guarantee a minimum price for small farmers' essential crops? Amara, you start.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Governments should guarantee a minimum price for essential crops, because small farmers face price crashes at harvest that wipe out a year of income.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Esther, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: But a guaranteed price is too costly for the state, since the state ends up buying surpluses it cannot sell.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Farmers who are sure of a price plant more of the guaranteed crop, which is exactly how those surpluses arise. I should say I grow lentils on a small farm myself.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying, Giulia, that the guarantee itself encourages overproduction?

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Exactly. That is why the guarantee should be limited to a fixed quota per farm.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: A quota is sensible, because it caps the amount the state must buy.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: But that ignores that officials setting the price would not know local production costs.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Not so: prices can be set from cooperative cost reports, since cooperatives already track their members' costs each season.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Amara, what about ordinary consumers?

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Stable farm prices protect consumers, because farmers who go bankrupt stop planting and food becomes scarcer. That is another reason to back the guarantee.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: So you are saying consumers end up paying when small farms fail.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Yes, and rice prices doubled in our region during the last drought, which shows it.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: My family ran a grain mill for thirty years. The scheme would also mostly pay out to large growers, which is one more reason it is too costly.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Amara, in other words, a per-farm quota keeps the state's bill under control. Thank you all.

spec.topic: Should public healthcare fund fertility treatment for people who are single?

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should public healthcare fund fertility treatment for people who are single? Hamza, you start.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Public healthcare should fund fertility treatment for single people, because a single person with infertility has the same medical need as someone in a couple.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: But waiting lists for fertility treatment already run over two years, so adding single people would only lengthen them.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: That ignores the fact that donor insemination costs a fraction of IVF, and it is all most single patients need.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: So you are saying that including single people would cost the health service very little.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Yes. The national donor bank already supplies sperm at low cost, which shows how cheap donor insemination is.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Single women are the fastest-growing group of applicants, which is another reason the waiting lists would grow.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The state should not fund it for single people, since children raised by single parents face greater hardship.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Clinics screen every applicant, single or coupled, for stability, and that is another reason to fund it.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: That hardship exists because single parents are more likely to live on low incomes.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Success rates for single patients match those of couples, so the medical need is just as real.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Excluding single people is discrimination on marital status, which is why the current rule is unfair.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Put another way, two people with the same condition get different care depending on who they live with.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: In other words, the health service should not be helping to create single-parent families. Incidentally, my sister went through IVF last year.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Thank you both. For the record, the first public fertility unit opened in 1998, and that is all we have time for.

spec.topic: Should ranked-choice voting replace plurality voting in legislative elections?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The first reason for that change is that plurality voting can allow a candidate to win a legislative election without majority support. A second reason is that ranked-choice voting allows voters to support a preferred candidate without wasting their ballot if that candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I first encountered ranked-choice voting in a civics textbook.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting gives voters a way to rank legislative candidates in order of preference.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My local ballots are printed on pale blue paper.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A common objection to replacing plurality voting is that ranked-choice ballots can confuse some voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clear instructions can be printed in multiple languages on ranked-choice ballots; for that reason, the transition to ranked-choice voting is practical.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, ranked-choice voting lets voters record a first choice and backup choices on one ballot.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The transition to ranked-choice voting is practical.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Candidates in legislative elections using ranked-choice voting have campaigned for support from voters whose first choices were competing candidates, and that campaign behavior shows that ranked-choice voting can encourage candidates to appeal beyond their core supporters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice tabulation proceeds through publicly visible counting rounds.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice results are produced by a transparent round-by-round count.

utterances.text: They should, because employees who choose their own courses stay engaged and learn skills they actually use.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, legislators may be accountable to voters while still having a personal party interest in drawing boundaries.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Exactly. That conflict of interest gives voters a reason to distrust boundaries drawn by legislators.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Yes, and public scrutiny makes electoral boundary decisions more legitimate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, public scrutiny increases the legitimacy of electoral boundary decisions.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha

spec.topic: Should governments fund research into extending healthy human lifespan?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether governments should fund research into extending healthy human lifespan. Dimitri, why should taxpayers support it?

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Governments should fund research into extending healthy human lifespan because such research could reveal ways to prevent age-related illness.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: The national ethics committee will publish its annual report in October. That report may help frame the public conversation.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Because healthy-lifespan research could reveal ways to prevent age-related illness, public funding for it could reduce future healthcare costs.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Research could also produce treatments that preserve people's independence in old age, because preventing age-related illness would keep more people well for longer.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Governments can reasonably invest public money in this research because preventing age-related illness would benefit the whole population, not just a small group.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Government funding would make any resulting healthy-lifespan treatments available beyond wealthy early adopters. But that promise does not justify diverting money from current patients.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: That raises the fairness question: should future benefits outweigh urgent needs today? Wilhelmina, what wider benefit do you see?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Longer healthy lives would let older adults remain active in their communities. Many could continue caring for relatives, mentoring younger workers, or volunteering.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So you are saying that longer healthy lives would let older adults remain active in their communities?

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: The phrase healthy lifespan means years lived without severe disease. That goal is more defensible than simply seeking extreme longevity.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether employees should repay professional qualification fees if they leave soon after receiving the training.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: The training team schedules professional qualification courses on Tuesdays.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: An employer-funded qualification gives an employee a portable credential. Because that credential remains useful after departure, an employee can leave soon after employer-funded training while keeping the qualification's benefits.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: For that reason, companies should require employees to repay professional qualification fees when they leave before eighteen months.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A repayment requirement could deter applicants from accepting a job. However, a short, clearly capped repayment period would make the policy fairer, because employees would not face an open-ended obligation.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Since most employees remain with the company for at least eighteen months, the proposed condition would affect relatively few people.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: So you are saying that the risk is that repayment requirements would discourage potential applicants.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: I would use a sliding repayment scale. That is why I think a sliding repayment scale would make the policy fairer.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: In other words, a sliding repayment scale means employees repay less the longer they remain with the company.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Because the company can prevent surprises by explaining the repayment clause before employees enroll, I support the eighteen-month condition.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: The company should publish the repayment schedule before employees sign up for a qualification.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: In other words, employees should see the repayment schedule before they sign up for a qualification.

utterances.speaker: Femi

utterances.text: Should political parties face strict limits on total campaign spending?

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Wealthy political parties can buy more campaign exposure than smaller parties.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: That imbalance is why unequal campaign exposure can distort political representation.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: And that distortion is why strict total campaign spending limits are necessary.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Odette

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Odette

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Odette

spec.topic: Should retailers be required to refund price differences when an item goes on sale shortly afterward?

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Retailers should be required to refund the difference when an item goes on sale shortly after purchase, because customers who buy just before a sale pay more than customers who buy it afterward.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: But retailers should not be required to refund later price differences.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: That is a firm objection. Incidentally, I keep most paper receipts in a drawer by the kitchen door.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Retailers can record the original purchase price and the sale price in one transaction record, because a standard record would let them calculate refunds quickly.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Quick calculations would keep compliance manageable for small retailers, which is why the administrative burden is not a decisive objection.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: A separate reason this would remain manageable is that retailers could issue store credit instead of cash to simplify the refund process.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Price protection would make customers more willing to buy at the current full price, and that is another reason retailers should be required to offer it.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: I prefer shopping early in the morning, regardless of how this rule is designed.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that you oppose any mandatory rule requiring retailers to refund later price differences.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Exactly; in other words, my position is that retailers should never have a legal duty to refund a later price difference.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: That consumer benefit is plausible because customers who expect fair price protection are less likely to postpone purchases while waiting for a sale.

spec.topic: Should doctors be permitted to prescribe psychedelic drugs for severe depression?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Our question is whether doctors should be permitted to prescribe psychedelic drugs for severe depression. Anika, why should the law change?

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Psychedelic-assisted treatment can produce rapid symptom relief for some people with severe depression. I say that because controlled trials have found rapid symptom relief in this group.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Many people with severe depression do not improve adequately with standard antidepressants.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Carmen, is that enough to justify prescribing permission?

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Because rapid relief matters and many patients do not improve with existing medicines, doctors should be permitted to prescribe psychedelic drugs for severe depression under medical supervision.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: But psychedelic drugs can trigger acute panic or psychosis, so I am not ready to support unrestricted permission.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: The risks can be substantially reduced in a supervised clinic because psychiatric screening can identify patients who face unusually high risks.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: So you are saying that supervised medical access, rather than general availability, is the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Specialist clinics should handle the treatment; that is one reason the risks can be reduced. Continuous observation during a patient's first treatment is another reason the risks can be reduced.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: I disagree with treating the possibility of panic or psychosis as decisive: acute panic and psychosis do not make carefully regulated psychedelic treatment unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: The national medical board has not yet published its draft guidance, but we will return to the safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Carmen, can you state your position in one sentence?

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal is for specialist clinics to handle psychedelic treatment for severe depression.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: What Carmen means is that supervised clinics can substantially reduce the risks of psychedelic treatment.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: A six-month follow-up study found that most participants who received supervised treatment retained meaningful symptom improvement, which supports offering additional treatment options.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Patients who have exhausted standard antidepressants need additional treatment options.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Specialist doctors who complete accredited training can provide psychedelic treatment responsibly.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Before the final response, a brief production note: the studio's fire certificate is current.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Because specialist doctors can complete accredited training and provide this treatment responsibly, a national prescribing pathway should authorize them to treat severe depression.

spec.topic: Should anonymous political donations above a small threshold be prohibited?

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Agenda item two: whether anonymous political donations above a small threshold should be prohibited. Nkechi, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: We should prohibit anonymous donations above five hundred pounds, because they let donors buy influence without voters ever knowing.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: But a ban would expose donors to harassment, since donor lists have leaked before.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So you are saying donors need protection from retaliation.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Exactly. Also, the committee room heating is broken again.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: The ban would only touch large donors, since most people give far less than five hundred pounds.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So you are saying ordinary small donors would be unaffected.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: I will grant this much: hidden money makes foreign interference harder to trace, because shell companies can route gifts without any donor's name attached.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: In other words, anonymity weakens oversight of elections, since oversight bodies rely on named donor records.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: A threshold can also be dodged, because one donor can split a gift among relatives, and as Sanna said, shell companies hide the true giver.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: That is to say, the ban would be hard to enforce, since gifts are so easily split.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Reporting names would add little cost for parties, because they already file returns every quarter.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So the proposal is to prohibit anonymous donations above five hundred pounds. Separately, the next meeting is on the fourteenth.

spec.topic: Should corporations be banned from donating directly to political parties?

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether corporations should be banned from donating directly to political parties. Wilhelmina, you support a ban; make your case.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Corporations can spend millions of dollars on political activity. Because those resources greatly exceed ordinary individual contributions, direct corporate donations give corporations disproportionate influence over political parties.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: That disproportionate influence is why direct corporate donations to political parties should be banned.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Before we go further, Wilhelmina's party publishes its financial accounts every June. Transparency already matters to many parties.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: A ban would push some corporate money toward shell groups, and that would make political finance less transparent.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Wilhelmina, are you saying the problem is corporate access itself, rather than every form of political spending? Please respond to Naveen's concern.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: In other words, corporations can use their wealth to exert disproportionate influence over political parties. I still think direct transfers are the clearest channel to close.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: The reduced transparency caused by shell groups is a reason to remove the direct donation route, even if other forms of spending remain legal.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal would prohibit corporations from giving money directly to political parties. That does not automatically prohibit independent campaigning.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: To restate my objection, a ban would divert some corporate money into shell groups. The money could still shape campaigns without appearing on a party's books.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Shell groups can conceal the identities of political donors. Concealed donor identities would prevent voters from judging who is influencing political parties.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: But should voters hear that as an argument against a ban, or as an argument for tighter rules around it?

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Small political parties often hold their internal meetings online. That practical detail should not decide the question before us.

spec.topic: Should women’s professional leagues receive equal public funding to men’s leagues?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether women's professional leagues should get the same public funding as men's. Elodie, you start.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Women's leagues deserve equal public funding, because public money belongs equally to every taxpayer.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: But equal funding would simply pay for empty seats, since men's leagues draw far larger crowds.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: The small crowds at women's games come from past underinvestment, not lack of interest, because attendance doubled in cities where clubs upgraded their stadiums. Which is another reason to back equal funding.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: So, Aiko, you are saying women's games are poorly attended because of past underinvestment rather than lack of interest.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Public funding should follow demand, not precede it, which is one more reason equal money would be wasted on empty seats. I say that as someone who coaches a boys' team on Saturdays.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: So, Quentin, what you mean is that women's leagues must prove they have an audience before they get public money.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Sponsors follow public investment, since women's clubs backed by city councils signed twice as many sponsors as unbacked ones.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: In other words, women taxpayers deserve the same return on their taxes as men do.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: And whatever happens, I have tickets to the women's cup final this Saturday.

spec.topic: Should governments impose a surcharge on homes left empty for most of the year?

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should put a surcharge on homes left empty for most of the year. Deirdre, you start.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Governments should impose that surcharge, because it would push owners to let their empty homes out.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Vancouver's tax returned thousands of homes to rental use. That shows owners respond to it, and it is the strongest reason to copy it.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: But a surcharge would unfairly punish families who work abroad for months at a time. I should add that I keep a flat I only use in winter.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: So you are saying, Rohan, that the surcharge would penalise people who have good reasons to be away.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Exactly, in other words, it treats mere absence as if it were hoarding.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: For the record, the council votes on a draft next month. We will take a call after the break.

spec.topic: Should contact sports require independent medical approval before an injured player returns?

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should an injured player in a contact sport need independent medical approval before returning? Gideon, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Independent doctors should have to clear any injured player before return, because club doctors are paid by the club and so have a reason to rush players back.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: But that ignores how well club doctors know their players, far better than any outsider would. I should say I have worked as a physio for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: So you are saying, Gideon, that no injured player should return without being cleared by someone from outside the club.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Exactly, and here is a further reason: concussion symptoms can appear hours after the final whistle.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: But independent approval would delay returns by days, which a weekly fixture list cannot absorb. On Sundays I coach my daughter's netball team, so I see how tight the calendar is.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: The deeper problem is that players often hide their symptoms, because places in the team are fiercely contested.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: So you are saying, Esther, that players cannot be trusted to report their own symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Yes, which is shown by two players in my county league last season who hid concussion to stay in the squad.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: In other words, a player's word alone is not evidence of fitness.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Rugby competitions that brought in independent doctors saw fewer repeat head injuries, which backs up my case.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: So what you want, Gideon, is for an outsider's decision to come before any player returns.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Most professionals surveyed nationally admitted playing on with a suspected concussion, and coaches rarely question a player who says he is fine, which is why players hide symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will leave it there.

spec.topic: Should schools require uniforms for all pupils, including those in sixth form?

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Item two: uniforms for every pupil, sixth form included. Samir, you start.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: I think we should require them for everyone, since uniforms reduce visible differences in family income between pupils.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: They also save parents money on everyday clothing, which is another reason to require them.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: But sixth formers should not be required to wear uniform, because they are close to adulthood and need to practise making their own decisions.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Noted. Unrelated, the sixth form common room needs repainting.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So you are saying that sixth formers should be trusted to choose their own clothes as preparation for adult life.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Yes, and also, since a rule for older pupils would be hard to enforce, it is another reason to drop it for them.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: We will vote next time. The governors meet on Thursday.

spec.topic: Should the state match small individual political donations with public funds?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Tonight: should the state match small individual political donations with public funds? Tariq, you first.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Yes, the state should match them. Matching funds make candidates court ordinary voters rather than wealthy donors.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Zainab, why would that follow?

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Because candidates who rely on many small donors depend less on a few rich backers.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: But this takes money from schools and hospitals, since the programme would cost the state about forty million a year.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: So, Hollis, Tariq is saying the state should subsidise small donations because candidates would then want ordinary voters' money.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: If you like. I was a campaign treasurer once, for what that is worth.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: The case is stronger than that, because matching schemes in other states have increased the number of people who donate.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: That ignores fraud: fraudsters could split large gifts into many fake small donations to claim matching money.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: The risk is manageable, since matching claims require verified donor identities.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I think we have run long, Harriet.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Let me sum up: matching funds would give candidates less reason to depend on a few rich backers. We stop there.

spec.topic: Should professional cycling teams be allowed to use performance data from implanted sensors?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should professional cycling teams be allowed to use performance data from implanted sensors? Seamus, you open.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Teams should be allowed to use that data, because implanted sensors would catch dangerous dehydration and heart problems before a rider collapses.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Padraig, you look unconvinced.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: But riders would be pressured into accepting implants, since a team can simply refuse to renew anyone who declines.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying riders would not truly be free to refuse.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Exactly. For the record, I raced professionally for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: In other words, Seamus, the implant works as an early warning system for the heart. Arrhythmia shows up in the data weeks before a rider ever feels it, and that is why such a warning is possible.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Teams already owe their riders a duty of care, which is another reason to allow the data.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, what about privacy?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That is one more reason to say yes: privacy can be protected if only an independent doctor sees the raw data, since the team would then receive only a fitness flag.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Two teams trialled wearable trackers last season.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Noor, is the safety case enough on its own?

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Early warnings protect the other riders too, which is one more reason to allow implants, since a rider who collapses at speed can bring down the whole peloton.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Implant data follows a rider for life, which is why any implant should be voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Put another way, Padraig, riders should decide for themselves.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Let me put my case another way: allowing implant data simply lets teams act on what a rider's body already reveals.

spec.topic: Should courts be allowed to empanel anonymous juries in cases involving organised intimidation?

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether courts should be allowed to empanel anonymous juries in cases of organised intimidation. Babajide, you start.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Courts should be allowed to do it, because jurors in these trials have been approached and threatened at home.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: A caller is waiting on the line, but first Adrian, your response?

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: But anonymity undermines the defendant's right to a fair trial, since jurors whom nobody can name feel less answerable for their verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: So you are saying, Adrian, that a hidden juror is a juror who is not held to account?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Adrian is right that the trial becomes unfair, and here is a further reason: defendants cannot challenge a juror they cannot identify.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: So what you mean, Jolene, is that with anonymous juries the defence loses its chance to screen jurors for bias.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Yes, and I served on a jury myself ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: That the threats are real is shown by last year's gang trial, where two jurors reported being followed home.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Would judges not hand out anonymity too freely?

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Judges can be trusted to use it sparingly, since an order is made only after the judge hears evidence of a real threat.

utterances.text: The government's own figures show that juror intimidation is rare.

utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

spec.topic: Should governments subsidise satellite internet for households without reliable broadband?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should subsidise satellite internet for households without reliable broadband. Thandiwe, you start.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Governments should subsidise it, because children in those households simply cannot do their homework online.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Karima, do you see it the same way?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: I do, and here is another reason: farms and small businesses in those areas cannot reach customers online.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: But public money would be better spent extending fibre to those villages.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: So you are saying fibre, not satellite, deserves the public money, Petra.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Karima, put another way, those businesses are cut off from their market.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: I installed a satellite dish for my uncle last spring.

utterances.speaker: Karima

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Theo
