spec.topic: Should hospitals publish the waiting times for every consultant-led treatment?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should hospitals publish the waiting times for every consultant-led treatment?

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Yes, hospitals should publish the waiting times for every consultant-led treatment because patients cannot compare access without that information.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would publication change beyond giving patients another set of figures?

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Published waiting times would reveal where patients face unusually long delays. A further reason for publication is that public attention to those delays would encourage hospitals to improve their services.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Have you seen patients use information of this kind?

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: I have helped patients choose between clinics during my work in hospital administration.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: I have also seen patients change their treatment choices after learning that another clinic had a shorter wait.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: A published waiting-time table would let patients choose among available treatment options.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: But that table alone would not tell patients whether a particular appointment suited their medical needs.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Waiting-time information would make differences between hospitals visible to patients.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Publicly comparable waiting times would create pressure on hospitals with the longest delays.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So your positive point is that a waiting-time table would help patients choose among treatment options, even though it is not a complete guide?

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Exactly. Every published waiting time should identify the date on which the clock starts.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Hospitals should explain whether a reported waiting time covers the period from referral to treatment or only the period after a specialist appointment.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: That is another reason to publish all consultant-led treatment waits: publication would make the health system more accountable to patients.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, you are calling for an explanation of the starting point used for each reported waiting time.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: For the record, I keep a blue notebook beside my desk.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you support a standard national format?

utterances.speaker: Siobhan

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Our question is whether vaccines should receive provisional approval before long-term safety studies are complete. Javier, you support that policy?

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Yes, vaccines should receive provisional approval before long-term safety studies are complete. I support it because provisional approval would let people at high risk access a vaccine sooner.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Another reason for my position is that regulators could require frequent safety reports throughout the provisional-approval period. The evidence already available can give regulators adequate protection during that period.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Harriet, what is your response?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: I disagree with that reassurance: provisional approval can expose the public to harms that the available evidence has not revealed. Long-term safety studies can take several years to complete.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: One practical safeguard is that provisional approval can be restricted to people facing an immediate outbreak danger.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: So you mean limiting provisional approval to people facing an immediate outbreak danger. That restriction would still need strict oversight.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: A further reason to permit provisional approval is that a regulator could withdraw it as soon as monitoring reveals a serious safety signal. For context, Harriet works as a hospital pharmacist.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Frequent safety reports would allow regulators to react while long-term studies were still running.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: So you are saying that frequent reports would let regulators respond before the long-term studies ended?

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Yes. Two further reasons support my recommendation: restricting provisional approval would reduce the number of people exposed before long-term evidence was available, and a provisional approval could be cancelled without waiting for the final study reports.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: The regulator could suspend distribution immediately after a credible safety warning.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Put another way, Enzo's proposal allows distribution to stop immediately after a credible safety warning.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: The central question is whether those safeguards justify early access. Provisional approval would preserve access during an emergency while keeping long-term safety studies in progress.

spec.topic: Should businesses abolish forced rankings of employees?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether businesses should abolish forced rankings of employees. Priya, make the case for abolition.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Forced-ranking systems require managers to place employees in a fixed order.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: In other words, forced-ranking systems reduce nuanced performance to a single ladder.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Sanna, does that description capture the problem?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Put another way, forced-ranking systems turn complex reviews into a first-to-last ordering.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: The same policy requires managers to rank employees against one another rather than assess each employee independently.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Priya, is the objection mainly about the ranking exercise itself?

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: That is to say, the policy imposes an artificial order when employees' contributions are difficult to compare.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Let us turn from the definition to the workplace effects.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: My practical concern is that forced rankings make employees compete instead of sharing information.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Because that competition discourages cooperation, abolishing forced rankings would protect collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Since employees would no longer be pitted against one another, they would be more willing to report problems early if forced rankings were abolished.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: That is why abolishing forced rankings could improve employee retention.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Isaac, what is the strongest argument for keeping the system?

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Forced rankings give managers a way to identify chronic underperformance.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: I once worked at a firm that used quarterly reviews.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Because that oversight is useful, abolishing forced rankings could leave persistent underperformance unaddressed.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Since rankings expose repeated failures, managers can direct coaching to the employees who need it.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: But that argument overlooks the fact that forced rankings can label a solid employee a loser when the whole team performs well.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Naveen, can a company preserve accountability without forced rankings?

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Without forced rankings, managers would struggle to hold employees accountable.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: On the contrary, clear role-based standards can preserve accountability without forcing a fixed distribution of low scores.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: The question, then, is whether the accountability benefit outweighs the damage to cooperation and fairness.

utterances.text: Businesses can replace forced rankings with regular developmental feedback, and that approach helps employees improve.

utterances.speaker: Sanna

utterances.text: Why take down any fences at all?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Artificial-intelligence tools can give students rapid feedback. Because of that, disclosed use can help students revise their work.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Since disclosed use can help students revise their work, schools should permit students to use artificial-intelligence tools for assessed assignments when the students disclose that use.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: But disclosure does not prove that a student wrote an assessed assignment independently.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Artificial-intelligence tools can produce polished drafts, which is precisely why schools should permit disclosed use rather than banning the tools outright.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Teachers cannot reliably verify every student's working process, which is why disclosure does not prove independent authorship.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that artificial-intelligence tools can produce polished drafts.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: In other words, Naveen's proposal is to permit artificial-intelligence use conditionally on disclosure.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Schools lack time to inspect every student's artificial-intelligence declaration because oral checks of every student's working process are impractical.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Before we move to enforcement, I want each of you to address fairness.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I have used an artificial-intelligence tool to plan a garden.

utterances.speaker: Leopold

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should every teacher receive mandatory training in recognizing and supporting young carers?

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Yes, schools should require that training because it helps teachers notice when a pupil's home responsibilities are affecting attendance or concentration.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why is formal training needed rather than relying on individual teachers' experience?

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Young carers are often identified only after their school performance has already declined. Early recognition gives schools more opportunity to prevent them from falling behind.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You have worked in schools for some time. What does your own background involve?

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Rosalind has taught science in secondary schools for eight years. Training should explain how to make flexible arrangements for homework and deadlines, and it should show teachers how to refer pupils to appropriate local services.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: I know the objection: mandatory training would take time away from teachers' existing planning and teaching duties. Even so, I recommend that the training include practical guidance rather than only general information about young carers.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are arguing that compulsory training should give teachers usable advice about supporting young carers?

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Exactly; in other words, the required course should focus on practical support for young carers.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposed training would be a practical course on identifying and helping young carers?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: We are speaking before the afternoon lesson period. What makes the policy workable in practice?

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: A short, well-designed course can fit into the school year without displacing substantial teaching time, which is why mandatory training remains reasonable. That same fact shows that practical guidance can be included without making the course excessive.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: A consistent national course would give teachers a shared process for responding to young carers; that is why schools should require it, and it also shows why the course should use practical guidance.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: The evaluation policy should require formal contributions from colleagues, because colleagues observe aspects of one another's day-to-day work that managers may miss.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Another reason to adopt the policy is that formal peer feedback can reveal teamwork problems that individual evaluations overlook.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: Equal opportunity is a further reason for the policy: formal peer input gives every employee an equal opportunity to comment on collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Kieran has raised a concern. What is the strongest objection to the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Formal peer input creates an auditable record of workplace contributions, which strengthens the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: But employees may retaliate against colleagues who give them critical feedback. For context, I have worked at the company for nine years.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: In other words, formal peer feedback can reveal teamwork problems that managers otherwise miss.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Put another way, colleagues see parts of one another's daily work that managers may not observe.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: I currently manage six employees, so I have seen how much information a manager can lack.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: So you are saying that formal colleague contributions create a record that managers can audit.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: To summarise Vikram's position, the evaluation policy should make colleague contributions a formal part of performance reviews.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: A workable peer-evaluation policy should protect contributors from retaliation.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Anonymous submissions reduce employees' fear of retaliation; that is why anonymity would make the protection credible.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Removing identifying details before comments are shared would protect contributors. That is another reason to build safeguards into the process.

utterances.speaker: Kieran

utterances.speaker: Jelena

utterances.speaker: Theo

utterances.speaker: Jin

utterances.speaker: Daniela

utterances.text: Welcome to tonight's debate. Should employers be required to compensate workers for mandatory commuting between job sites? Quentin, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Employers require some workers to travel between job sites during the workday. Because the employer determines both the destination and the timing, that travel is part of the workers' assigned duties.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: That is why employers should compensate workers for mandatory travel between job sites; treating it as unpaid personal time ignores who required the journey.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Workers incur transport costs and lose personal time during mandatory travel between job sites, which is another reason employers should compensate them.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The debate is being broadcast from Studio Four. Chidi, what is the strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Chidi

spec.topic: Should publicly funded infrastructure projects use domestic materials whenever reasonably possible?

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether publicly funded infrastructure should favor domestic materials. Dimitri, could you begin with the practical case?

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Domestic suppliers can provide structural steel within current project schedules. That makes domestic sourcing feasible for many contracts.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Domestic sourcing keeps public infrastructure spending circulating among domestic manufacturers.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Domestic suppliers are easier for public agencies to audit for labor and environmental compliance.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: A separate administrative note: the committee will publish the meeting minutes on Friday.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Recent overseas delivery disruptions have delayed infrastructure construction. A domestic-materials preference can still be waived when domestic bids fail the required quality standards.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Domestic infrastructure orders help retain skilled manufacturing jobs.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Long-term public contracts can encourage domestic manufacturers to expand production capacity.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Public agencies can define reasonable price and quality thresholds before applying a domestic-materials preference.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: The procurement office plans to hold a supplier workshop in May.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: In other words, the procurement office's May workshop is intended for suppliers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Because of the schedule evidence, the domestic economic benefit, the auditability advantage, the disruption evidence, the waiver safeguard, the jobs effect, the capacity effect, and the threshold plan, publicly funded infrastructure projects should use domestic materials whenever reasonably possible.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: I object to that recommendation because a domestic-materials requirement can raise project costs beyond reasonable limits.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposed policy is a conditional domestic preference rather than an absolute domestic purchasing mandate.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: The bridge project has three approved design options.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Put another way, the bridge engineers have three design choices available.

utterances.speaker: Carmen

spec.topic: Should creators be required to watermark realistic synthetic videos?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: I think creators should be required to watermark realistic synthetic videos, because viewers can no longer reliably tell them from real footage.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: But a mandatory watermark would not stop determined bad actors, since a watermark can be cropped out or re-encoded away.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Viewers really can't tell: in one survey most participants took synthetic clips for real footage, which backs Bongani's premise. Watermarks also give platforms an easy signal to label fakes, which is another reason to require them.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So you are saying a watermark is pointless against determined bad actors. Most harmful fakes come from casual users who never bother stripping marks, which is why a requirement still helps.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Put another way, the rule would only ever catch honest creators. I edit video for a living, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Small creators would face compliance costs they cannot afford, and that is why the rule falls on honest creators.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: So what you mean is that small creators couldn't afford to comply. Separately, casual users rarely know how to re-encode video, so marks would mostly survive, which supports Bongani's point about casual users.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: In other words, a watermark lets platforms label fakes automatically. Fakes spread fastest before anyone can check them, which is why that signal matters.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Put simply, creators should have to mark realistic synthetic videos. Sponsored posts already require disclosure, so this would be nothing new.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: I'm travelling tomorrow, so my replies will be slow.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: A modest daily allowance is not enough when jury service can occupy full working days and require people to miss paid employment.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Since jury service can occupy full working days, full-time wages would compensate jurors for the employment they miss.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Because jury service can occupy full working days, full-time wages would make service financially possible for workers who cannot afford unpaid days.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: The same fact matters beyond reimbursement: because jury service can occupy full working days, full-time wages would reduce the financial pressure that can distract jurors from their civic duty.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Since jury service can occupy full working days, full-time wages would make a summons feel like compulsory public service rather than a low-paid inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: And because jury service can occupy full working days, full-time wages would encourage a wider range of workers to serve.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: One practical concern is that the courthouse cafeteria is closed on Fridays. Still, the accessibility problem remains.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Full-time wages would make jury service financially accessible to low-income workers, while also treating it as paid civic work rather than a private sacrifice.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: For anyone checking the logistics, the courthouse cafeteria is closed on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Daniela

utterances.text: Governments should create a licensing system for buy-now-pay-later providers because consumers need protection from unaffordable buy-now-pay-later debt.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: For transparency, I have never used a buy-now-pay-later service. Arjun, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: A licensing system would require buy-now-pay-later providers to carry out affordability checks. Because of those checks, some purchases that applicants could not afford would be blocked.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Before we continue, the studio clock is five minutes fast. Arjun, please finish your argument.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Licensing would drive many small buy-now-pay-later providers out of the market.

utterances.speaker: Petra

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Petra, so you are saying that small buy-now-pay-later providers could survive licensing. Efua, does that preserve competition?

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Because small buy-now-pay-later providers could remain, competition among buy-now-pay-later providers would remain broad; that broad competition is why a national licensing register would give regulators more data about complaints against buy-now-pay-later providers.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A national licensing register would give regulators more data about complaints against buy-now-pay-later providers. Because of that information, regulators could suspend buy-now-pay-later providers that repeatedly harmed consumers, and that enforcement power is why governments should license them.

utterances.speaker: Efua

spec.topic: Should households set a maximum indoor temperature during winter to reduce energy use?

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should households set a maximum indoor temperature during winter to reduce energy use? Tariq, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Household heating is a major source of winter energy use. Because of that, a maximum indoor temperature would reduce household energy use.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That makes a maximum indoor temperature a reasonable response to substantial household heating use. Since most households could stay comfortable at 20 degrees Celsius, the limit would not be excessive.

utterances.speaker: Zainab

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Winter energy bills rise sharply when homes are heated above 20 degrees Celsius, which shows why heating limits deserve consideration.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: A maximum indoor temperature would not by itself guarantee lower energy use in poorly insulated homes. That is an important limitation, because heat escapes quickly from those buildings.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: In other words, Rashid is saying that most households could remain comfortable under a 20-degree Celsius maximum.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Many families already wear warm clothing indoors during winter. We will now hear brief closing comments before the audience vote.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The government should publish clear guidance before any temperature rule begins.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether releasing unwanted aquarium species into rivers should carry mandatory fines. Bruno, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Releasing an unwanted aquarium species into a river should carry a mandatory fine, because released aquarium species can damage native river ecosystems.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: I oppose a blanket rule. But mandatory fines would punish responsible aquarium owners who make accidental mistakes.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Bruno, what other evidence makes fines necessary?

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Some aquarium species carry parasites that can spread to wild fish. That is why the parasite risk justifies mandatory fines for releasing aquarium species into rivers.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: For context, I once kept a rescued goldfish in a forty-litre tank.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Beatriz, are you rejecting every fine, including one aimed only at deliberate releases?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: So you are saying every person who releases an unwanted aquarium species into a river should receive a fine. The city rescue centre receives many calls about injured water birds.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Bruno, can the proposal distinguish deliberate dumping from an accidental escape?

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Yes. The proposed fines would apply only when an owner deliberately releases an unwanted aquarium species.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed penalties would target intentional releases rather than accidental escapes.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: That limited rule is workable because aquarium shops usually keep records of their customers' purchases.

utterances.speaker: Femi

utterances.speaker: Jasper

spec.topic: Should stadiums reserve a fixed proportion of seats for standing spectators?

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: I oppose a fixed quota for standing spectators. A fixed standing allocation would prevent stadiums from adapting their seating plans to different events.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: But stadiums should reserve a fixed proportion of seats for standing spectators. That objection overlooks the consistency the policy would provide.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Because that fixed allocation would give spectators a predictable choice between standing and sitting, it would make the arrangement fairer.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Since the policy makes that choice predictable, ticket information would also become clearer.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Clearer ticket information would reduce disputes at stadium entrances, because people would know exactly what kind of place they had bought.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Because the policy reserves a defined area, stadiums could install suitable barriers and sightlines there.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Those suitable barriers and sightlines would make standing sections safer to manage, which is another reason for the fixed proportion.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A fixed proportion would give clubs a stable basis for staffing standing sections, because the expected capacity would not change from match to match.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Because staffing would be stable, stewards could monitor crowd movement more consistently.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Consistent crowd monitoring would make it easier to identify dangerous overcrowding, so the reserved proportion would improve supervision.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Because the standing capacity would be known in advance, emergency planners would have a reliable number for their calculations.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Reliable capacity calculations would improve emergency preparation, which is a final practical benefit of reserving the proportion.

utterances.speaker: Cillian

spec.topic: Should referees be required to explain controversial decisions publicly after matches?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Controversial refereeing decisions can undermine public confidence in sport. That is why a public explanation can help restore confidence after a controversial refereeing decision.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For that reason, referees should be required to explain controversial decisions publicly after matches.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some football matches attract more than fifty thousand spectators.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A public explanation can show whether a referee applied the relevant rule correctly. Showing how rules were applied can improve the public's understanding of the sport.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author once watched a referee reverse a decision after consulting a video assistant.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since explanations should be given after matches rather than during active play, they would protect the flow of the game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The strongest objection is that public explanations would inevitably expose referees to more abuse.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That risk is manageable because a controlled explanation process could reduce the risk of abuse. This is why leagues could limit the process to written statements or questions from accredited journalists.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Yet leagues can require explanations through designated officials without exposing referees to uncontrolled public contact. That arrangement works because leagues can limit the process to written statements or questions from accredited journalists.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal is a requirement for public explanations after matches.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, explaining rule application can teach spectators how the sport works.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To put it differently, leagues can demand accountable explanations while protecting referees from direct harassment.

spec.topic: Should small businesses receive tax relief for offering formal profit-sharing schemes?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Small businesses should receive tax relief for offering formal profit-sharing schemes, because such schemes align staff effort with the firm's results.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: They do so because staff with a stake in the outcome tend to waste less and stay longer. Retention alone is a further reason for relief, since replacing a departed employee costs a small firm several thousand pounds.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Small firms mostly avoid formal schemes, since the legal and accounting fees of setting one up are high. That is the reason relief is needed.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics object, though, that relief would merely subsidise firms that would have created schemes anyway.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Fewer than one in ten small firms currently run a formal scheme, so relief would mostly reach firms not yet running one, which is a reason to grant it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Relief should be limited to schemes open to all staff, since otherwise owners could use it to reward only themselves.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, relief should reward broad sharing, not director bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Relief should also be capped at a modest sum per employee, because a cap keeps the cost to the Treasury predictable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the Treasury would know its bill in advance.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I ran a six-person print shop for eight years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Turning employees into partners is worth a small cost to the Treasury, and that is the final reason to grant relief.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, shared results keep people in their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The scheme's first review should come after three years.

spec.topic: Should patients be allowed to record every medical consultation without asking permission?

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: I support letting patients record every consultation without asking permission because recordings help patients remember medical instructions accurately.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: I disagree. Patients should obtain permission before recording a consultation, because clinicians and other patients have privacy rights.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: A recording can document an error or omission during a consultation. That is a reason patients should have the right to record without first asking.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: So you are saying that a recording can document an error or omission during a medical consultation.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Some patients prefer to take handwritten notes during medical consultations. That choice should remain available.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Recordings help patients with memory difficulties retain important medical information; for that reason, patients should be allowed to record.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Since patients should be allowed to record consultations, clinics should offer patients a standard way to record them.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Third-party details may be captured without those people's consent. That is why recordings may expose private information about people who are present as bystanders.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Obtaining consent before recording protects trust between patients and clinicians, which is why permission matters.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: In other words, patients should obtain permission before recording a medical consultation.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Patients should receive copies of recordings made during their consultations. Patients need control over the record of their own care.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Third-party details may be captured without those people's consent, so the privacy risk is not limited to the patient.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: A standard recording policy would reduce disputes about what clinicians told patients. That would make complaints easier to assess.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Put another way, a standard recording policy would reduce disagreements about what clinicians told patients.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Copies of recordings let patients check what clinicians said later; therefore, patients should receive copies.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Digital recordings require secure storage and careful access controls. Those technical requirements cannot be ignored.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Because patients should receive copies and a standard recording policy would reduce disputes, clinics should permit patient recordings while using safeguards for privacy and storage.

utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether political advertisers should have to disclose AI-generated campaign material. Giulia, you start.

utterances.speaker: Quentin

utterances.speaker: Annelise

utterances.text: So you are saying, Giulia, that voters should be told when a machine made the material they are shown. Any last word?

utterances.speaker: Vikram

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Put another way, a screen leaflet is no substitute for a real conversation.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: I once bought emergency contraception for a friend, so I know how stressful it is.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Let us move on to practicalities.

utterances.speaker: Dalia

spec.topic: Should landlords be required to audit software used to screen prospective tenants?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Landlords should be required to audit the software they use to screen prospective tenants, because such software can reject applicants on the basis of errors in the data it draws from.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many screening reports mix up people with similar names. That is why applicants are sometimes refused housing because of records that belong to someone else.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A refusal of housing can cost an applicant a job and a school place for their children, and for that reason wrongful refusals impose serious harm.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But audits would be expensive for small landlords.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That ignores the option of placing the duty on the software vendors, who can spread the cost across thousands of clients.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a vendor can audit once and share the result with every landlord who buys the product.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Scores often hide how they weigh an applicant's history, and an applicant cannot challenge a decision whose reasoning is hidden.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since both are true, hidden scoring leaves applicants with no way of appealing, which is one more ground for requiring audits.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Auditing would show whether scores systematically disadvantage particular groups, since such a pattern would amount to unlawful discrimination.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I rented a flat last spring through an agency.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Landlords already take responsibility for checking the condition of the buildings they let. Put another way, checking the tools used to choose tenants is a similar duty of care.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Screening will keep growing as more rental listings move online.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: All of this shows that, in short, a legal audit requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Screening scores can reproduce biases from the historical data they are trained on.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That matters because a biased score can shut an entire group of applicants out of the housing market. And landlords who rely on such scores cannot tell whether they are discriminating unlawfully, which is another reason to require audits.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Would landlords be required to find out what their tools actually do? In other words, an audit requirement would force exactly that.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Small landlords with one or two flats cannot afford audits, and that is a serious objection to the whole proposal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But vendors can be made to supply the audit as part of the licence, so the cost does not fall on small landlords.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some will say audits would slow down the rental process.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That ignores that an audit is done once per software version, not once per applicant.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Audits reduce the number of applicants wrongly rejected. Put differently, applicants would no longer be rejected by errors nobody can explain.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I rented a flat last spring.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Auditing screening software is a basic safeguard, like inspecting a building's wiring.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Landlords already accept safety inspections for gas and electrics, which shows the comparison holds.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, requiring audits of screening software is a modest and justified step, and the law should say so.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Several cities already require audits of automated hiring tools, which is a further reason to act.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For the record, I have no financial interest in any screening vendor.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: People say rewilding threatens national food security, but the farmland involved produces under one percent of national output.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would farmers be paid for, then?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Farmers should be paid for ecological results rather than crop volume. I have advised farmers for fifteen years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that payment should follow results, not volume.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Yes, since results payments reward farmers who actually restore habitat.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And does that cost more?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Results payments cost taxpayers less than open-ended production subsidies, which is a further reason for the switch, since pilot schemes with results payments have come in under budget.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, paying for results is the cheaper option for taxpayers.

utterances.speaker: Bongani

spec.topic: Should all digital political advertisements display their funders and targeting criteria?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: All digital political advertisements should display their funders and targeting criteria.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Identifying an advertisement's funder allows voters to judge whose interests the message may serve. For that reason, funder disclosure supports the case for displaying both kinds of information.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Voters can compare a political message with the interests of the organization that paid for it. That comparison is why identifying the funder makes the advertisement more accountable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, voters can assess a political message by comparing it with the interests of its funder.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is a reason to require digital political advertisements to identify both their funders and their intended audiences.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A standard disclosure label would make funder and audience information easy to find. Because the label would be consistent, readers would not have to search through separate platforms or legal notices.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A consistent label therefore supports the broader requirement that digital political advertisements identify both their funders and their intended audiences. Put another way, the requirement is that both the payer and the intended audience be named.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universal disclosure could expose small political donors to harassment. That concern is serious, but it does not overturn the case for requiring disclosure of political advertising.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many campaign advertisements use photographs supplied by commercial image libraries.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I first became interested in political advertising during a local election.

spec.topic: Should landlords be required to accept rent payments through government-backed accounts?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should landlords be required to accept rent payments through government-backed accounts?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Yes. Landlords should be required to accept rent through those accounts, because they would protect tenants' payment data.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics worry that a compulsory system could create new privacy risks. How do you answer that?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A mandatory account system could expose tenants' payment data without safeguards. That is why government-backed accounts would need to protect tenants' payment data.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the policy help tenants who cannot always pay on the same day?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Tenants with variable incomes often struggle to pay rent on a fixed date, so government-backed accounts would make late rent payments less likely.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would the arrangement change for landlords?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: The payment system could process transfers automatically. As a result, automatic transfers would reduce landlords' administrative work.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Are there any practical qualifications?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Some landlords already accept rent through housing-benefit payment systems. The proposed accounts would need a clear procedure for correcting failed payments.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would landlords lose control over the rent they charge?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: No. Landlords would still be able to set lawful rent amounts, since the proposed accounts would change the payment channel rather than rent-setting powers.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So what is your overall assessment?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: In other words, government-backed accounts would improve the reliability of rent collection.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether professional clubs should be fined when their supporters commit discriminatory abuse. Dolores, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Discriminatory abuse by supporters is a recurring problem at some professional clubs. Because that problem persists, professional clubs should be fined when their supporters commit discriminatory abuse.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Would you require clubs to do anything beyond paying the fine?

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Yes. The same recurring problem is also why professional clubs should publish annual reports on how they address discriminatory abuse.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Professional clubs can identify supporters who use club platforms to organise discriminatory abuse. Since clubs can identify those organisers, they should be fined when they fail to do so.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Because clubs can identify organised abuse through their platforms, fines would encourage them to improve their reporting and monitoring systems. For the record, I have attended three football matches this season.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: A professional club that repeatedly reports abusive supporters to the authorities can reduce discriminatory abuse around its matches. That is why such clubs should receive smaller fines.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Bongani, you think the policy could punish clubs for conduct they cannot control.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Some supporters make discriminatory comments independently of anything a professional club says or does. For that reason, a professional club should not automatically be fined for every discriminatory comment made by a supporter.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Professional clubs should face financial penalties for discriminatory abuse committed by their supporters.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: In other words, clubs should lose money when their supporters engage in discriminatory abuse.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposed policy would make clubs financially accountable for discriminatory abuse by supporters. The studio audience includes several former professional players.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: So you are saying that clubs, rather than only individual supporters, should bear a financial consequence for discriminatory abuse.

utterances.speaker: Bongani

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Emergency shelters are unavailable to some people on many nights. Since shelters are unavailable, criminalizing sleeping in public punishes people for lacking an available shelter.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: But public sleeping can block entrances and create sanitation problems. For that reason, keeping public sleeping a criminal offence is necessary to protect access and sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: My bicycle has a loose chain. A practical fact for this discussion is that emergency shelters often fill before evening.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma

utterances.speaker: Nkechi

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I think we should recommend a ban, because late polls push undecided voters to follow whoever looks like the winner.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: But a ban would restrict the public's access to information, and that is a serious objection.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: So you are saying a blackout would amount to censorship of what the public can learn.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Fair enough. My brother works at a polling firm, by the way, so I have heard their side.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Several neighbouring countries already run a final-week blackout, so it is workable in practice, whatever else we think of it.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: In other words, Petra, you want us to recommend a ban on polls in the last week.

spec.topic: Should governments place a temporary windfall tax on industries benefiting from sudden price shocks?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments place a temporary windfall tax on industries that profit from sudden price shocks? Helga, you start.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Governments should place a temporary windfall tax on energy firms, because their profits have doubled purely on a war-driven price spike.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Amir, your reaction?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: But a windfall tax would discourage investment, since investors could no longer trust that the rules will stay stable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Aurelio, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Spain's windfall tax paid for bill rebates for four million families, which is another reason to adopt one. My cousin works at a refinery, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: I back it because the tax expires when prices normalise, leaving long-term returns untouched. The excess profits come from luck, not new investment, which is a further reason.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that, because the tax expires, long-term returns are untouched.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Yes, and that works because governments can write an automatic end date into the law. Only profits above the pre-crisis average would be taxed, which is why returns stay untouched.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Governments rarely let such a tax lapse, since the British levy was extended twice.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: In other words, Amir, you think a promised expiry is worth nothing.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Poor households spend a quarter of their income on energy, which is why the revenue should go to household rebates.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So the money would protect the poorest households.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: I used to work at an energy regulator. Put differently, nobody will fund a new power plant under this tax.

spec.topic: Should possession of small quantities of drugs be treated as a civil violation rather than a crime?

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: I think possession of small quantities should be a civil violation, not a crime, because a criminal record for possession damages a person's chances of finding work for years.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But that ignores the fact that decriminalising possession would remove the deterrent that keeps casual use low.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Side note, my cousin works as a probation officer, so I hear a lot of these stories.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: It would not remove all deterrence, since a fine or a mandatory health assessment would still discourage casual use.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Hm, go on, what else do you have?

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Police time would be freed for tackling dealers and violent crime, because police resources are limited.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: So you are saying civil penalties would free up the time police now spend on possession arrests.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Yes. By the way, I have read about a few European countries that changed their drug laws.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: My worry remains that treating possession as a civil matter would send a message that drug use is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Put another way, you think drug use should be handled as a health matter, not a moral one? Then we agree.

utterances.speaker: Kai

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: There is another reason to ban them: surveys show problem gamblers report more urges to bet after seeing adverts during live games, so the adverts hurt vulnerable viewers.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: To put my first point another way, young viewers come to see betting as a normal part of sport.

spec.topic: Should voters be able to recall elected legislators before their terms end?

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether voters should be able to recall elected legislators before their terms end. Naveen, why do you support that power?

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Voters should be able to recall elected legislators before their terms end because elected legislators are agents of the voters.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Recall campaigns can punish legislators for unpopular votes. I worry that a legislator who follows evidence rather than opinion could be targeted.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Legislators need freedom to take unpopular positions. Because they need that freedom, recall campaigns can punish legislators for unpopular votes.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: A signature threshold can reduce frivolous recall petitions, which is why recall should be available. The threshold would separate serious complaints from passing anger.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: A fixed recall election gives voters an orderly remedy; that is another reason to allow recall.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Recall elections would impose significant administrative costs, so I would not create them lightly. I once attended a legislative hearing that lasted six hours.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Regular elections are too infrequent to correct serious failures by legislators. Because voters need a remedy between elections, recall should be available.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So you are saying that voters should have the power to remove elected legislators before their scheduled terms end?

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: No. Recall is not a substitute for ordinary elections; on the contrary, it could turn every difficult policy decision into a campaign.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: A recall vote can remove a legislator who has lost public trust, which is why voters should have this power.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: For example, a five-percent signature threshold can screen out weak recall petitions. That concrete threshold shows how the broader safeguard could work.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: In other words, regular elections provide voters with a delayed opportunity to judge legislators.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: A fixed recall date prevents repeated petition drives. That scheduling rule makes the remedy more predictable.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: What you mean is that a recall ballot should be held on a fixed date rather than whenever organizers choose.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: I prefer reading committee reports to watching campaign debates.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: A replacement election can be held within sixty days after a successful recall. Because that keeps a vacancy brief, it makes removing an underperforming legislator a workable remedy; for the same reason, voters should have recall power.

spec.topic: Should medical schools reserve places for applicants from disadvantaged communities?

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether medical schools should reserve places for applicants from disadvantaged communities. Naveen, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Equal treatment in admissions does not guarantee equal opportunity for applicants from disadvantaged communities. Because of that, medical schools should reserve a defined share of places for such applicants even when their entrance-exam scores are lower.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: I understand the concern, but score-only admissions can perpetuate unfairness between applicants who had unequal opportunities to prepare. That is why treating every score as an identical measure of merit is not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Because equal treatment alone cannot remove those unequal starting conditions, reserving places would broaden socioeconomic diversity in medical-school cohorts.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: The admissions committee will publish its annual report next Tuesday. Naveen, how would you answer the concern about standards?

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Because unequal opportunity narrows the applicant pool, the reservation policy would make medical-school student bodies more socioeconomically diverse. In other words, reserving places would broaden socioeconomic diversity in the cohorts.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: For context, I volunteered at a community health clinic during the previous summer. I still think the policy needs a safeguard.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Because equal treatment alone is insufficient, a reservation policy should retain a published academic minimum for every admitted student. That requirement does not support reserving places for applicants with lower scores regardless of competence.

spec.topic: Should retailers be forbidden from destroying unsold usable goods?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should shops be stopped from throwing away goods that nobody has bought?

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Yes, retailers should be forbidden from destroying unsold usable goods, because it is indefensible waste.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why do you call it indefensible?

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Those goods have already consumed energy and materials in manufacture, which is why binning them is so hard to justify. France, incidentally, has had a ban in place since 2020.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about the cost to retailers?

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Retailers claim a ban would be too costly for them, but the real cost is small.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why is it small?

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Several charities collect surplus stock free of charge, so retailers barely pay anything to pass it on.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying a ban would cost retailers very little.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Yes. Voluntary pledges cannot be relied on, because some brands still destroy unsold stock to protect their prestige.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How do you know so much about this?

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: I spent ten years working in retail logistics.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So what should be done?

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Legislation is needed to end the destruction, since pledges cannot be relied on. In other words, only a law will stop it.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether artificial-intelligence developers should pay licensing fees for copyrighted material used in training. Isaac, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Yes. Artificial-intelligence developers train models on copyrighted books, images, and recordings at commercial scale. Because they use those works commercially, artificial-intelligence developers should pay licensing fees for copyrighted material used in training.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: But licensing fees would raise costs for small artificial-intelligence developers. I started coding before sunrise on the day of the debate.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Fees would compensate creators for the use of their work in artificial-intelligence training, which is a reason developers should pay. Developers paying licensing fees would encourage a functioning market for permissions, and that follows from the payment requirement.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Rohan, what would a workable system look like?

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: A statutory licensing scheme could simplify permission for artificial-intelligence training; that is another reason developers should pay. Voluntary negotiations over training rights are too slow for the scale of artificial-intelligence development, so mandatory fees are needed.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: That cost increase would make it harder for small developers to compete, because higher training costs would fall most heavily on them.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Large technology companies can absorb licensing fees more easily than small developers, which is why the fee requirement remains feasible. In other words, the burden of licensing can be scaled toward companies with deeper pockets.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Rohan's research group releases an annual artificial-intelligence safety report.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Elif, are you asking for payment to be compulsory even when a creator has not negotiated with a developer?

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: A registry identifying rightsholders would make licensing practical for artificial-intelligence developers, which is why the fee requirement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: To put Isaac's position plainly, developers should pay licensing fees for copyrighted material used in artificial-intelligence training.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The proposed collecting agency would be based in the capital. Clement, the remaining issue is how the fees are administered, not whether creators deserve payment.

spec.topic: Should councils charge higher business rates for premises that remain vacant?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Vacant premises reduce local footfall. The reason this matters is that vacant premises impose costs on councils.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Vacant premises also attract vandalism that councils must address; this is another reason for the public costs of empty properties.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Higher business rates can motivate owners to reopen vacant premises.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A pilot scheme found that higher rates led owners to let or sell more empty premises, which shows that the incentive can work.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For those reasons, councils should charge higher business rates for premises that remain vacant.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: There is, however, a serious objection: higher business rates could push financially fragile businesses into closure.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, a vacancy surcharge could harm businesses that are already struggling.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second objection is that higher business rates could be passed on to tenants and customers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The policy can nevertheless be limited because councils can exempt premises that are being actively marketed for rent or sale.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed charge would apply only to premises whose owners are not genuinely trying to find occupants.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author once worked in a shop that stood empty for six months before becoming a café.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A surcharge should begin only after a property has been vacant for twelve months.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is to say, the policy should wait a full year before imposing the higher rate.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A twelve-month threshold would target deliberate property holding rather than brief periods between tenants, which is why the threshold is important.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many councils send their annual business-rate bills in the autumn.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Councils could use the additional revenue from the surcharge to fund grants for town-centre improvements.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put differently, higher rates on persistently vacant premises would create a useful incentive for owners to act.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Councils should adopt a vacancy surcharge with exemptions for genuine hardship and active marketing.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since a twelve-month threshold would target deliberate holding and the revenue could fund town-centre improvements, councils should charge higher business rates on premises that remain vacant, subject to reasonable safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: The national employment survey was released in April. Workers on short fixed-term contracts can lose income abruptly when their contracts end.

utterances.text: That experience may be relevant, but I want to focus on the effect on workers.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for requiring severance?

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Severance pay gives workers time to find their next job.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: In other words, severance pay provides workers with a financial bridge after a short contract ends.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Employers can predict the payroll cost of severance for short fixed-term contracts.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Many employers already calculate similar payments when permanent jobs end.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: Can the proposed obligation be administered without creating excessive paperwork?

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Because employers can predict the payroll cost, and because many employers already calculate comparable payments, a severance requirement for short fixed-term contracts would be administratively manageable for employers.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: So you are saying that employers could administer severance payments for short contracts without major difficulty.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Some employers would avoid hiring short-term workers if severance became mandatory.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: Cillian, give us your position clearly.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Employers should be required to provide severance pay when short fixed-term contracts end, because workers can lose income abruptly, because severance gives them time to find their next job, and because employers can predict the cost.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: But that recommendation is too broad: many short fixed-term contracts cover genuinely seasonal work that ends when the season ends.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Because some short contracts are genuinely seasonal, and because those contracts end as expected, a blanket severance rule could impose costs on those employers.

utterances.speaker: Margit

spec.topic: Should nuclear power receive the same renewable-energy subsidies as wind and solar power?

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: I think nuclear should get the same subsidies as wind and solar, because nuclear emits almost no carbon while running.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: But subsidising nuclear is a slow way to cut emissions, since plants take over a decade to build.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Fair point, a decade is realistic, since approvals alone take seven years in most countries.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Side note: my electricity bill went up again last month.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: So you are saying nuclear is almost carbon-free once it is running.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Yes. Nuclear runs around the clock, which is why grids that lose wind and sun at times need it.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Subsidies should go to whichever low-carbon option is cheapest. My cousin put solar panels on her roof last year.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: In other words, you want subsidies only for the cheapest option.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Wind turbines need replacing after about twenty-five years, which is why wind's cheap headline price hides replacement costs.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Meanwhile a nuclear plant keeps producing power for about sixty years.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: So you are saying a nuclear plant keeps generating power for around six decades.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: A per-unit subsidy pays out only once a plant is running, which is why construction delay risk would fall on investors rather than taxpayers.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Long-term waste storage costs are still uncertain, so nuclear's true cost is hard to estimate.

spec.topic: Should whistleblowing reports be handled by an independent external body?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Reports should go to an independent external body rather than internal HR, because staff simply do not trust internal teams with them.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: And they don't trust them since the HR team is paid by the same company that is being reported on.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: But an external body would take months to understand each complaint, because it knows nothing about the workplace.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: In other words, you think outsiders are too slow to handle complaints?

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: That ignores that external regulators already handle financial fraud tips within days.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I used to work in a regulator's call centre, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Independent bodies also protect whistleblowers from retaliation, since the employer never learns who made the report.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: So you are saying the main benefit is that the reporter's identity stays hidden from the employer.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Yes. Several countries already legally require external reporting channels as well, which is another reason for my view.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That is to say, the law already treats external reporting as normal practice.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: That distrust is earned, because internal handling often fails to act, as a third of reporters in the latest survey said nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: In other words, internal teams often just sit on reports.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I do accept that outsiders are slow, because the regulator's complaint queue is currently four months long.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Off topic, but my company's HR has just changed its phone number.

spec.topic: Should governments build new nuclear reactors to reduce carbon emissions?

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether governments should build new nuclear reactors to reduce carbon emissions. Emeka, why do you support the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Nuclear reactors emit very little carbon during operation. Because of that, nuclear power is a low-carbon source that can replace fossil-fuel generation.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Before we turn to the opposing view, a reminder that the debate is being broadcast from the capital tonight.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: That is why governments should build new nuclear reactors to reduce carbon emissions: their very low operational emissions make nuclear a practical replacement for fossil fuels.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Reactors provide steady electricity when wind and sunlight are unavailable. This supports Emeka's point that nuclear power can replace fossil-fuel generation, and it strengthens the case for building reactors.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But new nuclear reactors take too long and cost too much to reduce emissions soon. A climate policy needs results sooner than these projects usually deliver.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: In other words, Tariq's objection is that new nuclear reactors would be too slow and expensive to deliver near-term emissions cuts.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: As a separate point, my local energy cooperative installed new solar panels last spring.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So you are saying that governments should build new nuclear reactors as part of their emissions reduction policy. Tariq, does that fairly capture Emeka's recommendation?

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: We have heard the case for dependable low-carbon power and the objection about speed and cost. I will now ask each of you for a brief closing statement.
