spec.topic: Should supervised drug-consumption facilities receive legal protection from prosecution?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether supervised drug-consumption facilities should receive legal protection from prosecution. Efua, why do you support that protection?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Any legal protection would excuse every offence committed on the premises. That is too broad a shield for the public to accept.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: These facilities give people who use drugs a route into treatment and support. They are not simply places where consumption is tolerated.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The law can protect staff without granting immunity for trafficking or violence. A carefully written statute can draw that boundary.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Gwen says the proposal is dangerously broad, while Efua and Elif describe a limited form of protection. Efua, make the case for that limited form.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: In other words, supervised facilities should receive protection for possession-related work, rather than blanket immunity. That protection would let them operate without staff fearing arrest.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are saying these facilities reduce fatal overdoses by providing immediate medical intervention. Because that intervention happens on site, some deaths can be prevented.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Put another way, the law can protect staff while excluding trafficking and violence. But that directly contradicts the idea that every offence would be excused.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Because legal protection would let facilities remain open when staff might otherwise fear arrest, people would have a safer alternative to consuming alone.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: That same protection would keep the doors open; because the doors stay open, people who use drugs could reach supervised care instead of consuming alone.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Legal protection would also make it easier to recruit qualified medical staff. Since qualified staff improve safety, the facilities would be safer places to seek help.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Because these facilities provide immediate medical intervention, that intervention would prevent some overdose deaths.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Preventing some overdose deaths is a strong public-interest reason to protect the facilities, since the law should reduce avoidable loss of life.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The argument from Efua and Elif is therefore that limited protection keeps facilities open, supports qualified care, and prevents deaths. Gwen, you have the final response.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: The studio audience has submitted more questions than this programme can answer.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: For the record, I have chaired televised health debates for six years. Thank you all for joining us.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should online platforms offer independent appeals against moderation decisions? Elodie, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because moderation errors are frequent and users currently have nowhere to turn.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Do you have evidence for that?

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: I do, since one recent audit found that a fifth of removed posts were restored on review.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: But independent appeals would be far too slow, since platforms remove millions of posts every single day.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So what you mean, Petra, is that independent appeals would be too slow to work.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Urgent cases could be decided within days, because appeals bodies can sort cases by the harm at stake.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, sorting by urgency removes the delay problem.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I moderate a small hobby forum myself, so I see this up close.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: A levy on the largest platforms could cover the cost, since they earn most of the advertising revenue.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Put another way, the big platforms should foot the bill for appeals.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Appeals would also raise users' trust in platforms, because people could challenge decisions they consider unfair.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: By the way, the national oversight board was only set up two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Thank you all; that is all we have time for.

utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether companies should publish the results of anonymous employee surveys. Abena, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Anonymous employee surveys reveal concerns that employees may not raise publicly. Because publishing those results would expose such concerns to management and the wider workforce, it would improve corporate accountability.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: For context, I have worked at three different companies.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: I joined the programme from the studio lobby, so I will keep this brief.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: That is why companies should publish the results of anonymous employee surveys.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: I disagree with Abena's recommendation: companies should not publish raw survey results, because publishing results from small teams can make individual employees identifiable.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: In other words, Sipho's position is that companies should not publish raw survey results.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: A safer approach is to publish aggregated survey summaries, which can protect employee anonymity. Employees are also more likely to trust surveys when management reports the findings.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Because those two benefits work together, aggregated publication is a workable standard for reporting survey results.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Put another way, Abena's proposal is that companies should publish anonymous employee-survey results.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: In other words, Dimitri's point is that aggregated survey summaries protect employee anonymity.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: A written publication policy would tell employees in advance how their responses will be reported.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Since aggregated publication is a workable reporting standard, and since a written policy gives employees that advance information, companies should adopt a written policy for publishing aggregated survey results.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The panel therefore distinguishes between publishing raw responses and publishing carefully aggregated results.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should releasing sulphur particles into the atmosphere be researched as a climate intervention? Deirdre, you start.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Tariq, you are not convinced.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: I flew in from Lisbon this morning, so forgive the tired voice. But researching this would reduce the pressure to cut emissions.

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Odette

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Research is not deployment, since a model run releases nothing into the air. That is one more reason to go ahead with it.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: In other words, studying it commits nobody to using it.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Exactly. And the tipping points matter, because current emissions cuts are too slow.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Anything else to support your case, Deirdre?

utterances.speaker: Deirdre

spec.topic: Should businesses give workers formal seats on their governing boards?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether businesses should give workers formal seats on their governing boards. Tariq, you start.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Businesses should give workers formal board seats, because workers know the daily reality of a firm better than outside directors do.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of that?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Staff on the shop floor spot safety problems months before managers do, and that is why they know the firm's reality better.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: But worker seats would slow decisions down, since boards would have to consult staff representatives before every major decision.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Germany has given workers board seats for decades and its large firms remain among the most competitive in Europe, which is another reason to back Tariq's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Dimitri, what you are saying is that worker seats would make firms sluggish at deciding.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: I was a union organiser for twelve years before I entered politics.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Worker directors would help narrow executive pay gaps, because executives would have to justify pay awards to staff at the board table.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Swedish firms with worker directors have smaller pay ratios, which shows that point in practice.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Worker representatives on boards would leak confidential strategy to rivals.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: That ignores the law: every director, including a worker director, is bound by the same confidentiality duty.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So what you mean is that worker directors carry the same legal duty of confidentiality as any other director.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: I ran a small bakery for fifteen years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Is cost a worry for you?

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Small firms could not afford the training that worker directors need.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: A single board training course costs several thousand pounds per director, and that is the reason.

spec.topic: Should executive pay be capped at a fixed multiple of median employee pay?

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should executive pay be capped at a fixed multiple of median employee pay? Vikram, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Executive pay should be capped at a fixed multiple of median employee pay because large gaps between executive pay and median employee pay undermine employee trust.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: But a fixed multiple would punish firms competing for scarce executives. A cap sounds simple, yet it could ignore differences between industries.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Some industries compete intensely for scarce executives, and that is why a fixed multiple would punish those firms.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Median employee pay can be distorted by a company's large part-time workforce. That measurement problem deserves attention before any law is drafted.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: A cap can make long-term investors more confident, because predictable pay rules reduce reputational risk.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A fixed cap makes executive pay rules more predictable; that is why reputational risk falls.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: So you are saying that a cap can make long-term investors more confident. Arjun, what is your strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Boards need room to reward exceptional performance. A rigid ceiling could make that difficult.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: In other words, you mean that boards need room to reward exceptional performance.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Because boards need room to reward exceptional performance, a fifteen-times ceiling leaves room for exceptional rewards. Since that ceiling leaves room for such rewards, a fifteen-times ceiling is workable.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: The annual shareholder meeting is scheduled for Tuesday. I mention that only for viewers following the companies involved.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: We have heard the case that a cap builds trust and investor confidence, alongside the objection that it may restrict recruitment. We will return after the break.

spec.topic: Should people be expected to bring gifts when invited to an ordinary dinner?

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should people be expected to bring gifts when invited to an ordinary dinner?

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: An ordinary dinner invitation is a social occasion rather than a gift exchange. I think the distinction matters.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: That is why guests should not be expected to bring gifts to an ordinary dinner.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: For the same reason, hosts should value guests' company rather than the presents they bring.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Dinner guests have different financial circumstances, so a required gift could embarrass guests who cannot afford much.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: A small bottle of wine or bunch of flowers can be a considerate gesture. That is why guests may bring a small gift, but guests should not be expected to bring one.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Dinner hosts usually plan their food and drink before guests arrive, since a mandatory gift can duplicate something the host has already bought.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: But I reject that softer rule: guests should be expected to bring gifts to an ordinary dinner.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: In my family, we usually serve dessert after dinner.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Personally, I prefer arriving at dinner without carrying anything.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: A dinner gift should be a voluntary thank-you rather than an admission price.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: So you are saying that a dinner gift should be a voluntary thank-you rather than an admission price.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: In other words, the moderate position is that guests may give thanks with a gift, but hosts should not require one.

utterances.text: Tonight we are debating whether apartment residents should vote before their building allows short-term guests to stay. Milos, you support a vote?

utterances.text: Apartment residents should vote before the building allows short-term guests to stay because short-term guests can increase noise and security burdens in shared areas.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: A resident vote would also let residents set conditions for protecting shared spaces, which is another reason for requiring a vote.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: I have lived in this building for six years, and I do not think residents should control every arrangement made by individual owners.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Bruno, what is your main alternative to a building-wide vote?

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: For context, the building's lift was replaced last spring.

utterances.speaker: Bruno

utterances.speaker: Bruno

utterances.speaker: Milos

utterances.speaker: Bruno

spec.topic: Should schools allow students to take vocational qualifications alongside academic subjects?

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Our question is whether schools should let students combine vocational qualifications with academic subjects. Leilani, why do you support that option?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Students who take vocational qualifications alongside academic subjects practise skills used in real workplaces. Because that practical experience broadens their options, schools should allow students to take both kinds of qualification.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: I disagree that the policy is automatically beneficial: taking two demanding programmes can overload students.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Vocational qualifications can prepare students for apprenticeships as well as examinations. That wider preparation is why schools should offer students both vocational and academic routes.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools should make the combination available without requiring every student to take it?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Exactly; I believe that each student should retain the choice of route.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: The workload concern is not theoretical, since students already struggle when their timetables contain too many compulsory classes.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Schools can reduce that pressure by scheduling vocational lessons in different timetable blocks. For that reason, flexible scheduling can make taking vocational and academic qualifications together manageable.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: In other words, Xavier says that flexible scheduling can make dual study manageable.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Because the arrangement is manageable, students can pursue a vocational qualification without abandoning academic study.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Vocational qualifications include assessed projects and practical examinations.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal preserves academic study while adding a practical route.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Staffing every possible vocational subject is expensive, so schools should add vocational courses only where local demand is clear.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: To restate Xavier's point, schools should use local demand to decide which vocational courses to add.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Can a school offer these qualifications without spreading its staff too thinly?

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Because schools can target courses to local demand, allowing the combination can widen access to careers that university-focused timetables overlook.

spec.topic: Should governments be barred from calling early elections except after a formal parliamentary vote?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Governments should be barred from calling early elections except after a formal parliamentary vote, because a prime minister who can choose the date will choose the moment when the polls are best.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: But that ignores that a government with no working majority needs a quick way back to the voters. A parliamentary vote could take weeks, and the government would be paralysed meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: No, a government without a majority would simply lose a confidence vote and reach an election through parliament. Those votes are usually held within days, after all.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: So you are saying parliament could always bring about an election when one is needed.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Yes. And a vote forces the government to justify an early election in public debate, which is another reason for the rule, since open debate exposes purely tactical motives.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: But a government with a large majority would win that vote easily, because its own members rarely rebel.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Even a vote that is won has to be defended in the open, and that is why the rule matters.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: The rule would hand the opposition a veto over election timing, so I think it is a bad idea overall.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: So you are saying the opposition would end up controlling the election calendar.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Exactly. I watched the last confidence debate live, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Giving the opposition a say over timing is acceptable, since the opposition is the proper check on a government.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: So what you mean is that the opposition should have some say over when elections are held.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Yes. I should add that I campaigned for such a rule in my own party.

utterances.speaker: Petra

utterances.speaker: Petra

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Another reason to give residents priority is that the rule would reduce the travel distance for many allotment holders.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Although I remain concerned about fairness, one reason to favour resident priority is that it would help preserve allotments as a shared local resource.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Finally, resident priority is defensible because it would make the allocation process easier for the council to explain to local taxpayers.

utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether school boards should publish detailed breakdowns of spending by category each year. Adrian, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: School boards should publish detailed spending breakdowns by category every year because those reports would help families judge whether school priorities match their needs.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: I served on a school board in 2019, and the paperwork was already substantial.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Publishing spending breakdowns would be practical for most school boards, since most boards already record spending by category.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: But detailed public reports could expose information that identifies individual pupils. That privacy risk should not be treated as a minor detail.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: I have taught mathematics for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: So Adrian's proposal is for school boards to publish detailed annual spending categories.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: What you mean is that annual category reports would help families assess school priorities.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Put another way, annual publication of spending categories is the proposal under discussion.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: That proposal is needed because school boards should explain unusual spending differences between schools.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Those explanations would make officials answerable for budget decisions, which is why they matter.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: That accountability would improve public confidence in school budgets.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Margit, is the administrative burden your strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: No. The administrative burden of preparing the reports would be modest, so school boards could publish them without hiring large numbers of extra staff.

utterances.speaker: Magnus

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Raw financial tables are often difficult for families to interpret. Because of that, each published breakdown should include plain-language explanations of the main figures.

utterances.speaker: Magnus

spec.topic: Should citizens be able to trigger binding national referendums by collecting enough signatures?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should citizens be able to force a binding national referendum by collecting signatures?

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Yes, they should be able to trigger binding national referendums, since a high signature threshold keeps frivolous proposals off the ballot.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How high is high enough?

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Take Switzerland: only a handful of initiatives reach the ballot each year, which shows that a threshold really does filter. I covered those votes as a journalist in Bern for three years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say a binding vote lets a majority override minority rights.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: That ignores that constitutional courts can strike down results that violate minority rights, and that is another reason to allow binding referendums. Those courts can act since constitutions entrench such rights.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So in other words, courts act as a safety net for minorities.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Exactly, that is the idea.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the people should have the last word.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Yes, because parliaments drift away from voters between elections, which is why citizens need a way in. My own town ran a petition vote last spring.

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether public funding should follow each student to whichever accredited school the student chooses. Lucia, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Families in low-income neighborhoods are often assigned to schools with fewer advanced courses than nearby alternatives. That gap should not be determined by a family's postcode.

utterances.speaker: Rashid

utterances.text: So you are saying, Vikram, that officers should simply decide for themselves when to test. We will take a call after the break.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Respecting an adult's autonomy includes respecting the adult's informed refusal of medical treatment. That principle should apply even when doctors judge the decision irrational.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, honoring an adult's refusal of treatment is one way of respecting that adult's autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For that reason, adults should be allowed to refuse life-saving treatment even when doctors consider the refusal irrational.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, an adult's right to refuse treatment is a practical expression of personal autonomy, which supports my position.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Adults generally have the legal and moral authority to make decisions about their own bodies. Because refusal concerns the patient's own body, that authority supports allowing the refusal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Allowing doctors to override irrational refusals would make bodily authority depend on a doctor's judgment of rationality. Since that standard would weaken personal authority, it is another reason to protect the refusal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Patients are more likely to trust medical professionals when those professionals respect patient decisions. That increased trust supports respecting an adult's refusal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Respect for refusal can preserve a patient's trust even when the patient rejects medical advice, which is a further reason to protect the patient's decision.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Doctors can explain the consequences of refusing treatment without coercing a competent adult. This shows that medical guidance does not require forced treatment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, a doctor's belief that a refusal is irrational does not by itself prove that the adult lacks decision-making capacity. That objection limits the case for overriding the refusal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, respecting an informed refusal means allowing an adult to retain control over a medical decision.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Medical ethics courses often present difficult treatment refusals as emotionally challenging cases.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I find conversations about end-of-life care especially difficult to discuss with family members.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That same ethical principle supports the rule that a capable adult's refusal of life-saving treatment should ordinarily be respected.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because adult authority matters, the proper medical test is whether an adult has decision-making capacity, rather than whether the adult's choice seems sensible. In other words, a refusal should be judged by the person's understanding, not by its appeal to the physician.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Respect for bodily authority also supports careful capacity assessment, because such an assessment can distinguish an autonomous refusal from a decision made without understanding.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The same respect means that an adult does not have to provide a medically wise justification for refusing treatment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, adults may refuse treatment without proving that their reasons are medically sound.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This principle offers another reason to protect refusal: compulsory treatment can damage a patient's trust in future medical care.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In practical terms, forced treatment can undermine the relationship that makes later care possible.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some doctors would take the opposite position: doctors should override an adult's refusal whenever the doctors judge the refusal irrational.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That view should be rejected. Adults should remain free to reject life-saving treatment despite medical disapproval.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Hospitals should record the patient's stated reasons in the medical file, although that administrative question is separate from the right to refuse.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Families often find these decisions emotionally difficult, but their distress does not settle the patient's legal or ethical authority.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Respecting a competent adult's refusal of treatment protects trust between patients and doctors, which is another reason to respect the refusal.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.text: Because capacity assessments examine understanding and choice, hospitals should use safeguards to check capacity before overriding a refusal.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, doctors may call a refusal irrational without establishing that the patient lacks decision-making capacity.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, doctors can describe a refusal as irrational without proving that the patient is unable to choose.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That distinction is why doctors should record a capacity finding separately from their opinion about the wisdom of a refusal.

utterances.speaker: Author

spec.topic: Should websites verify users’ ages through government identification documents?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether websites should verify users' ages with government identification. Leopold, you start.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Websites should verify ages with government ID, because children reach adult content far too easily.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Is that your whole case?

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Which is another reason: a document check is the only method that cannot be beaten by typing a false birthday. Several countries already require such checks for online gambling, which shows it can work.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: But collecting government documents creates large databases that will eventually be breached, since several age-check vendors have already leaked records.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So, Fatima, you are saying ID checks make every site that holds the documents a target for hackers.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Exactly, because those documents are very valuable to identity thieves.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Bilal, you run a website yourself.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: I run a forum with about four thousand members. Small sites like mine would simply close.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Why would they close?

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Because verification would cost us more than we earn in a year.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Put another way, small sites cannot afford age verification.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Eamon, is there a middle way?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: I spent ten years at a media regulator. Regulators could license a few certified providers so that websites never see the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: So you are saying the sites never handle the documents.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: In other words, a site only receives a yes or no on whether the user is an adult. And it is safer, since certified providers can be audited.

spec.topic: Should airport expansions be rejected when their projected emissions exceed local reduction targets?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Welcome. Tonight's question: should an airport expansion be rejected when its projected emissions exceed the local reduction targets? Daniela, you first.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Yes, expansions should be rejected in that case, because a target that an airport can override is not a target at all.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: For viewers, the airport opened in 1962. Tobias, your response?

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: But rejecting an expansion simply moves the flights to an airport across the border. Incidentally, my flight in this morning was late.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: The airport's own forecast shows its emissions rising thirty percent above the local target, which is another reason to reject expansions like this one.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: I would approve expansions only together with binding emission caps, because caps written into the operating licence can be enforced with fines.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: In other words, you would approve expansion on condition that the airport stays within emission limits.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Yes. Binding caps would also let the region keep the two thousand jobs the airport provides, and that is a further reason for them.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: So, Daniela, what you are saying is that a local target only counts if the airport cannot get around it.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Exactly. Offsets are no substitute for real cuts, since a planted forest takes decades to absorb what a flight emits in hours.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Thank you both. We will take viewer calls after the break.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Welcome. Tonight we ask whether carbon capture should get public money before emissions are substantially cut. Yara, you first.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Yes, it should get funding now. Some industrial emissions from cement and steel cannot be eliminated by any other known method, which is why I say so.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Carmen, you are sceptical. Why?

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Let me add why the money must be public: capture only becomes cheap after many plants have been built and run. That is the reason public money is needed to get the first plants built.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Carmen, your response?

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Public funding for capture will let polluters carry on emitting.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: The Norwegian Sleipner project has stored carbon under the sea since 1996.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: But funding is not the same as excusing emissions, because the grants I propose would carry binding cuts.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So, Carmen, what Rania is saying is that capture grants should be tied to binding emission cuts.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Yes, grants tied to binding emission cuts are what I could support.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: My town hosts a pilot capture plant, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Still, the money would be better spent on renewables, because renewables cut emissions more cheaply per tonne than capture does today.

spec.topic: Should probation fees be abolished for people unable to pay them?

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether probation fees should be abolished for people unable to pay them. Camille, you support abolition?

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Yes. People unable to pay probation fees often have to choose between those fees and essential needs, so probation fees should be abolished for people unable to pay them.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Abolishing probation fees would remove a source of funding for probation services, because those fees currently contribute to their budgets.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: However, probation services need fee revenue to maintain their current staffing. That makes the loss of funding a serious objection to abolition.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: In other words, unaffordable probation fees force some people to sacrifice basic needs. That financial pressure can make people disengage from supervision.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Because financial pressure can make people disengage from supervision, abolishing unaffordable probation fees would improve compliance with supervision.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: So you are saying that ending unaffordable probation fees would make probation supervision more successful.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Since that simpler approach would avoid repeated tests of a person's finances, abolishing unaffordable probation fees would reduce disputes about who qualifies for relief.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Put another way, abolishing unaffordable probation fees would spare probation staff many arguments about a person's ability to pay. Staff could spend the time recovered from those arguments monitoring risk.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Because better use of staff time would improve supervision, better monitoring would make breaches of supervision easier to detect early.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Early intervention can prevent minor breaches from becoming new offences, since problems are easier to address before they escalate.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: If early intervention prevents minor breaches from becoming new offences, preventing those breaches from escalating would reduce pressure on the courts.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Because reduced pressure on the courts would benefit the public, it would be a further public benefit of abolishing unaffordable probation fees.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Therefore, abolishing probation fees for people unable to pay them is justified despite the lost fee revenue.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: I have never worked in a probation office.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Esther, does that address the funding concern?

utterances.text: I brought a blue notebook to the debate.

spec.topic: Should farmers be paid to plant crops designed primarily to absorb atmospheric carbon?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should farmers be paid to plant crops designed primarily to absorb atmospheric carbon?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Yes. Farmers should receive public payments for planting such crops because those crops remove carbon from the atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some critics worry that this policy could harm food production. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: That is a serious objection to my proposal: paying farmers to plant carbon-absorbing crops could divert farmland from food production.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that you support paying farmers to plant crops whose main purpose is absorbing atmospheric carbon?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: I do, provided the payments are tied to carbon that actually stays in the soil.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Independent measurements can show whether carbon remains in farm soil for many years.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Because those measurements can verify stored carbon, contracts can reward farmers for verified storage; long-term contracts then make carbon planting financially predictable for farms.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: In other words, long-term contracts give farms predictable financial support for planting carbon-absorbing crops, because carbon-planting payments reduce the income risk faced by participating farms.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How would the policy be tested before it became national?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: The proposed pilot would include farms in three agricultural regions.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: I began farming after studying environmental science.

spec.topic: Should constitutional amendments require approval in a binding public referendum?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should constitutional amendments require approval in a binding public referendum? Saanvi, you start.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because the constitution belongs to the people and not to the legislature. Any change to it needs the people's direct consent.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: But a referendum turns a complex amendment into a yes-or-no question.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying, Adrian, that voters cannot judge the details of an amendment on a yes-or-no ballot.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Ireland has held dozens of constitutional referendums since 1937.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Turnout in such votes is often below forty percent, which shows that the results can misrepresent what the public wants.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: So what you mean is that a low-turnout result may not reflect the will of the public.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: For context, I spent six years working as an election observer.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: A two-thirds parliamentary vote is enough protection for the constitution, since it forces cross-party agreement.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that a supermajority in parliament is a sufficient safeguard for amendments.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: A referendum requirement would be a heavy burden on the state and on voters, because organising a national ballot takes months of administrative work.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Which is another reason: each national referendum costs tens of millions.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Adrian, anything to add on the burden?

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Yes, and a third reason is that voters tire of being called to the polls repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

utterances.speaker: Leopold

utterances.speaker: Matteo

utterances.speaker: Elodie

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Local governments should require supermarkets to provide publicly accessible toilets.

utterances.text: The main reason is that requiring supermarkets to provide toilets would improve public access to essential facilities.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This is because publicly accessible toilets reduce barriers for people who need facilities during shopping trips.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That benefit matters since many shoppers spend enough time in supermarkets to need a toilet during their visits.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a size threshold would make a supermarket toilet requirement administratively workable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To put that differently, the requirement should allow exemptions where a building cannot safely fit a toilet, making an unqualified requirement objectionable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I usually plan my shopping trips around the location of nearby cafés.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some supermarkets already make their toilets available to the public.

utterances.text: Police should be allowed to request footage from privately owned smart doorbells. That is because smart-doorbell footage often helps identify people involved in nearby crimes.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Homeowners should receive notice whenever police request their smart-doorbell footage. The reason is that a notice gives homeowners a chance to challenge an improper request.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: In other words, homeowners should be notified about police requests for their smart-doorbell footage.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: A written notice creates an auditable record of the request, and that is why homeowners should be notified.

utterances.speaker: Elodie

utterances.speaker: Ulla

utterances.speaker: Femi

utterances.speaker: Ulla

utterances.speaker: Elodie

utterances.text: Employers should be required to provide paid leave for employees caring for sick relatives, because paid leave would prevent employees from having to choose between earning wages and caring for sick relatives.

spec.topic: Should doctors routinely use artificial intelligence to identify patients at risk of deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Yes, doctors should routinely use AI to flag patients who may deteriorate, because the paper-based warning scores we use today miss many slow declines.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: The models read every vital sign from the bedside monitors continuously, which is why they can detect subtle trends hours before staff would notice them.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: But the alerts are often false, and nurses start ignoring them. That worry is real, since alert fatigue already affects hospital wards.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Still, alert thresholds can be tuned for each ward, so false alarms can be kept low.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Put another way, each ward can choose its own alert sensitivity. I run a respiratory ward myself.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Trials in two hospitals found fewer emergency transfers to intensive care with AI alerts, which shows these tools help patients.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: In short, AI alerting should become part of ordinary ward care. Incidentally, we installed our system in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Ivana

utterances.text: That practice is worthwhile because children are more likely to mention their worries when they know that parents respect their privacy.

utterances.speaker: Ivana

utterances.speaker: Zainab

spec.topic: Should universities record every lecture and make recordings available to enrolled students?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universities should record every lecture and make the recordings available to enrolled students. The simplest reason is that students who miss a lecture through illness or work shifts can catch up from a recording.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second reason is that students learn better when they can rewatch difficult explanations. In other words, rewatching a hard explanation at their own pace lets them absorb it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The usual objection is that recorded lectures make students stop attending in person.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But attendance in my own department fell by only five percent after recording began.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Recordings also help students who are not native speakers of the language of instruction, because they can pause, replay and look up unfamiliar terms.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is why recording every lecture is an equity measure as much as a convenience; put differently, it gives every student the same chance to follow the course whatever their circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once sat through a lecture in a hall with a broken heater, and I remember nothing of it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, universities should record every lecture, since the equipment costs little compared with a teaching budget.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some lecturers may worry about being judged on their recorded performance.

spec.topic: Should laboratories be prohibited from using animals when non-animal methods are available?

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Yes, I think laboratories should be prohibited from using animals where validated non-animal methods exist, because animal tests often fail to predict how humans will respond.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Organ-on-chip models built from human cells can already reproduce liver toxicity more reliably than rodent tests, which is another reason. And animal studies are slower and more expensive than those alternatives, which is a further reason.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Critics will say a ban would slow medical research.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: But that ignores that the ban would cover only cases where validated alternatives already exist, so it would not slow research.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: I spent six years in a toxicology lab myself. It has since closed, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: I would phase the ban in over five years, since regulators in many countries still demand animal data before approving products.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: That is also why the phase-in matters: revising regulatory guidelines typically takes around three years.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: In other words, animal testing should end wherever a proven alternative exists.

utterances.text: One month is too short for some interns to receive meaningful training. That is why I think the law should not permit unpaid internships beyond one month.

utterances.text: Unpaid work becomes unfair when interns perform ordinary staff duties, so companies should not be allowed to use unpaid interns for more than one month. The longer such placements last, the more regular work can be shifted onto people who are not paid.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre

utterances.speaker: Lucia

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe

utterances.speaker: Fatima

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: So you are saying that tracking collars would make it possible for wildlife agencies to respond quickly to released predators?

utterances.speaker: Lucia

spec.topic: Should businesses guarantee paid internships rather than offering unpaid placements?

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Businesses should guarantee pay for interns, because unpaid placements shut out students who cannot afford to work for free.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: But a guaranteed wage would force small firms to cancel placements altogether.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Paid placements in our pilot scheme had half the dropout rate of unpaid ones, which is another reason to guarantee pay.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: So, Jasper, you are saying that many small firms would simply stop offering placements?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Exactly, because most small firms run on margins of only a few percent. I did my own placement unpaid, in a garage, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Amir

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Experience is itself a form of payment.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: So what you mean is that interns get paid in learning rather than in money.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Put another way, unpaid roles exclude people who lack family money.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Jasper, is there a middle path?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: A stipend would be a fairer compromise than a full guaranteed wage. A stipend eases the cost for interns without sinking small firms.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Guaranteeing pay is still workable, since a public subsidy could cover the cost of intern wages for small firms.

utterances.speaker: Amir

utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: This thread asks whether central banks should put employment before inflation when they set interest rates.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Inflation can become entrenched when demand remains excessive, while interest-rate rises can cause immediate job losses.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Because of that trade-off, central banks should prioritise employment over inflation when setting interest rates.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Since rate rises can cause immediate job losses, interest-rate decisions should give job losses more weight than temporary price rises.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: The same trade-off shows why an employment-first approach is preferable when central banks face a conflict between jobs and prices.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Because delaying action on inflation can allow it to become entrenched, inflation should remain the first priority even when unemployment is high.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: The possibility of immediate job losses is why central banks should avoid raising interest rates during periods of severe unemployment.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Keeping interest rates lower during a jobs crisis is justified. Employment should come before inflation in the central bank's interest-rate decisions.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Several members of this forum work in industries that depend heavily on consumer spending. Employment should come before inflation in the central bank's interest-rate decisions.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: The central bank is scheduled to publish its next rate decision on Thursday. The central bank should put protecting jobs ahead of controlling prices when the two goals conflict.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: In other words, my employment-first view, Seamus's formulation, and Fatima's formulation all say that central banks should prioritise employment over inflation when setting interest rates. That conclusion rejects the claim that inflation should remain the first priority even when unemployment is high.

spec.format: opinion essay by a single author
spec.topic: Should the death penalty be replaced with life imprisonment in every case?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The death penalty should be replaced with life imprisonment in every case. Execution can permanently punish an innocent person when a conviction is later shown to be mistaken, so this possibility is a strong reason for replacement.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Courts sometimes convict innocent defendants despite following established procedures. Because such mistakes occur, an irreversible sentence is unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Life imprisonment can protect the public by keeping dangerous offenders away from society. That protection is another reason to replace executions.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: New evidence can lead to a review or correction of a life sentence. Since a life sentence can be revisited in this way, it is less final than execution.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Death-penalty cases usually require more costly and lengthy legal procedures than life-imprisonment cases. That expense is an additional reason to abandon executions.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some victims' families regard execution as the only adequate form of finality. Their desire for finality deserves serious respect.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that concern overlooks an alternative: victims' families can obtain finality without an execution because life imprisonment permanently confines the offender. Because execution adds no necessary protection, this alternative supports replacement.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The proposed policy would use life imprisonment instead of execution for every offence currently carrying the death penalty. This is not a proposal to release offenders.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, life imprisonment can keep dangerous offenders away from the public for the rest of their lives.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The death penalty has not been shown to deter crime more effectively than life imprisonment. That evidence supports replacing it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The certainty of punishment matters more for deterrence than the maximum severity of punishment. Since life imprisonment can be imposed with certainty, it need not be weaker as a deterrent.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author keeps a notebook of sentencing decisions.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put briefly, the policy would abolish execution as a punishment and make life imprisonment the maximum sentence.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author has never attended an execution.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether members of the upper legislative chamber should be elected rather than appointed. Isaac, you support changing the system.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: I do: members of the upper legislative chamber should be elected rather than appointed, because elected members would be directly answerable to voters.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Election would also give citizens a direct say over the composition of the upper chamber, which is another reason to replace appointments.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: But election campaigns could make candidates dependent on wealthy donors. That financial dependence is a serious risk.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Voters could remove elected members who repeatedly ignored public concerns, so elections would create a real mechanism of accountability.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: The upper chamber would duplicate the lower chamber if its members were elected in the same way. It would then lose its distinct constitutional purpose.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Election campaigns would require candidates to state their positions publicly, and that would make the upper chamber's choices more transparent.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: The upper chamber should preserve a different method of selection from the lower chamber. For that reason, members should remain appointed.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Appointed members can examine legislation without constantly preparing for the next campaign, so members of the upper chamber should remain appointed.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So Isaac is arguing that elections would make upper-chamber members accountable to voters. Karima, does that settle the issue?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: No. Long, non-electoral terms allow upper-chamber members to consider consequences beyond the next election; appointed members can therefore take a long view of legislation.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: I once attended a public hearing of the upper chamber, and it was more technical than partisan.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Put another way, the appointed chamber can take a long view of legislation; because of that capacity, the upper chamber should retain appointed members so that long-term review remains possible.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Appointment gives the upper chamber greater continuity when governments change.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: In other words, appointment helps the upper chamber remain institutionally stable during changes of government.

spec.topic: Should long-term contractors receive the same benefits as permanent employees?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Long-term contractors should receive the same benefits as permanent employees. A contractor who has sat beside staff for three years does the same work, and that is the first reason.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a person's role in the team, not their paperwork, ought to decide their benefits package.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some will object that it would cost firms far more than they save by using contractors, but that overlooks what the arrangement is for.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My own firm has employed contractors since 2015.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Contract status is often just a device for avoiding the cost of sick leave and pensions, and that is a further reason to equalise benefits.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Firms in surveys name lower labour costs as their main reason for using contractors, which shows the device is deliberate.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, contracts are used as a cheaper substitute for employment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Contractors also lose out on parental leave when a baby arrives, so that gap is another reason to equalise benefits.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Pension rules differ from country to country.

spec.topic: Should employers consider criminal convictions only when directly relevant to the role?

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether employers should consider criminal convictions only when those convictions are directly relevant to the role. Leopold, you support that approach?

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I do. Employers should consider a criminal conviction only when the conviction is directly relevant to the duties of the role.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Because employers would use that rule, considering convictions only when they are directly relevant gives employers a consistent standard for assessing applicants.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Because the rule limits attention to direct relevance, considering convictions only when they are directly relevant reduces arbitrary exclusion from employment.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Can you give us a concrete example?

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Because the proposed rule focuses on direct relevance, embezzlement is relevant to a finance role.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Considering a conviction only when it is directly relevant lets employers explain hiring decisions more clearly, because they can point to the duties that created the concern.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Yara, what is the strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Some serious convictions should be considered even when the convictions are unrelated to the duties of the role. That conflicts with Leopold's rule.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Marisol, is relevance enough on its own?

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: A direct-relevance test is sufficient for deciding whether employers should consider criminal convictions.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Because a direct-relevance test is sufficient, employers can distinguish job-related risk from broad moral judgment.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Because a direct-relevance test is sufficient, a conviction for falsifying safety records can be considered for a safety-inspector role.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying employers need a direct-relevance test instead of a broader system for considering conviction information.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: However, a direct-relevance test is not sufficient because rehabilitation and the age of a conviction also matter.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Because a direct-relevance test is sufficient, employers can reject broad character judgments about applicants.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I served on a hiring panel last year, and the cases were more complicated than this debate suggests.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Let us turn to transparency. Yara, what should an applicant be told?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Employers should explain to applicants how a conviction affected a hiring decision.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Because employers should explain their decisions, applicants can identify factual errors in conviction records.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Because employers should explain their decisions, hiring processes become more accountable.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: In other words, applicants deserve a clear explanation of how a conviction affected an employer's hiring decision.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: To put Yara's point plainly, employers should tell applicants how conviction information influenced the hiring decision.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: That means employers must say how conviction information changed the hiring decision.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Both sides agree that employers need a principled process, even though they disagree about how narrowly relevance should be defined.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: The decision should focus on the role rather than on a permanent judgment about the person.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: The studio audience has been unusually quiet during the debate.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: That is all we have time for. Thank you to all three panelists.

spec.topic: Should recruitment software be prohibited from rejecting applicants without human review?

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether recruitment software should be prohibited from rejecting applicants without human review. Beatriz, you support the prohibition.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: The recruitment software rejects applicants without human review, and we should prohibit that because my internal audit found that 18 percent of applicants rejected by the software later met the basic qualifications.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Automated screening can rank routine applications in seconds. That efficiency matters when employers receive thousands of applications.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Applicants deserve to know which criteria a recruitment system uses. Transparency is a separate issue from the speed of hiring.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: A human reviewer can catch an erroneous rejection before it reaches an applicant. Because the software can reject without review and because a human can catch such errors, recruitment software should be prohibited from rejecting applicants without human review.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Requiring human review of every rejection would slow hiring sharply because automated screening can rank routine applications in seconds. But that delay does not overturn the proposed prohibition.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So Beatriz is saying that the software makes final rejection decisions without a person checking them. Is that the concern you want the panel to address?

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, a person reviewing an application can identify a rejection that the software got wrong.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: For a workable safeguard, human review should focus first on applications that the software marks as borderline.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Put another way, reviewers should examine borderline applications flagged by the software before other applications.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: The final recruitment policy should be published in plain language.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The panel has identified both the risk of unreviewed rejection and the concern about delay. We will now take questions from the audience.

utterances.speaker: Jolene

utterances.speaker: Chidi

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Anonymised totals cannot be traced back to one person, which is why that works. In other words, aggregate figures stay and only individual tracking goes.

utterances.speaker: Chidi

utterances.speaker: Adrian

utterances.text: Gwen, you work on this locally.

utterances.text: I sit on the planning committee. Permeable surfaces let rain soak into the ground where it falls, which is why the runoff drops.

utterances.speaker: Gwen

utterances.speaker: Milos

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: The reason is a survey of eleven towns, which found that flood reports fell by a third after the rule.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: So, in other words, the rule works in practice.

utterances.speaker: Milos

utterances.speaker: Sipho

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take your calls after the break.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo

utterances.speaker: Karima

utterances.speaker: Pradeep

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Lorenzo, in other words, you are saying that athlete protests can turn a shared celebration into a political confrontation.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: A rule allowing a brief peaceful statement during a medal ceremony can be applied consistently. Because the rule can be applied consistently, it would reduce arbitrary punishment of athletes.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Therefore, the committee should adopt a rule permitting athletes to make a ten-second peaceful statement during medal ceremonies. We will put that proposal to a vote.

utterances.text: Siobhan's proposal is that councils should make a developer contribution a condition of planning approval.

utterances.speaker: Theo

utterances.text: We have heard the case for the condition and the concern about its effect on smaller developments.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should stadiums prohibit alcohol sales during youth and family fixtures? Maeve, you start.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Stadiums should prohibit alcohol sales at youth and family fixtures, because children should not be exposed to heavy adult drinking.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: They copy the adults around them, which is why it matters. My nephew plays for an under-twelves team, so I see this every weekend.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jin, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: A ban would push drinking into car parks and nearby pubs, since drinking outside the ground is far less supervised than drinking inside it.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: In other words, Jin, you are saying a ban just moves the problem outside the stadium.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Exactly, and inside is safer because licensed stadium bars have trained staff who refuse to serve drunk people.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: But incident reports at family fixtures peak in the hour after the bars close, so inside is no safer. That is another reason to prohibit sales.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: I would go for a middle route: a zoned, alcohol-free family stand would protect children without a ban. Three clubs that introduced one saw complaints fall.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Birgit, put another way, separating families from drinkers is enough?

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Seventy percent of surveyed parents want to be able to buy a drink at matches, so a ban would be unpopular.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: So what you mean, Jin, is that parents would resent a ban.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: That unpopularity is why a ban would be widely ignored.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Stewards are already stretched thin, which is another reason.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Stewards at family fixtures report abuse from drunk adults more than at any other match, which is another reason to prohibit sales.

utterances.speaker: Jin

spec.topic: Should former ministers face a two-year ban on lobbying their previous departments?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether former ministers should face a two-year ban on lobbying their previous departments. Arjun, could you start us off?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Former ministers should face a two-year ban on lobbying their previous departments. A cooling-off period would reduce the former ministers' immediate influence over their previous departments, which is why I support the ban.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: I disagree. A two-year ban would unfairly prevent former ministers from offering legitimate expertise to their previous departments.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: For clarity, the proposed ban would cover only lobbying former ministers' previous departments.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Former ministers retain personal contacts in their previous departments. Because of those contacts, former ministers can obtain privileged access to their previous departments.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: So you are saying that former ministers' personal contacts can give them privileged access to their previous departments.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: A two-year interval would give departments time to make decisions without former ministers' direct lobbying, and that is another reason to adopt the ban.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Public confidence would improve if former ministers had to wait two years before lobbying their previous departments; that supports the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Keiko

utterances.speaker: Pablo

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should repeat-offender laws impose substantially longer sentences for a third conviction? Felix, you start.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Yes, a third conviction should carry a substantially longer sentence, because a small number of repeat offenders commit a large share of serious crime.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Margit, your response?

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: But that ignores how crime works: longer sentences would not deter anyone, since offenders rarely weigh sentence length beforehand.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Margit, you are saying that longer sentences would simply fail to deter.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: Exactly. Incidentally, the studio air conditioning is broken again.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Deterrence is not the point; longer sentences protect the public through incapacitation, since a person in prison cannot offend against the public. That is another reason for lengthening the third-conviction term.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Long sentences keep ageing inmates locked up after they stop being a danger, because most repeat offenders are over forty by their third conviction.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: So you are saying that the late years of such a sentence protect nobody.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Yes. I should add that I testified before the legislature on this last year.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: That is another reason the policy fails to deliver: states with three-strike laws saw no fall in violent crime, which shows that longer terms do not deter.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
