utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether public healthcare should cover cosmetic procedures that significantly improve a person's ability to work. Pradeep, you support coverage.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Reconstructive hand procedures can restore a patient's grip after an accident. Because restored grip can make employment possible again, public healthcare should cover cosmetic procedures that improve a patient's ability to work.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: But coverage should be limited to cosmetic procedures that significantly improve a patient's ability to work; a smaller benefit should not qualify.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: In other words, public healthcare should pay for cosmetic procedures when those procedures improve a patient's ability to work.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: So you are saying that your proposal is to cover cosmetic procedures that improve a patient's ability to work.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Fairness is an important consideration in deciding which healthcare services the public should fund.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Untreated visible physical differences can prevent a person from getting or keeping a job. Occupational specialists can assess whether a proposed procedure would significantly improve a patient's ability to work.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Put another way, some cosmetic conditions can prevent a person from working or finding employment.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: The national health service publishes its annual budget in March.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: A workplace-medicine review found that patients returned to work sooner after eligible procedures. Occupational specialists can assess whether a proposed procedure would significantly improve a patient's ability to work.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: I support coverage only under a significant-work-benefit test. utterances.text: I think election administrators should be appointed through nonpartisan public-service competitions. Appointments made by elected officials tie administrators' careers to the officials who chose them.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Agreed, and that is the key point, since administrators whose careers depend on partisan patrons cannot be trusted to run elections impartially.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: But competitive exams would shut out capable people who lack a polished academic background.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: I'd say that is because exams test the ability to take tests, not the ability to run elections.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: For what it's worth, I have worked as a poll clerk in two counties.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Competitions could include practical simulations of running a polling place, not only written exams.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: So you are saying the competition should assess practical election skills as well as test-taking.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Off topic, but the county I live in has had three different election chiefs in six years.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put another way, public-service competitions would make the selection of administrators fairer than appointment by officials.

spec.topic: Should companies be legally responsible for unpaid wages owed by labour agencies they hire?

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Our question is whether companies should be legally responsible for unpaid wages owed by labour agencies they hire. Gareth, make the case for responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Agency workers can lose earned wages when a labour agency becomes insolvent. Because that loss falls on vulnerable workers, companies that hire labour agencies should be legally responsible for the unpaid wages.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Because companies would face that responsibility, they would have an incentive to vet labour agencies more carefully.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: So you are saying that hiring companies should bear legal responsibility when the labour agencies they use fail to pay workers?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Yes. That incentive matters because companies would have reason to audit agency payment records when careful vetting affected them financially.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: This monitoring would deter labour agencies from deliberately underpaying workers.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: In other words, a wage-liability rule would discourage labour agencies from deliberately withholding workers' pay.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Agency workers often move between several short-term contracts during one year.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: But holding hiring companies responsible would be unfair because those companies do not control agency payroll systems.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: That deterrent effect would lead hiring companies to demand proof of wage payments from their agencies.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: They could identify unpaid wages before renewing an agency contract because payment records would expose the problem.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So Jelena's point is that hiring companies could check whether an agency had failed to pay workers before extending that agency's contract.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Some small companies have only one employee handling their payroll administration. Ifeoma, can the law still be made workable?

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Yes. Since hiring companies could identify unpaid wages before renewing contracts, a statutory liability rule could be limited to wages that a hiring company could reasonably verify.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: That limit would make a hiring company's potential cost predictable.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Put differently, a hiring company could predict its financial exposure if the law covered only wages it could reasonably verify.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: The proposed limit would make wage liability a foreseeable business cost rather than an unlimited risk.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: The debate has addressed worker protection, fairness and the possible limits of liability. Gareth, give us the final recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Because the potential cost would be predictable, Parliament should make companies legally responsible for unpaid wages owed by the labour agencies they hire.

spec.topic: Should people tell neighbours before holding a large gathering at home?

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether people should tell neighbours before holding a large gathering at home. Pradeep, you support that idea?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Yes, people should tell their neighbours before holding a large gathering at home, because large gatherings can create noise and parking pressure for neighbours.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Neighbours need advance warning when a gathering may disrupt sleep, so I understand the case for notice. But a notice can feel like a demand for permission rather than a courtesy.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Advance notice gives neighbours time to raise practical concerns. They can request a quieter finish before the gathering begins.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Advance notice also lets neighbours rearrange childcare or work shifts, which supports the point that they need warning. Hosts should state an expected end time in the notice.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: A stated end time makes advance notice useful. Hosts should also cap the number of guests at a large gathering, because that makes the disturbance more manageable.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Still, I would not impose the same rule on every event: a blanket notification rule would burden people holding small family dinners.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So your objection is that the rule should not apply to every kind of gathering?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Exactly. The host should set a guest limit for a large gathering. For context, I once hosted a birthday lunch for twelve people.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A text message is sufficient for notifying neighbours about a gathering, because a text message is quick and leaves the gathering details in writing.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Our building has a shared courtyard behind the kitchens, so sound carries differently from room to room.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So Pradeep's proposal is that hosts should give neighbours advance warning of a large gathering?

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: In other words, the guest limit is part of the proposed approach to responsible hosting.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Put another way, an end time makes the advance notice worthwhile.

spec.topic: Should businesses appoint a senior manager specifically responsible for accessibility?

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Businesses should appoint a senior manager responsible for accessibility, because without a named senior owner nobody owns the problem.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: But a dedicated manager lets everyone else treat accessibility as someone else's problem. Mine is a twelve-person firm, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: So you are saying staff would stop caring once there is a manager. Still, a senior person with budget authority can make every team fix problems, which is a reason to appoint one.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: A small firm cannot afford a salaried accessibility manager, since the pay would swallow a big share of its budget.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Part of someone's time is enough, so the role can go to an existing senior person, and that is one more reason firms should appoint one.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: So you are saying a small firm just adds a title to someone's job. That person would be too busy to do it properly.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Why would they be too busy?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Because part-time owners rarely deliver on extra duties.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Not quite: measurable targets set by the board protect the time the role needs, so a small firm can run it that way.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Fine. What would the manager actually report on?

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Complaints data would give clear priorities, since complaints show where real people are blocked.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: In other words, the work would be driven by where customers hit barriers.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Exactly. I chaired a similar working group at my last job.

utterances.text: Welcome. Should local authorities impose noise limits on outdoor home-improvement work during weekends? Darius, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Outdoor home-improvement noise wakes residents on weekend mornings.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Weekend mornings are the only time my family cooks breakfast together.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: For that reason, local authorities should impose a noise limit on outdoor home-improvement work before 10 a.m. on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Matteo

utterances.speaker: Carmen

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Most indoor sanding and drilling can be done after 10 a.m. on Saturdays, so the proposed limit remains practical.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Infants and night-shift workers need quiet weekend mornings; that is another reason to adopt the proposed limit.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: A complaint-based noise rule could be enforced through residents' timestamped recordings, which shows that the proposed limit would be workable.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: In other words, Darius's position is that local authorities should impose a noise limit on outdoor home-improvement work before 10 a.m. on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Residents can report noise violations through the council website. Because that channel is already available, the council should publish a simple procedure for enforcing weekend noise limits.

utterances.speaker: Cillian

utterances.speaker: Cillian

utterances.text: Schools should provide artificial-intelligence tutors as substitutes for some classroom instruction. I say this because such tutors can adapt practice exercises to each student's level.

utterances.speaker: Meera

utterances.speaker: Bongani

utterances.speaker: Zofia

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether witnesses should be allowed to give evidence anonymously in gang-related prosecutions. Cillian, why do you support that approach?

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Gang members can threaten or harm witnesses who testify against them, because some witnesses may refuse to testify when their identities are revealed.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Since allowing witnesses to testify anonymously can secure evidence that would otherwise be lost, the courts should not dismiss that evidence automatically.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: That is why courts should allow anonymous evidence in serious gang-related prosecutions when judges impose safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Anonymity can prevent the defence from probing a witness's possible bias and connections. Because of that problem, anonymous evidence should never be admitted in a criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: So you are saying that anonymity can prevent the defence from investigating a witness's possible bias and connections. For that reason, anonymous evidence should be excluded from criminal prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Cillian, is judicial supervision enough to protect defendants?

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: I have worked as a criminal barrister for twelve years, and I have seen how fear can silence a witness.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Thank you both. The next televised debate will examine protections for jurors.

spec.topic: Should governments ban employers from requiring workers to repay training costs after resigning?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Governments should ban employers from requiring workers to repay training costs after resigning.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Workers can face repayment demands worth thousands of pounds when they leave a job. Those large demands deter workers from changing employers, because leaving becomes a financial risk.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many workplace training courses now include online modules and recorded lessons.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics object that employers should be entitled to recover training costs when workers leave soon after expensive training.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That concern does not justify repayment clauses, because employers can treat training as part of compensation and recruitment rather than as a debt imposed on departing workers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, a ban would mean that employers could not make workers repay training costs after resignation.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The policy remains workable because employers can protect themselves through reasonable probation periods and retention incentives.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A reasonable probation period allows an employer to recover value from training before confirming a permanent appointment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, probation gives employers time to obtain value from the training they provide.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author once completed a workplace course during a quiet week in February.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public subsidies can help small employers provide training without imposing repayment clauses.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is to say, public funding can replace repayment demands as support for small employers' training programmes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Portable training makes it easier for workers to move between employers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because trained workers can move freely, employers can compete for them through better pay and working conditions. That is why banning repayment demands is preferable to binding workers to an employer through debt.

spec.topic: Should small businesses accept late-payment penalties as a standard clause in every customer contract?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should a late-payment penalty be a standard clause in every small-business contract?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Yes, but it should be clearly drafted and include a reasonable grace period. A standard clause gives small businesses a consistent starting point.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Because the clause is used consistently, customers receive advance notice of the financial consequences of paying late.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: The standard wording is also useful because it makes the business's payment expectations easier to explain and administer.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: It improves predictability in enforcement, because everyone can see in advance what happens when an invoice is overdue.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What safeguards would you put around that standard wording?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: The penalty must be proportionate and must not apply during a reasonable grace period. That is important because a proportionate charge protects the business without turning an ordinary delay into a punitive dispute.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: The grace period is another reason for the approach: it gives customers time to correct a minor administrative mistake before any charge is imposed.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: The contract should explain exactly when the penalty starts and how the amount is calculated. Clear timing and calculation are essential because customers should not have to guess what they owe.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that the clause gives customers advance warning about the cost of late payment?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: In other words, customers should know about the late-payment charge before they sign the contract.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And the standard wording makes the payment rules straightforward to communicate?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Put another way, the same payment expectation can be explained to every customer.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could the clause damage an important customer relationship?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: A penalty clause can alienate a valuable customer who experiences an exceptional cash-flow problem, but that objection overlooks the grace period and the requirement that the penalty be proportionate.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: I keep a paper copy of my preferred contract template beside my computer. Some small businesses review their customer contracts at the end of each financial year.

spec.topic: Should cities charge higher waste-collection fees to households that produce more rubbish?

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Cities should charge higher waste-collection fees to households that produce more rubbish, because those households create greater collection and disposal costs.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: I oppose that policy for a fairness reason: higher rubbish-producing households, including large families, could face a disproportionate financial burden. Since greater rubbish creates greater costs, that burden is a real concern.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Cities can measure each household's rubbish by weighing bins or counting official waste bags. In other words, household rubbish can be measured through bin weights or official bag counts.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Because those measurements would be reliable, variable waste-collection fees would be practical. A practical variable fee would then give households a financial reason to reduce their rubbish.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: So you are saying that a variable fee would financially encourage households to produce less rubbish.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Exactly; reducing household rubbish would lower collection and disposal costs, because fewer discarded materials would need to be handled.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: That potential burden is why cities should give every household a free basic waste allowance before charging higher fees. The allowance would protect households with limited incomes from excessive charges.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Put another way, every household should receive some rubbish disposal without an extra charge.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: The savings from reducing rubbish could also fund reuse and repair facilities. Cities could use those savings to expand such facilities.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: In other words, savings from producing less rubbish could finance larger city reuse and repair programmes.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Because better reuse and repair facilities would give residents alternatives to throwing things away, they would make higher waste-collection fees more acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: So your point is that expanded reuse and repair facilities could make variable rubbish fees easier for residents to accept.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: I will be away from the forum next weekend.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: The forum's mobile application received a new colour scheme this month.

utterances.text: Should expert witnesses be paid by the court rather than by the party calling them?

utterances.text: The court should pay expert witnesses rather than the parties that call them, because payment by a party can create perceived pressure on an expert witness.

utterances.text: Why is that pressure a serious concern?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Party-paid experts can be chosen for conclusions that suit the paying side. That is the reason party payment creates perceived pressure, and that is why the court should pay experts.

utterances.text: Critics say court funding would solve one problem without guaranteeing neutral evidence.

utterances.text: But court payment would not guarantee impartial expert evidence. A published fee schedule would make court payment predictable, which is another reason to adopt court payment.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How could the system reduce the risk of official favoritism?

utterances.speaker: Keiko

utterances.text: Should governments require large farms to maintain uncultivated strips beside streams? Yusuf, what is your view?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What evidence makes that requirement necessary?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Streams beside large farms currently receive excess nutrients from agricultural fields. That is why voluntary measures have not been enough.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say the rule would impose costs on farmers. How do you answer them?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Requiring uncultivated strips would reduce the amount of land available for large farms to cultivate. I still support the rule, because compensation for the lost land would make the requirement fair to large farms.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would enforcing the rule require new technology?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Most large farms already use GPS systems to map their fields.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Because most large farms already use GPS systems, large farms could mark the required streamside strips without buying new mapping systems.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are proposing that governments require large farms to leave uncultivated strips beside streams?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf

utterances.speaker: Yusuf

utterances.speaker: Yusuf

utterances.speaker: Yusuf

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Uncultivated strips would provide habitat for pollinators and increase visits to flowering crops.

utterances.text: The agenda asks whether software companies should face a fixed legal deadline for notifying customers about known security vulnerabilities. Efua, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Known vulnerabilities can be exploited while customers wait for voluntary notice. Because of that risk, the law should require companies to notify affected customers within thirty days of confirming a known vulnerability.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: In other words, companies should have a legal thirty-day deadline for notifying affected customers about confirmed vulnerabilities.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Before we continue, the catering invoice is awaiting approval.

utterances.text: Verifying a suspected vulnerability can take several weeks. Because verification takes that long, the law should allow companies thirty days to notify affected customers after confirming a vulnerability.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Rushed verification can produce false alarms; that is another reason for allowing a defined reporting period.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Customers cannot patch or isolate affected systems until they receive credible details about a vulnerability. Therefore, prompt disclosure lets customers begin mitigating the vulnerability.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: For the same reason, customers should receive notice before a company makes a vulnerability public.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Put another way, rushed verification can produce false alarms. That is why a thirty-day maximum balances verification time with prompt warning.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Amir, do you see any danger in the proposed deadline?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Yes. But a thirty-day legal deadline could force companies to disclose inaccurate information.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: We will record that objection and ask the group to consider whether the rule needs an exception for emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: That concludes this item.

spec.topic: Should public officials be required to publish their calendars and gifts received?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public officials should be required to publish their calendars and the gifts they receive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Access to an official is a form of power, because whoever gets the meeting gets to shape the decision. That is why calendars belong in public.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I wrote this essay in the week the ethics bill was tabled.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Gifts are a quieter channel of influence than meetings, which is another reason the rule should cover them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Even a small present creates a sense of obligation in whoever accepts it, and that is why gifts count as influence. In other words, a present is a favour paid in advance.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics fear that published calendars will make people less frank when they meet officials.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But the entries need list only names and dates, not what was said.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Several governments already publish their ministers' diaries, which shows that publishing is workable, one more reason to adopt the rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Voters cannot hold anyone to account for influence they cannot see; for that reason alone the duty should be law.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put differently, hidden influence is influence that nobody can vote against.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The state ethics commission, for what it is worth, has only five members.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Compliance would take officials little effort, because a threshold of fifty pounds would keep trivial gifts off the register.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Most officials already keep electronic diaries, which is a second reason compliance would be easy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, the public is entitled to know whom officials meet and what they accept.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Exactly. In other words, a total ban is unnecessary for informed adults; that position conflicts with banning every loot box.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: I prefer playing single-player games at weekends.

utterances.speaker: Gideon

spec.topic: Should subscription services be required to let customers cancel with a single click?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: A lengthy cancellation process causes some customers to give up before ending their subscriptions. Because of that, subscription services should be required to let customers cancel with a single click.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: I am not convinced that a legal requirement is necessary. What benefits would the rule provide?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Because customers sometimes abandon difficult cancellations, a single-click requirement would reduce the number of customers who give up.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: That same abandonment problem is why subscription services would have less opportunity to keep customers subscribed through unnecessary obstacles. For that reason, customers would also receive a clearer and more consistent cancellation experience.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Because the current process can make cancellation difficult, a single-click rule would make it easier for customers to compare cancellation policies across services.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: The abandonment risk is also a reason to expect the rule to reduce the time customers spend searching for a cancellation option.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Since a lengthy process discourages some customers, a common cancellation standard would make subscription contracts more understandable.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Here is my concern: a single-click rule would cancel a subscription immediately even when the customer still owed a bill.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: No, the rule would not erase legitimate payment obligations; it would only stop future renewal. In other words, the rule would stop future billing without cancelling an outstanding debt.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: I can accept that identity checks may be required before the final cancellation action.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: So you are saying the proposal can require identity checks but must make the final cancellation action a single click.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: I usually read subscription terms on my phone.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: My broadband plan renews on the first day of each month.

spec.topic: Should nurses be allowed to diagnose and prescribe independently for common conditions without physician sign-off?

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Item two: whether nurses should diagnose and prescribe for common conditions without a physician signing off. Hollis, you start.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Nurses should be allowed to diagnose and prescribe independently for common conditions, because the wait for a minor-illness appointment at our clinic is nine days.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: The reason is also that sign-off is nearly always a rubber stamp for our nurse practitioners, and it adds a day or more to each prescription.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: But a nurse working alone could miss a rare cause of chest pain, since nurses complete far fewer diagnostic training hours than physicians.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying the training gap makes unsupervised diagnosis risky.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Our nurse practitioners hold master's degrees, so they can be trusted with common conditions, and that is exactly why independent prescribing is justified.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Exactly the risk I mean, and the cause is that without a second check, antibiotics get overprescribed under pressure from patients.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: So what you mean is that nurses would overprescribe antibiotics.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: The pilot ward data cut against that, and it supports letting nurses prescribe on their own: nurse antibiotic rates matched physician rates.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Put another way, you are saying nurses and doctors prescribe antibiotics at the same rate.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: A compromise: nurses prescribe only from a fixed formulary of common drugs.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So the idea is that independence would be limited to a fixed list of drugs.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: That would work for us, since common conditions need only around forty drugs.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Noted for the record: the pharmacy contract renews in March.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: I could accept it, as a fixed list limits the harm a missed diagnosis can do.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: In other words, a short list caps the damage of any error.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Unrelated, but my clinic opens at seven in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Naveen

utterances.speaker: Hollis

utterances.speaker: Hollis

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Physicians would be freed for complex cases, and that would shorten the overall waiting list.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Put another way, independent prescribing would shorten the waiting list for minor ailments.

utterances.speaker: Soren

spec.topic: Should research grants be awarded partly by lottery among proposals that meet a quality threshold?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether research grants should be awarded partly by lottery among proposals that meet a quality threshold. Efua, you support the idea.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Research grants should be awarded by lottery among proposals that meet a quality threshold. The reason is that a quality threshold excludes proposals with fatal methodological flaws.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: In other words, expert screening can exclude proposals with fatal methodological flaws. Since panels can do that reliably, a lottery could still fund weaker proposals than a system based on panel rankings.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Established institutions receive higher scores from grant panels. Because of that, a lottery reduces the influence of institutional prestige on grant awards.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Screening can reject unsound proposals before those proposals enter the lottery, which is why I think the proposal is safe enough to test.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So you are saying the lottery would operate only among proposals that expert reviewers have screened.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: A pilot found that reviewers rejected nearly all applications with fatal flaws.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: That result shows that expert screening can identify proposals with fatal flaws.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Put another way, the lottery would be a post-screening way to reduce prestige bias.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru

utterances.text: Research panels can identify proposals that meet a basic scientific quality standard. Because that threshold protects the grant pool from proposals that fail the basic standard, it is a sensible first filter.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Clement, how would the lottery operate after that filter?

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Because panels can identify qualifying proposals, a lottery can be restricted to proposals that meet the quality threshold. A restricted lottery would give equally qualified applicants a more even chance.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: In other words, the lottery would give proposals that pass the threshold an equal chance of receiving a grant. That could reduce the influence of individual panel preferences.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Soren, what is the strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Soren

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Therefore, a thresholded lottery would preserve expert screening while sharing final selection among qualifying proposals.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Put another way, panels would decide who enters the draw rather than who receives every grant.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed system would preserve the quality gate while randomizing final selection among qualifying proposals. utterances.speaker: Efua

spec.topic: Should hospitals be required to staff wards to a legally fixed nurse-to-patient ratio?

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should hospitals be required by law to staff wards to a fixed nurse-to-patient ratio? Agnieszka, you start.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Yes, they should. Each extra patient per nurse raises the risk of death after surgery, which is why the law has to set a ratio.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: But a single fixed number is far too blunt, since a ward of stable patients needs far fewer nurses than an intensive care unit.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Yara, you run a ward. What do you see?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I have run a surgical ward for nine years, and last year it lost eleven nurses to exhaustion, which is a reason to put a legal minimum in place.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Rural hospitals already cannot recruit enough nurses, so a legal ratio would force them to close beds.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: So, Eamon, you are saying a ratio law would leave rural areas with fewer hospital beds.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Exactly. And the regional health board still has not published its vacancy figures.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: The law can give rural hospitals a phased timetable, so it need not close a single bed overnight.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Nurses leave because of pay, not because of ratios, so a ratio law would not fix retention.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: In other words, you think a ratio law would not keep nurses in their jobs. Yet turnover fell in California after its ratio law passed, which is another reason to back one.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Bruno, is that one number cannot suit every ward.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Yes, since a ratio set for cardiac wards would be wasteful on a day-surgery unit.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: A legal ratio would also protect nurses from being blamed when a ward is short-staffed, and that is one more reason to legislate.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Put simply, Yara, a ratio would shield nurses from blame for shortages. We have to leave it there.

spec.topic: Should local governments offer tax discounts to businesses that occupy long-vacant premises?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Local governments should offer tax discounts to businesses that occupy long-vacant premises, because a shop that stays empty for years drags down the footfall of every neighbouring business.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, on a street with empty units the neighbours lose customers and some of them close.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is why filling a vacant unit protects the businesses around it, and why it should be encouraged.

utterances.speaker: Author

spec.topic: Should statutes of limitations be abolished for all child sexual abuse offences?

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: The agenda asks whether statutes of limitations should be abolished for all child sexual abuse offences. Padraig, please outline the case for abolition.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Some survivors report child sexual abuse decades after it occurred. That delay is one reason I support abolition.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Because statutes of limitations can expire before survivors report child sexual abuse, the law can close the route to prosecution too early.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Since that deadline can close before disclosure, abolishing statutes of limitations would ensure that every survivor has a viable route to prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Trauma can delay disclosure of child sexual abuse for many years. Milos, how should the committee address the fairness concerns?

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Because trauma can delay disclosure for many years, some survivors report child sexual abuse decades after it occurred; in other words, the reporting delay can be extremely long.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: I oppose abolition for every offence. A universal abolition could make fair trials harder because evidence and memories deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: In other words, abolishing statutes of limitations for all child sexual abuse offences could make fair trials harder as evidence and memories deteriorate.

utterances.text: The meeting room has three large windows. We will record both the access-to-justice argument and the fair-trial objection.

spec.topic: Should students be allowed to graduate with unpaid library or accommodation debts?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universities should not withhold degrees over unpaid library fines, because the block is out of proportion to the sum owed.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The disproportion is plain, since a degree certifies three years of work.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Accommodation debt is a different matter from library fines, since it often runs to several thousand pounds.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I paid a six-pound library fine myself in my second year.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some say a degree block is the only lever a university has. But universities can recover debts through the ordinary civil courts.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That belief is partly there because courts are slow and costly for small sums. In other words, chasing a small debt in court costs more than it recovers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universities should offer payment plans instead of blocks, because a blocked graduate cannot easily take up work that needs the degree.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a degree block turns a debt into a barrier to earning.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Most graduation ceremonies at my university take place in July.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That barrier is real because a withheld certificate can cost a graduate a job offer, given that employers routinely ask for degree certificates.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Students should be told about their debts early, because early notice lets them settle what they owe in time.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, no student should learn of a fine on graduation day.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Our question is whether inheritance tax should be replaced with a tax on lifetime gifts received by each person. Adrian, you support the change?

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Inheritance tax should be replaced with a tax on lifetime gifts received by each person. I support that change because the proposed tax would use each recipient's total lifetime gifts as the tax base.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Inheritance tax currently raises substantial revenue from estates.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: But wealthy donors could avoid the proposed tax by giving assets away through complicated arrangements.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Adrian, how would your proposal work in practice?

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: The proposed system would tax the lifetime receipts of beneficiaries rather than the donor's estate at death. In other words, the proposed system would tax the lifetime receipts of beneficiaries rather than the donor's estate at death.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Recipients, rather than estates, would be responsible for paying the proposed tax. Because recipients would be responsible, people who receive illiquid assets could be forced to sell them to pay the proposed tax.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Because recipients, rather than estates, would be liable, the proposed tax would follow transferred wealth into the hands of beneficiaries.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: So you are saying that the people who receive lifetime gifts, rather than donors' estates, would be liable for the tax.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: A further advantage is that annual reporting would expose lifetime gifts before the donor's death. Since reports would arrive during donors' lives, earlier reporting could help the tax authority detect attempts to split gifts among nominees.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Because annual reports would arrive during donors' lives, the tax authority would receive information about taxable gifts earlier than it does under inheritance tax.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposed system would give the tax authority gift information during donors' lives instead of only after their deaths.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: My main practical concern is that family businesses could lack enough cash to pay a tax when ownership shares are gifted. That is why some family businesses might have to change their ownership structure to meet the tax bill.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: We have heard arguments about fairness, avoidance, administration, and the effect on family firms.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: I have not decided how I would vote on the proposal.

spec.topic: Should universities count public outreach, such as school talks, when deciding which scientists get promoted?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universities should count public outreach, including school talks, when deciding which scientists get promoted.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because of that policy, promotion panels would gain evidence about a scientist's ability to explain research to non-specialists.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The university's astronomy building has a glass roof.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since universities would count outreach, scientists would have a stronger incentive to spend time speaking with schools.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, universities should treat public outreach as a legitimate part of a scientist's promotion record.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That policy would make promotion decisions better reflect the range of work that academic scientists actually perform, because it would recognize outreach.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The campus radio station broadcasts at noon on weekdays.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, public engagement should be considered alongside research and teaching in promotion decisions.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because outreach would count in promotion, scientists could build more durable relationships with local schools.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This means that counting outreach would recognize communication with the public as part of academic work.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because the promotion criteria would include outreach, they would send students a broader message about what universities value.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, counting outreach in promotion could reward polished publicity instead of careful science.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, universities should include public outreach among the activities that can strengthen a scientist's case for promotion.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because outreach would count in promotion, outreach records could help committees identify scientists who contribute to the wider community.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because universities should count outreach, a university could require evidence of outreach quality rather than simply counting the number of public appearances.

spec.topic: Should convicted people be allowed to seek compensation automatically when their convictions are overturned?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should people whose convictions are overturned be allowed to seek compensation automatically?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: An overturned conviction is strong evidence that the state wrongly deprived someone of liberty. For that reason, people whose convictions are overturned should be allowed to seek compensation automatically.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why should access be automatic rather than dependent on a separate finding of official wrongdoing?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Automatic eligibility is important because applicants should not have to prove official fault before their compensation claims are reviewed. Removing that initial burden makes the compensation remedy accessible to more people.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics worry that this would make every overturned conviction an immediate compensation case.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: The objection is that automatic eligibility could compensate people whose convictions were overturned for technical reasons. The appellate court issued its decision in March.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does automatic access also mean that payment is guaranteed?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: No payment should be presumed merely from filing a claim. A compensation review panel should assess documented financial and personal loss.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, automatic eligibility means that every person with an overturned conviction may file a compensation claim without preliminary permission.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: A compensation review panel should assess documented financial and personal loss. The interview room has two microphones.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How would you prevent agencies from postponing these cases?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: The compensation process should start when the final order overturning a conviction is entered. A fixed starting point prevents disputes from delaying the compensation process.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would compensation serve a wider public purpose?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Public confidence falls when state errors leave wrongly convicted people to bear the costs. Compensation can restore public confidence by acknowledging the state's error.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the scheme expose the government to an unlimited number of claims?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: The pool of potential claimants would remain limited because only people whose convictions were actually overturned would qualify to use the scheme.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are proposing an automatic route into review, not an automatic award?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The proposal is automatic access to a compensation review after a conviction is overturned.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: An independent panel should review each compensation claim because government agencies should not decide their own liability.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, an independent body should assess the state's liability for an overturned conviction.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Parliament should create automatic eligibility to seek compensation after a conviction is overturned because an overturned conviction signals state error, removing the initial burden improves access, and independent review protects fairness.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Amateur citizen scientists should be allowed to run unsupervised biology experiments in community laboratories, since community laboratories already require every member to complete a safety course before getting a bench.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say that unsupervised amateurs could accidentally release dangerous organisms.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that ignores the fact that community laboratories only permit the lowest biosafety level of work, which uses harmless organisms such as baker's yeast and common soil bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason to allow unsupervised work is that constant supervision would make community laboratories too costly for most members.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Supervision is simply not necessary for harmless work. Put another way, insisting on supervision amounts to saying that only professionals may handle harmless work.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I joined my own community laboratory two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Community laboratories should keep an open logbook of every project.

spec.topic: Should athletes be allowed to challenge refereeing decisions personally rather than through team officials?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Athletes should not be allowed to challenge refereeing decisions personally; formal challenges should go through team officials.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Personal confrontations with referees lengthen stoppages in play, because players often argue emotionally rather than using a defined procedure.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Team officials can use established appeal procedures without surrounding the referee with players. That is why the officials-only route protects the flow of the match.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, a personal challenge can correct an obvious refereeing error before play continues.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Officials who understand the rules and communication protocols are better placed to present a precise appeal. Since that expertise reduces confusion, it is a further reason to keep formal challenges with team officials.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal keeps conversations about refereeing decisions between referees and designated team representatives.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Elite matches attract millions of viewers online.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many athletes practise set pieces every week.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: An appeal handled by a team official creates a record of the referee's decision and its basis. That is another reason to require athletes to use representatives.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A recorded appeal allows the league to review recurring refereeing errors after the match. This is also why personal challenges should not replace the official process.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, athletes should leave formal challenges to team officials rather than confronting referees themselves.

spec.topic: Should households keep a no-phones rule at the dinner table?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether households should keep a no-phones rule at the dinner table. Theo, you start.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Yes, households should keep a no-phones rule at dinner, because dinner is often the only time the whole family is together.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: But a blanket rule is unrealistic, since many parents need to be reachable for work in the evening.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Naveen, what does the evidence say?

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Children talk far more at meals when phones are put away, which matters because mealtime conversation is where they build much of their vocabulary. That is another reason to keep the rule.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: That ignores teenagers, though: a rule handed down to them only breeds resentment. My own family eats dinner at six sharp.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Bruno, you were nodding at that.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Teenagers hide phones in their laps under the table, which shows the rule breeds resentment.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Theo, can the rule survive work calls?

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: One parent's phone can sit on a shelf for emergencies, so the rule is perfectly workable.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: So, Theo, you are saying the rule can bend for emergencies without being abandoned.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Families should set their own exceptions, since every household's evenings are different.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: So you are saying, Emeka, that each family should write its own rules. Households with a rule also report calmer meals, which is one more reason to keep it.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Put another way, Theo, dinner is the family's single shared slot in the day.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: What you mean, Bruno, is that one single rule cannot fit every household.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: In other words, phones belong away from the dinner table. My own children are grown up and living away from home now.

spec.topic: Should lie-detector evidence be admissible in criminal trials?

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Lie-detector results should not be admissible in criminal trials. The main reason is that polygraph error rates are far too high.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: But a court can weigh unreliable evidence sensibly, since eyewitness testimony is often wrong and is still admitted.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Besides, jurors overweight anything that looks scientific, which is another reason to exclude it.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: In other words, you think jurors cannot be trusted with it.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Anxious innocent people often fail the test, and that is a reason to keep it out. I sat on a burglary jury once, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: I would allow it only if the defence consents, since defendants who want to clear their name should have a means to do so.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: So you are saying a defendant can volunteer for the test.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Exactly. Some jurisdictions already allow such stipulated tests, which shows it can work.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: But consent is not truly voluntary, because a defendant who refuses a test would look guilty.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: My cousin is a court clerk, and we have had this argument at dinner.

spec.topic: Should landlords be banned from raising rent more than once a year?

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should landlords be banned from raising rent more than once a year? Enzo, you start.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Landlords should be banned from raising rent more than once a year, because tenants cannot budget when their rent can change at any time.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Most wages are only reviewed once a year, which is exactly why tenants cannot plan around a second rise.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: But a limit on how often rent can rise would just make landlords impose bigger rises once a year.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: So you are saying landlords would front-load bigger rises into one annual increase. Separately, the housing minister is due to publish a rent review next month. Milos, you are a landlord.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: I own six flats myself. Since my insurance premium can jump at any point in the year, I would have to price that risk into one big annual rise.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Frequent rises also force families to move in the middle of the school year, which is another reason for the ban.

utterances.speaker: Kieran

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: But most family moves are caused by jobs, not by rent.

utterances.speaker: Olumide

utterances.speaker: Petra

utterances.speaker: Josefa

utterances.speaker: Ivana

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Many residents lack enough indoor space to dry clothes. That is why allowing outdoor washing would help residents who lack indoor drying space.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: The residents' association surveyed forty-two households about outdoor washing. The survey supports a limited approach because most households in it supported limited permission for outdoor washing.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: The neighbourhood's written rule bans washing that is visible from public paths. Since the rule identifies the prohibited visibility, the committee can explain and enforce a rule consistently.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: A six-month pilot would reveal whether allowing outdoor washing increases complaints. For that reason, the committee should test limited outdoor washing for six months.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Separately, the caretaker repainted the laundry-room door on Monday.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: The next committee meeting is scheduled for 14 June.

utterances.speaker: Josefa

utterances.speaker: Ivana

spec.topic: Should supermarkets be banned from selling cut flowers flown in from overseas?

utterances.text: Welcome to the programme. Fatima, should supermarkets be banned from selling cut flowers flown in from overseas?

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, supermarkets should be banned from selling them, because a flown-in bouquet has a carbon footprint many times that of a locally grown one.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Imported stems arrive at prices local growers cannot match. That is why local growers are going out of business, which is another reason for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: So what you mean is that local flower growers are going out of business.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes. Overseas farms also use pesticides banned in Europe, which is a third reason for a ban, since workers on some of them have suffered poisoning.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: But a ban would destroy jobs in Kenya, because Kenyan flower farms employ around ninety thousand people.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: So, Odette, you are saying a ban would take away livelihoods abroad.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Put another way, the flower trade is a lifeline for those households. Incidentally, the Aalsmeer flower auction opened in 1912.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Clear carbon labels would be a better policy than a ban, since labels have already changed what shoppers buy when it comes to eggs.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: So you are saying the shopper, not the law, should decide.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: That is what I mean, because labels let shoppers choose while Kenyan jobs stay in place. I bought tulips from a supermarket yesterday, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: A ban would also push supermarkets to buy from local growers, which is one more reason for it.

utterances.speaker: Odette

utterances.text: Because uninterrupted recovery reduces burnout, lower employee burnout improves staff retention.

utterances.text: To put Alina's point another way, retaining experienced staff benefits businesses.

spec.topic: Should heads of government be limited to a maximum of two terms in office?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I think heads of government should be limited to a maximum of two terms. A government needs enough time to work, but unlimited re-election invites leaders to treat office as a permanent possession.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: I am not convinced. Term limits encourage leadership renewal, but they can also remove an effective leader simply because the calendar says so.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: That is a fair concern, but the accountability gained from a two-term limit outweighs the loss of an occasionally capable long-serving leader. This is also why I disagree with the claim that leadership renewal is automatically a sufficient argument against limits.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: The strongest reason for a cap is that a fixed maximum prevents a head of government from using public resources to build an unfair electoral advantage.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Regularly changing leaders gives governing parties an incentive to develop successors, which is another reason to support a maximum of two terms. My local football club has changed its manager three times this season.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: A two-term maximum makes political power less dependent on one individual's personal network, so it supports the limit.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Voters are not powerless under this rule: they can still reward a successful government by choosing its party's next candidate. That is why I do not see term limits as an attack on electoral choice.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: A term limit creates a predictable transfer of power instead of leaving succession to a sudden crisis. For the record, Imogen prefers reading printed newspapers to reading news on a phone.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: So you are saying that term limits encourage leadership renewal. That point supports the two-term proposal.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: In other words, a two-term cap is a rule that prevents any head of government from becoming electorally permanent.

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Education campaigns teach households to plan portions. Because that planning prevents unnecessary purchases, portion planning reduces avoidable household food waste.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: That is why education campaigns reduce household food waste: they give families a practical way to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that education campaigns reduce household food waste. That position challenges the proposal to use fines instead.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Fines make households pay attention to household waste rules. Since ignoring those rules can cost money, fines prompt households to change their waste habits quickly.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: That quick change is why local authorities should use fines rather than education campaigns to reduce household food waste.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Council inspectors can record repeated overfilled household bins. Those records allow consistent enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Because repeated-bin records make enforcement consistent, local authorities can enforce food-waste fines consistently.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, does that approach depend on new technology? The council's annual waste report is due in July.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: In other words, Dalia's position is that education campaigns help households reduce food waste. I am not convinced that a fine teaches anyone what to do differently.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Joaquin, your response.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

utterances.text: I do. A hereditary monarch lacks a democratic mandate, and citizens deserve a direct choice of their head of state.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: My concern is that a directly elected head could turn a ceremonial office into a partisan contest. Legislators can instead choose someone who remains above party competition.

utterances.speaker: Jin

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Cillian, what is your answer to the concern about party politics?

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: For the record, I keep a handwritten list of constitutional books.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Because a hereditary monarch lacks a democratic mandate, the head of state should be directly elected.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: A fixed term would give a directly elected head institutional continuity; that is why direct election is workable.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: A direct election would make the head accountable to voters because voters could remove a poor head of state at the next election.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that Cillian's case is that the head of state should be directly elected?

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Choosing the head through the legislature is preferable to direct election because legislators can choose a neutral figure above party competition and because they can reach a cross-party agreement.

utterances.speaker: Cillian

utterances.text: So you are saying that direct election would give the office a democratic mandate from voters.

utterances.text: Yes. The legislative option would allow parliament to select a broadly acceptable figure; put another way, it would let parliament choose a broadly acceptable head of state.

spec.topic: Should councils set a maximum height for new buildings in historic town centres?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Councils should set a maximum height for new buildings in historic town centres.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The first reason is that tall new buildings destroy the skyline that makes a historic town centre recognisable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second reason is that visitors come because of a centre's character, and tourism supports local shops.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say a height limit would stop developers from building the housing that towns badly need.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But several towns that cap heights at five storeys still approve dense, well-designed housing within that limit.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A height cap protects a town's character; in other words, it keeps the old centre looking like itself.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I grew up in a market town with a medieval church spire.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put differently, the council would simply be refusing to let the skyline be changed by one-off towers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Planning committees meet monthly in most councils.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To sum up, a cap is a modest rule that leaves room for new building while protecting the old centre.

utterances.text: I do. Households should face fines for repeated contamination because sorting facilities must remove non-recyclable items, which makes recycling more expensive.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Fines could punish households for occasional sorting mistakes. For context, I have served on the city recycling committee for six years.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Targeted enforcement is possible: inspections can identify households that repeatedly contaminate their bins because inspectors can compare contamination records from tagged bins over time.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying fines should apply only when a household has repeatedly contaminated its recycling bin.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Exactly. Since the policy attaches a financial consequence to repeated contamination, it would deter careless sorting.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Clear education and reminders work better than fines for improving recycling habits. Households respond better when labels clearly identify acceptable items.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: In other words, Rashid proposes using education and reminders instead of financial penalties.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will return to enforcement after a short audience question. The council meeting on waste policy begins at seven o'clock tomorrow.

utterances.text: A warning should come before any fine, because a warning gives a household time to correct its recycling practices.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: The city can issue recycling warnings by attaching tags to contaminated bins, because bin tags cost less than sending inspectors to every household.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: To put that another way, the proposed enforcement system would warn households before escalating to fines.

spec.topic: Should doctors be banned from accepting gifts or paid meals from pharmaceutical sales representatives?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should doctors be banned from accepting gifts or paid meals from drug company representatives?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Yes, they should be banned from accepting them, because even small gifts create a sense of obligation in the doctor who receives them.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Surely a sandwich does not change how anyone prescribes?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Prescribing data show that doctors who accept meals write more brand-name prescriptions than those who do not, which shows how small gifts create obligation. And brand-name drugs cost health systems far more than generics, which is another reason for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying a free lunch quietly steers doctors toward costlier drugs.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Defenders of representatives say they give doctors useful information about new drugs, but that ignores that the information is selected to promote sales.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would replace the representatives?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Independent bodies can give doctors drug information instead, which is a further reason a ban is workable, since independent drug summaries have no sales motive.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, doctors would get their drug news from neutral sources.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Exactly. Several teaching hospitals that banned representatives saw their prescribing costs fall, which is one more reason for the ban. I should say the pizza at my own training hospital was excellent.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Won't doctors resent being treated like suspects?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: I think doctors will accept a ban without resentment, since airline pilots and judges already live under gift rules without it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the deeper point for you?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: A ban protects patients' trust in their doctors' advice, and that is why it matters, because patients cannot tell whether a doctor's advice has been influenced by gifts.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the ban is ultimately about keeping patients' trust.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: I am writing a book on this subject next year.

spec.topic: Should public water supplies be fluoridated to reduce tooth decay?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether public water supplies should be fluoridated to cut tooth decay. Meera, you first.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Our water should be fluoridated, because children in unfluoridated areas have far more tooth decay than children elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: But fluoridation is mass medication without anyone's consent, since the dose cannot be tailored to each person.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: The decay gap is not imaginary: a dental survey found five-year-olds in the unfluoridated north had twice as many cavities as those in the south.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: I have worked as a dental nurse for twenty years, so I see these mouths every week.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: The dose really cannot be tailored, because people drink very different amounts of water. Farm workers, for instance, get through several litres a day.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: So you are saying that a fixed dose in the tap water ignores individual differences.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Whichever of you is right, the regional water board votes on this next month.
