spec.topic: Should governments set a maximum ratio between a company's top executive pay and its median wage?

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: I think governments should cap the ratio between top executive pay and median wage, since pay ratios have ballooned to hundreds of times the median at some big firms.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: But a legal cap would just push firms to outsource their lowest-paid jobs so the median looks higher.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Typing this from a train, so forgive the typos.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Isaac, is that a cap would make firms reshuffle who counts as an employee rather than change what executives earn.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Right. I would rather shareholders decided executive pay through binding votes than have a government cap.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Binding votes already exist in several countries, which is a reason to think they work.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: By the way, my own company published its pay ratio last year.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: So you are saying, Isaac, that shareholder votes are a better tool than a cap for controlling executive pay.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: I doubt it, because large institutional shareholders usually back whatever pay proposals the board puts forward, so votes rarely restrain pay.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether local authorities should be allowed to levy a tourist tax on overnight stays. Priya, you first.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because visitors who stay overnight put real strain on local streets, bins and public transport.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Jelena, you are not convinced.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: But a tourist tax would push visitors towards cheaper neighbouring towns.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: That ignores what happened in my town, where hotel bookings stayed steady after a small nightly charge was introduced.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: So, Olumide, what you mean is that a small charge does not change where people choose to stay?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Not for everyone. Visitors would simply choose another town once a tax is added to the bill. I should say I run a guesthouse near the old harbour.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: The money would be spent on cleaning and transport for visitors and residents alike, since it is residents, not visitors, who pay for that extra work today.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Put another way, the tax would leave local people better off by shifting the cost onto visitors.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

utterances.text: You run a community group that wants councils to stop mowing local verges. Why?

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Councils should let communities turn unused verges into wildflower meadows, because verges mown every fortnight give insects almost nothing to feed on.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Many residents say unmown verges simply look neglected.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: But small signs explaining the project make them acceptable, so there is no good reason to refuse. I have lived on Mill Lane for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that signs solve the appearance problem.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Exactly. Safety matters too, though: tall growth can block drivers' sightlines at junctions, which is why verges there should still be cut.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, only verges away from junctions would be left to grow.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Yes. Meadows also save councils money, since a verge cut once a year costs about a third less than one cut fortnightly, which is another reason to agree.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say wildflower seed is expensive.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: But most verges need no bought seed, because the native seed bank in the soil recovers within two summers. So meadows stay cheap.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In short, meadows cost councils less than mown verges.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Our group meets at the library on Thursday evenings if anyone wants to join.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Item four: whether the council should use predictive software to choose where housing inspectors go. Javier, you followed the trial.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: We should adopt it, because the software lets inspectors reach the worst flats first.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: In the trial, sixty percent of the homes it flagged had damp, which supports adopting it.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Housekeeping note for the minutes: we currently have four housing inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: I am wary, though. Tenants who rarely complain would be overlooked, because the software learns from complaint history.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: In other words, the tool would simply repeat the gaps in the complaint records.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: So you are saying, Amir, that it would miss the tenants who need help most.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Yes, and so officers should review the ranking every month, since a person can notice quiet streets that have no complaints.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: I can accept that, since the review would take only two days of one officer's time. Separately, the pilot was run in Northfield ward.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: To put it another way, Amir wants staff to check the ranking each month.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Authorities that add a monthly human check have reported fewer missed hazards, which shows the review is worth doing.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: And on cost, the licence is cheaper than one inspector's yearly salary, which supports adopting it.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Thank you both. We will vote on this at the next meeting.

spec.topic: Should rugby clubs be allowed to field players aged over thirty-five in under-twenty-one development leagues?

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether rugby clubs should be allowed to field players over thirty-five in under-twenty-one development leagues. Leilani supports the proposal, while Josefa opposes it.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Rugby clubs should be allowed to field players over thirty-five in these leagues. The reason is that older players can provide tactical knowledge that younger players have not yet developed.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Josefa, what is your main objection?

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Many under-twenty-one rugby leagues currently attract fewer spectators than senior competitions. That attendance issue should be considered separately from the age question.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: But allowing players over thirty-five would undermine the developmental purpose of under-twenty-one leagues.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal would permit clubs to use over-thirty-five players in under-twenty-one development matches. Clubs could use those older players as on-field mentors, which is why permission would help the young athletes.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The proposal therefore concerns participation by older players, not replacing the younger members of the squad.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Large age differences may expose younger players to greater injury risks during physically mismatched contests. Because of that, medical staff would need to manage the greater injury risks created by those contests.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Several clubs have recently replaced grass training pitches with artificial surfaces. Let us return to the safety question.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So you are saying that large age differences could make contests less safe for younger players?

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Yes, and Leilani's mentoring point is, in other words, a claim that older players would serve as coaches during matches.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: A supervised mentoring role would give clubs a practical way to transfer senior experience to developing athletes. That is another reason the clubs should be allowed to field older players.

spec.topic: Should schools be allowed to use software that monitors students' private messages on school-issued laptops for signs of self-harm?

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether schools should be allowed to monitor private messages on school-issued laptops for signs of self-harm. Thandiwe, you support that policy?

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Yes. Schools should be allowed to use the software because it can flag messages that indicate a student may be in danger.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: But monitoring students' private messages violates their privacy and can damage their trust in schools.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: A school's duty to intervene when it sees credible evidence that a student is in danger is a reason to allow this software. An alert can connect a student with a counselor before a crisis occurs, which is another reason.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Zofia, what concerns you most about the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: The software can flag ordinary private conversations, and false alarms from the software can distress students because of that.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: The district has used these laptops for several years. Does that affect your view?

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: School safeguarding teams already follow procedures for escalating credible warnings, so the software would add a useful early-warning layer.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Adrian, are you saying that the existing procedures make monitoring unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: No. So you are saying that schools should be permitted to use the software to detect possible signs of self-harm in student messages.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: The software can connect a student with a counselor before school staff otherwise notice the danger. That is why I think the policy deserves a chance.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposed software is an emergency safety net rather than routine surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Students use the same school-issued laptops for mathematics lessons, so any monitoring system would operate across much of their school day.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Adrian, your response to the promise of safeguards?

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: I disagree with allowing the system: safeguards do not solve the privacy problem created by monitoring private messages.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposed software is an emergency safety net and not routine surveillance.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Requiring a trained counselor to review every alert is another reason to allow the software.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: The panel therefore agrees that any permitted system would need strict limits, although you disagree about whether those limits can protect privacy.

spec.topic: Should smart speakers be prohibited from keeping voice recordings after a request has been processed?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Smart speakers should be prohibited from keeping voice recordings after the requested task has been processed.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The first reason for that position is that keeping recordings after processing gives companies unnecessary access to intimate information.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My smart speaker came with a one-year warranty.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A further reason is that stored voice recordings could be exposed in a data breach.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.text: Our question is whether adult education centres should receive public funding for courses leading to local shortage occupations. Eamon, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Adult education centres should receive public funding for those courses because the courses fill vacancies that local employers cannot otherwise fill.

utterances.speaker: Eamon

utterances.text: But public funding should be directed to employers rather than adult education centres. Employer contributions would reduce the cost to the public, which is the reason for directing the money to employers.

utterances.speaker: Tobias

utterances.speaker: Margit

utterances.speaker: Femi

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: I disagree with the proposal: wage subsidies for employers would address local shortages more effectively than funding adult education centres. Wage subsidies would reach employers at the moment when they hire workers, and that is why they would be more effective.

utterances.speaker: Eamon

utterances.speaker: Margit

utterances.speaker: Kieran

spec.topic: Should teacher-training programmes require a year of supervised classroom practice before qualification?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Teacher-training programmes should require a year of supervised classroom practice before qualification, because graduates who have only studied theory struggle to manage a class.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is hardly surprising, since classroom management is a craft that is learned only through repeated attempts in a real classroom.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Supervised practice also catches bad teaching habits early. In other words, a mentor can correct a habit before it hardens.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics will object, though, that a year of practice is unaffordable for many trainees, since many already carry heavy debt.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The practice year should be paid as a salaried residency, because schools gain an extra adult in the classroom during it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Mentors need protected time for the work, since mentoring on top of a full timetable produces only superficial feedback.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I did my own training in a town with only two secondary schools.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Placements should span at least two different schools, because a trainee who sees only one school's culture learns only that school's habits.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Trainees should be assessed on observed teaching rather than on essays. Put another way, what a trainee does in the classroom should count for more than what they write about it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The qualifying body's consultation on the reform closes in March.

utterances.text: Governments should tax fast-fashion garments according to the environmental cost of making them, because the industry's emissions and water use are currently paid for by everyone else.

utterances.speaker: Elodie

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

utterances.speaker: Joaquin

utterances.speaker: Efua

utterances.speaker: Elodie

spec.topic: Should supreme court judges serve a single fixed term of eighteen years instead of holding office until retirement?

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether Supreme Court judges should serve one fixed eighteen-year term instead of holding office until retirement. Tobias, make the case for changing the system.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: A Supreme Court judge can remain in office for several decades under the current system, and judges currently leave the Court at widely varying ages.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: That long duration matters because it makes vacancies arrive at unpredictable times. Because judges leave at widely varying ages, the United States should replace Supreme Court life tenure with a single fixed eighteen-year term.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Tobias has taught constitutional law for twelve years. Hamza, what is the strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: I object to that proposal because fixed terms could make Supreme Court judges anticipate political retaliation after leaving office.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Because that retaliation risk could weaken judicial independence, fixed terms could weaken judicial independence. A second consequence, for the same reason, is that fixed terms could encourage judges to make strategic retirement decisions.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: An eighteen-year term would give each president roughly two Supreme Court appointments during a four-year presidency.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Because appointments would then follow a known rotation, an eighteen-year term would make Supreme Court vacancies predictable. Because of that same rotation, an eighteen-year term would make confirmation battles occur at more regular intervals.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: In other words, an eighteen-year term would schedule Supreme Court vacancies instead of leaving them to chance.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Because that schedule would be public, lawmakers could prepare nominees before a seat became vacant. Since the schedule would also be public, it would reduce the temptation to keep elderly judges on the Court for political reasons.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: To restate the confirmation point, confirmation battles would occur at regular intervals rather than clustering unpredictably.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Because confirmation intervals would be regular, the appointment process would be easier for the Senate to plan. Regular intervals would also make the appointment process easier for advocacy groups to monitor, because they would know when to prepare.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.text: Still, a street name is an honour to the person, and honouring someone with a contested legacy offends residents whose families were harmed by it, so renaming is justified.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: In other words, a petition shows residents are really offended.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The council meets next month to hear the first petition, as it happens.

spec.topic: Should courts have the power to strike down laws passed by the national legislature?

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: The agenda asks whether courts should have the power to strike down laws passed by the national legislature. My position is that they should.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: I therefore propose that courts should have the power to strike down laws passed by the national legislature.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Constitutional rights need enforceable protection; that is the first reason for supporting the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Judges are insulated from short-term electoral pressure, which is another reason to give courts this power.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: National legislatures sometimes pass laws that violate constitutional rights. That is a further reason to support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Before we continue, the meeting-room projector is showing a low-battery warning.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Since the constitution has higher legal authority than an ordinary statute, courts need authority to reject statutes that conflict with it.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Judicial review can prevent a temporary majority from removing protections from an unpopular minority, so that supports the proposed power.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Courts cannot protect constitutional limits if they have no power to invalidate conflicting laws; that is why I support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: But judges should not override the democratic mandate of an elected national legislature. That is my objection to the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: So you are saying that courts should be able to invalidate laws enacted by the national legislature.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: The finance committee will circulate its travel policy next week.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal gives courts authority to cancel national legislation.

spec.topic: Should school sports teams be required to accept any pupil who wants to join?

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether school sports teams should be required to accept every pupil who wants to join. Rohan, you oppose the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Competitive school teams need selection in order to train effectively. If every willing pupil must be admitted, coaches may no longer be able to build balanced squads.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: The current selection system excludes many pupils from school sport, especially those who have never played for a community club.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Malik, should the rule apply to every team, including the most competitive ones?

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: The school should require every sports team to accept any pupil who wants to join. The school has not yet received its new scoreboard. But requiring admission is still preferable to allowing competitive standards to exclude beginners.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Because the school would have to admit every willing pupil, every interested pupil would get a genuine chance to play for a school team.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Since the rule guarantees a place for willing pupils, coaches could create beginner squads alongside the main team.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: That addresses access, but what would the policy change in practice?

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Because every willing pupil would have to be admitted, tryouts would become a route into school sport for pupils with no prior club experience.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: The requirement would give pupils without experience in community clubs access to school sport, because they could no longer be turned away at selection.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Because the teams would include a wider range of abilities, team captains would learn to include players with different skill levels.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Leilani, you have been listening to both sides. What is your assessment?

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: In other words, the current selection system leaves some pupils without any school-sport opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Because that exclusion deprives some pupils of school sport, a universal joining rule is needed.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: The school gym windows need replacing, although that is a separate facilities issue.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now move to closing statements.

spec.topic: Should councils limit the number of fast-food outlets near secondary schools?

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether councils should limit the number of fast-food outlets near secondary schools. Imogen, why do you support a limit?

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Councils should limit the number of fast-food outlets near secondary schools because a high concentration of outlets makes unhealthy food the easiest choice for pupils.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: A district survey found that pupils buy fast food more often when several outlets are close to their school. That is a further reason for a limit.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: I have worked with secondary-school pupils for six years, so I know how varied their eating habits can be.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: But a numerical cap on fast-food outlets would punish businesses that already follow the rules.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: So you are saying that councils should limit the number of fast-food outlets near secondary schools. Arjun, what is your response?

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Council inspections found that many fast-food outlets near schools sell meal deals that are high in salt and sugar. That finding is another reason to support a limit.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: For the record, I have moderated three school debates this month.

spec.topic: Should schools publish exam results for each individual teacher's classes?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Should schools publish exam results for each individual teacher's classes? Chloe, you first.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Schools should publish them, because parents have a right to know how well their children are being taught.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Publishing would also improve teaching across the school, which is another reason to do it.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: I'd add that teachers whose results are visible work harder with their weakest pupils, which is why publication improves teaching.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: The pilot in my borough bears that out: bottom-quartile grades rose after results went public.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: But it would unfairly penalise the teachers who are handed the weakest classes.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: I taught exactly that kind of Year 11 set myself for six years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Priya, what about the parents who would read the figures?

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Most parents rarely understand what a single class average means.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying raw class figures would mislead parents.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Small classes make it worse, since one pupil can shift the average by several points, and that makes the figures unreliable.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Exam boards already give every school a detailed breakdown by class.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: In other words, the numbers already exist and only the publishing is missing.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: The local paper ran a league table of schools just last week.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Parents at private schools already scrutinise results closely.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Put another way, you are saying that kind of scrutiny is already normal in the private sector.

spec.topic: Should a minimum share of legislative seats be reserved for women?

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Good evening. Our question is whether a minimum share of legislative seats should be reserved for women. Alejandro, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: I do, because equal citizenship should lead to a legislature in which women can win a guaranteed minimum share of seats.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Women currently hold only 31 percent of the seats in the national legislature. That figure is unacceptable, although the quota proposal deserves more scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: A legislature cannot fully represent the public when women are seriously underrepresented. For that reason, I support reserving a minimum share of seats for women.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Women bring experiences to lawmaking that are still missing from many legislatures. Those experiences matter because policies affecting childcare and safety receive more sustained attention when women participate equally.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Policies affecting childcare and safety are more likely to receive sustained attention when women participate equally in lawmaking.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: But a reserved quota can make legislative seats appear to be rewards for identity rather than achievement, so I cannot accept that the quota is automatically fair.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: So you are saying that quotas make people doubt whether women legislators earned their seats?

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: Put another way, a legislature that lacks women cannot fully represent the public. The remedy should address how candidates are selected, not merely set a symbolic target.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Political parties often recruit women late and place them in unwinnable constituencies. Because of that pattern, a reserved minimum share would force parties to nominate women in competitive constituencies.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Since competitive nominations would give more women a realistic path into legislative office, the quota would change who can seriously contest power.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: That evidence shows that a realistic path into office would broaden the range of experience in the legislature.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: Consequently, broadening legislative experience would improve the quality of democratic decision-making.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: The debate will continue after a short commercial break.

spec.topic: Should cricket's lengthy test matches be shortened to four days worldwide?

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Item two: whether Test matches should be cut to four days worldwide. Theo, you start us off.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: I say yes, we should shorten Tests to four days worldwide. Many five-day Tests end in draws, because rain and slow play eat into the schedule.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: And draws leave casual spectators feeling that nothing was decided, which is why fewer of them would help.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Side note: I already have a ticket for the Lord's Test in July.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: But five days is the defining tradition of the format, and a shorter game would damage it.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: In other words, you want to keep the schedule, though four days would still cut the draws, since the draws are the real problem.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Teams could add more overs per day to fit the same play into four days.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Longer days would exhaust bowlers and raise injury risk, since fast bowlers already break down at a high rate under the current workload.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: The calendar is crowded too, so a shorter Test would free dates for other series, which is another reason to do it.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: So you are saying, Camille, that the tradition of five days matters more than the draws.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Noted. The committee meets again in March.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Fewer draws would make Tests more appealing to casual spectators.

spec.topic: Should local authorities allow dogs off-leash in designated areas of public parks?

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Item two: off-leash areas in parks. We have the room only until five o'clock, so let's be brisk. Felix, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Councils should allow dogs off-leash in designated areas, because dogs need room to run freely to stay healthy.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: But off-leash dogs cause problems for other park users. We had twenty complaints about loose dogs last summer, which shows it.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: That ignores that designated areas can be fenced off from walkers. Leeds's fenced dog areas have had no reported incidents, which shows it works.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: So you are saying fencing keeps dogs and walkers safely apart.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Another problem for other park users is that off-leash dogs chase wildlife. Ground-nesting birds in the park have declined, which shows it.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: In other words, you say off-leash dogs harm the park's wildlife.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Areas can be sited away from the nesting zones, which is why the proposal can still go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: So what you mean is that the nesting zones would stay protected from dogs. For what it's worth, I walk my sister's spaniel on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Local dog clubs have offered to fund the fencing, which is another reason to trust the fenced approach.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Put another way, Tobias, you think loose dogs endanger nervous walkers.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Dog walking brings neighbours together, which is another reason for councils to allow it. That is because dog walkers make up much of the park's regular visitors.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Thank you both. We will vote next week.

utterances.text: Item two: dogs off-leash in designated areas of the park. Felix, you raised it.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: I think we should allow dogs off-leash in designated areas of the park. The reason is that dogs with regular off-leash exercise are calmer and less likely to behave aggressively.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Tobias, your view?

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: And fewer aggressive dogs means fewer incidents involving other park users, which is why it supports the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: But off-leash areas would lead to more injuries to children and joggers, since the park already gets about a dozen complaints a year about loose dogs.

utterances.speaker: Felix

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: In other words, the fences would separate the dogs from children and joggers.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Fine. I should say Felix walks his spaniel at the park every morning before work.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: A fenced area costs about eight thousand pounds, so the parks budget cannot absorb it this year.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: The council has an unspent grant for community green space, so it can pay for the fencing from that.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Good, let us go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Then I suggest the trial should run for six months with a review at the end.

utterances.speaker: Tobias

spec.topic: Should wild beavers be reintroduced to rivers despite complaints from neighbouring landowners?

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether wild beavers should return to our rivers despite complaints from neighbouring landowners. Amir, why support reintroduction?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Wild beavers create wetlands that support many river species. Beaver dams create those wetlands by slowing and spreading river water, which is why the ecological case is strong.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Deirdre, you represent several farming communities. What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: A limited beaver reintroduction programme is feasible, but wild beavers should not be reintroduced while neighbouring farms face an unacceptable flooding risk. That risk is a serious objection to Amir's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Wild beavers should be reintroduced with safeguards for neighbouring landowners. Regular dam inspections would allow authorities to remove dangerous dams quickly, and designated stretches would keep the trial manageable.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Maeve, do the proposed safeguards answer the landowners' concerns?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: I am not sure the councils can deliver that level of oversight. I have visited a river valley where beavers were successfully reintroduced, though, and the landscape recovered noticeably.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: A reintroduction programme restricted to designated stretches is feasible. More specifically, wild beaver reintroduction can be restricted to designated river stretches, so the animals need not occupy every tributary.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: A compensation scheme would protect landowners from verified beaver damage. That gives neighbouring farmers a practical remedy rather than leaving them to carry the whole risk.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: So, in other words, Amir's safeguarded reintroduction means returning beavers while monitoring dams and compensating affected landowners. Is that the proposal before the audience?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Yes. The programme can be limited to designated river stretches; in other words, reintroduction can be restricted to designated stretches rather than the entire river system.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Deirdre, what would you require before supporting even a limited trial?

spec.topic: Should offside rules in football be abolished at amateur level?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Gareth, should amateur football abolish the offside rule?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Yes, offside rules should be abolished in amateur football because volunteer referees often lack enough time to apply them consistently.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What practical difference would that make?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Amateur officials often struggle to apply offside consistently, which is itself a reason to abolish the rule. Because of that difficulty, removing offside would make amateur matches easier to referee.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the change affect the flow of matches?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Removing offside would reduce stoppages in amateur matches, and that is another reason to abolish it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So what exactly are you proposing?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: In other words, my proposal is to remove offside from amateur football.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say defenders would suffer.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: That objection has force, but abolishing offside would make amateur matches unfair to defenders.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Can you state that concern another way?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Put another way, defenders would lose an important protection if offside disappeared.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: One final background point: when are most amateur matches played?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Many amateur football matches are played on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And how did you become interested in refereeing?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: I began refereeing amateur football at the age of nineteen.

spec.topic: Should wet wipes containing plastic be banned from sale?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Our question is whether wet wipes containing plastic should be banned from sale. Meera, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Wet wipes containing plastic can shed microplastics when they are flushed. I usually buy fragrance-free wipes, although that is a separate preference.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: Wet wipes containing plastic persist in waterways for a long time, and that is why they should be banned from sale.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Some medical services depend on wet wipes containing plastic. However, that dependence is an objection to banning every such product.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Plastic-free wet wipes are available in many supermarkets, which is a reason the sale ban is practical.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: So you are saying that wet wipes containing plastic should not be sold?

utterances.speaker: Meera

spec.topic: Should councils require residents to separate food waste or face penalties?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Food waste in mixed rubbish contaminates recyclable material. Because mixed rubbish carries food residue onto recyclables, separating food waste reduces contamination.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since separating food waste reduces contamination of recyclable material, councils should require residents to separate food waste.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many residents already compost some of their food waste at home.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clear instructions and free caddies make food-waste separation easier to follow. For that reason, councils should provide clear instructions and free caddies for food-waste separation.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The council's annual waste report is due in October.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Warnings give residents a chance to correct mistakes. Therefore, a small penalty is fair only after repeated refusal despite warnings.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, penalties can burden low-income residents.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, the concern is that penalties may impose a financial burden on vulnerable residents.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To put that provision plainly, councils should give residents guidance and containers for food-waste separation. Because councils can give residents that practical support, councils should enforce food-waste separation with warnings followed by modest penalties.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether the metric system should become compulsory in everyday commerce across English-speaking countries. Malik, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: The metric system should be compulsory in all everyday commerce in English-speaking countries. Retailers can use their existing scales to print both metric and customary units.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: But compulsory metric rules would burden small shops that currently display familiar customary measures. I learned to estimate distances in miles during childhood.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Dual-unit labels can be adopted without major expense, because existing retail scales can support labels showing both units. That is why the cost objection should not block a common standard.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Most retailers already use digital weighing and pricing equipment. A retailer with that equipment would not need to replace every machine during the transition.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Seamus, does the proposal create practical problems beyond the cost of changing labels?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Metric pricing would make online comparisons across English-speaking countries easier, because online shoppers compare prices across borders every day.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: So the disagreement is partly about whether convenience for shoppers outweighs disruption for established businesses. Seamus, what would a workable transition look like?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: So you are saying that compulsory metric commerce would create a common measurement language. I keep a handwritten list of traditional recipes in my kitchen.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: To put Seamus's concern another way, compulsory metric rules would burden small shops using familiar measures.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: The change to compulsory metric commerce would be manageable for retailers, because most retailers already use digital weighing and pricing equipment and because a gradual timetable would give retailers time to adjust their labels and equipment.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: That leaves the audience with a choice between one compulsory standard and continued dual practice. We will take closing remarks after the break.

utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether political parties should be legally required to field gender-balanced candidate lists. Babajide, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Several comparative studies find that gender-balanced candidate lists increase women's electoral success. Because of that evidence, gender-balanced candidate lists increase the number of women elected.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Women face structural barriers in political party recruitment. Since those barriers affect who reaches the ballot, gender-balanced candidate lists would make elected institutions more legitimate.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Transparent reporting would make a legal candidate-balance requirement workable. That is why political parties should be legally required to field gender-balanced candidate lists.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: I disagree with that requirement. Mandatory gender-balanced lists could undermine political parties' autonomy because mandatory gender-balanced lists could produce token candidacies.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Poorly designed quota systems can produce token candidacies, which is another reason to set clear legal standards rather than leave the matter entirely voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Babajide, your objection is that mandatory gender-balanced lists could undermine political parties' autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Separately, the next general election will use a redesigned ballot paper.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: So you are saying that women face structural barriers in political party recruitment. That is precisely why voluntary promises have not been enough.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: Young voters are more likely than older voters to support independent candidates.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: The central disagreement is now clear: Amara sees a legal requirement as a remedy for exclusion, while Babajide sees a risk to party autonomy.

spec.topic: Should self-defence law include a duty to retreat before using lethal force in public places?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: I think the law should include a duty to retreat before lethal force in public places. A person who can step away safely does not need to kill anyone, and that is my reason.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: But retreat is not safe when an attacker is armed and chasing. That is because running from an armed attacker can get the victim shot in the back.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: A duty to retreat would not force anyone to run when escape is unsafe, because most statutes with the duty carry a safe-escape exception.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: These rules put the burden on the victim rather than the aggressor, since victims are made to prove after the fact that they could not have escaped.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: So you are saying the victim, not the aggressor, ends up carrying the burden. Agreed.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Juries are poorly placed to judge whether escape was possible, because they second-guess a frightened person's split-second decisions with hindsight.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: I watched a trial last year on exactly this question.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Countries with a duty to retreat have fewer fatal public confrontations, which shows that fewer killings in public places is a reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: Fatality figures differ across countries for many reasons besides self-defence law.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: The duty protects bystanders in crowded places, since stray bullets in crowded places kill bystanders.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: My tram stop gets very crowded at rush hour.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Retreat should be required only where escape is clearly safe. In other words, the duty should apply only when the person can escape without risk.

spec.topic: Should daylight saving clock changes be abolished on health grounds?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Daylight saving clock changes should be abolished on health grounds. I live in a country that still changes its clocks twice a year.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The first reason is that hospital admissions for heart attacks rise in the days after the spring change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, losing one hour of sleep in March puts a measurable strain on the heart.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second reason for abolition is that the lost hour disrupts sleep for a week or more.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A third reason is that teenagers, whose body clocks run late, are made to wake in the dark every spring.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I wrote this essay on the Sunday the clocks went back.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some argue that lighter evenings get people out exercising, but that ignores how small the gain is beside the harm of a week of broken sleep.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason I call the gain small is that a survey of gym attendance found no change when the clocks moved.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason to end the changes is that road accidents rise on the Monday after the spring change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Permanent standard time is the best replacement, because it keeps the body clock aligned with the sun.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Permanent summer time would be a mistake, since it would keep winter mornings dark until after nine.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Which is another reason to reject it: it would push the sleep problem into every winter.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the twice-yearly clock change has to be ended.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is not a trivial loss, because studies in several countries report a rise in heart attacks in the days after the change. In other words, the spring change is a mass dose of sleep loss imposed on the whole population.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Bodies keep time by daylight, and the clock change pulls social time away from the body's own rhythm. People who live on the late edge of a time zone already suffer this mismatch every day.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Defenders say the extra evening light encourages people to exercise after work.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But the evening exercise benefits are small and unproven, so they do not outweigh the documented harms.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Traffic safety reports show hospital admissions for car crashes rising in the week after the spring change, and tired drivers are a danger to everyone on the road.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My own children took a full week to settle after last March's change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Permanent standard time would match social time to the body's rhythm better than permanent summer time, which is why the sleep specialists' professional bodies back it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clock changes began as a wartime fuel-saving measure. Yet modern energy savings from the change are negligible.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because modern energy savings are negligible, the original purpose of the clock change no longer justifies keeping it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put differently, the clocks should stop changing.

spec.topic: Should smokers be required to quit before receiving elective joint replacement surgery?

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether smokers should have to quit before receiving elective joint replacement. Rohan, you support the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Smoking substantially increases the risk of complications after joint replacement surgery. Because quitting before surgery reduces the patient's risk of complications, patients should quit first.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: That is why elective joint replacement should require patients to quit smoking first as a medical safety measure.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: I have worked in orthopedic care for twelve years. Our clinic usually has a full appointment book in winter.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: But a mandatory quitting requirement could delay joint replacement surgery for months. Because that delay keeps patients inactive, prolonged inactivity while patients wait for surgery can worsen their mobility.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Smoking-cessation counseling can double quit rates among surgical patients. Because counseling can double quit rates, hospitals should offer smoking-cessation counseling to patients awaiting joint replacement.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposed requirement is a medical safety rule rather than a punishment for smokers?

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: A documented quit attempt provides a clear eligibility threshold for elective surgery. Because that threshold is clear, the hospital can schedule elective joint replacement after a patient makes a documented quit attempt.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal would schedule surgery after a patient makes a documented quit attempt.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Nicotine replacement and counseling improve smoking cessation before surgery. That is why hospitals should fund nicotine replacement and counseling for patients preparing for joint replacement.

spec.topic: Should secondary schools replace the traditional summer holiday with several shorter breaks spread across the year?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether secondary schools should swap the long summer holiday for several shorter breaks. Abena, you start.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Schools should replace the long summer holiday with several shorter breaks, because pupils forget much of what they learned during a ten-week summer gap.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Magnus, your response?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: But shorter breaks would wreck the summer jobs that older pupils depend on, since many families need that income.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Josefa, you have studied this.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: In a study of three thousand pupils, September test scores averaged eight percent below June scores, which shows the forgetting is real. I taught for twelve years before moving into research.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Magnus, is that pupils' summer wages hold many family budgets together.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: But employers can hire pupils during the short breaks too, since local shops took on extra staff at half-term last year.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: In other words, Josefa, the learning loss over the summer can be measured.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Abena, are there other benefits?

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Pupils are exhausted by the seventh week of a term, so frequent breaks keep them rested.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Abena, frequent breaks would keep pupils fresh.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Teachers would welcome shorter breaks, because marking piles up in long terms. That is a point in favour of replacing the summer holiday.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Put another way, teachers would be less worn out by the end of a term.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: For me, keeping pupils rested is the reason to scrap the ten-week summer.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: My own school's summer holiday lasts ten weeks.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Wrestlers and other scripted-sport performers should be covered by athlete drug-testing rules, because their bodies take real punishment every night.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I grew up watching Saturday wrestling with my uncle. Heavy drug use appears in the records of many performers who died young, which is another reason to test them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A wrestler works some two hundred dates a year, far more than most athletes, and that is a further reason to bring them under the rules.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some say testing is pointless because the results are decided in advance. But that ignores the fact that testing exists to protect health, not to police results, which is why the rules suit performers too.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, performers should face the same tests as any sprinter or boxer. A new season of the main league starts next month.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Who should pay? Promotions, not taxpayers, should fund the testing, since they profit from the performers' bodies.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: They already employ medical staff at every event, which is a second reason.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That makes a programme cheap to run, since a few hundred tests a year would cover a whole roster.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Panels in other sports show that a single test costs very little, which is a further reason to think it is cheap.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, the industry should pay for its own testing.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To put it differently, testing would barely dent a promotion's budget.

spec.topic: Should legislators be paid the average national wage rather than a premium salary?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether legislators should be paid the average national wage rather than a premium salary. Josefa, you start.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: They should take the average wage, because then they would understand the financial pressures that voters face.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Noor, your response?

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: And the reason I say that is that a premium salary cuts legislators off from the daily costs borne by ordinary households.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: But capping pay at the average wage would keep able candidates with professional careers from standing, since only wealthy people or people with outside income could afford to serve.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: I would note that Josefa sat on a county council for six years before entering the national legislature.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Pay too low also invites bribes, because legislators would be open to them. In the end I believe a premium salary is the only way to attract able candidates.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Vikram, what do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: So you are saying that low-paid legislators would be easier to bribe than well-paid ones, Noor.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are running over time, so one more round.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Voters can already judge their legislators at the ballot box, whatever the pay.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: In other words, Josefa, an average wage would be the only fair deal for the voters who fund it.

spec.topic: Should coastal councils fund engineered sea defences instead of relocating threatened communities?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should councils spend scarce money on engineered sea defences, or should they relocate people from places that are becoming unsafe?

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Coastal councils should generally fund engineered sea defences instead of relocating threatened communities. They should do that because well-designed sea defences allow threatened residents to remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say that approach treats every coastline as if it can be defended. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Not entirely. However, several isolated coastal villages cannot be protected safely by engineered sea defences. As a separate practical matter, the council's summer ferry timetable has already been published.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that councils should usually protect threatened communities rather than move them?

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Yes, and a second reason is that protecting existing roads, water systems, and schools lets councils preserve essential services for coastal residents. I should add that I grew up in a fishing town on the east coast.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What makes relocation especially difficult in practice?

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: A managed retreat plan requires years of preparation. A regional survey also found that most residents of threatened communities want a direct say in relocation decisions.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, managed retreat is not an overnight policy.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: That survey shows that abandoning these communities without their consent would face sustained opposition. Finally, repeated emergency repairs can cost councils more than maintaining a properly designed defence.

utterances.text: Why summer in particular?

utterances.text: Turf needs the most irrigation then, since evaporation peaks in those months. I should say I live beside one of those reservoirs.

utterances.text: Golf clubs say recycled water makes their courses sustainable.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: But that ignores that recycled supply is already fully allocated to farms, because the treatment plants send nearly all their output there, which is another reason to refuse.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that councils should simply say no.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Yes. The regional council votes on the next application in March.

spec.topic: Should hosts of dinner parties expect guests to arrive exactly on time?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Hosts should not expect guests to arrive exactly on time, because a guest who knocks on the stated minute catches most hosts half-dressed.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason is that home kitchens rarely run to the minute; sauces split and ovens sulk.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the perfectly punctual guest gets in the host's way. I have hosted dinners for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some call lateness rude, but ten minutes is nothing next to the pleasure of a calm host.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Guests should aim to arrive within fifteen minutes after the stated time, because that window lets the host finish the last tasks.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, dinner is seldom ready at the minute it was promised.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My sister, for the record, is always forty minutes late.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ambulance services should be allowed to decline callouts that a phone assessor judges non-urgent.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason is that every crew sent to a minor complaint is unavailable for a cardiac arrest elsewhere in the area.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is not a hypothetical worry, since response times for life-threatening calls have lengthened as non-urgent calls have grown.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But assessors working only from a phone conversation misjudge some cases. In other words, a calm voice on the line can hide a developing stroke.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My cousin has driven an ambulance for eleven years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Callers whose callouts are declined should get a nurse call-back within the hour, because a call-back would catch most patients whose condition worsens.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That holds because in the Aldwick pilot, nurse call-backs caught nearly all patients who deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put differently, the call-back is a safety net under the decision to decline a callout.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Dispatch centres run twenty-four hours a day.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, an ambulance service should be free to decline a call that is truly non-urgent.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Regular board renewal brings independent scrutiny to company decisions; because of that scrutiny, renewal is valuable.

spec.topic: Should doctors be required to retake licensing examinations every ten years?

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether doctors should be required to retake licensing examinations every ten years. Darius, why do you support the requirement?

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Medical knowledge can change substantially during a doctor's career. Because of that, a ten-year licensing retest would reveal knowledge gaps before those gaps endanger patients.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: The existing license-renewal process includes a fixed fee. Chloe, my concern is whether another examination would improve care enough to justify its burden.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Since a retest would reveal knowledge gaps, regulators could require targeted refresher training before renewing a license.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: That targeted training would make a ten-year retest a practical patient-safety policy.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So you are saying, in other words, that the proposal would create a universal examination every decade for doctors.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Exactly. Because the examination would be universal, it would also test doctors with clean professional records.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: But testing doctors with clean records would consume appointments that could be used for patients. Using those appointments for retesting would reduce doctors' appointment capacity.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: The policy would present an access objection because retesting would reduce appointment capacity.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Put another way, the policy's access objection would be the loss of clinical time.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Thank you both. We will now hear brief closing statements.

spec.topic: Should pupils who repeatedly fail core subjects be required to repeat the school year?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should pupils who repeatedly fail core subjects be made to repeat the year? Priya, you start.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Pupils who keep failing maths and English should repeat the year, because they simply cannot cope with the following year's work.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: But being held back makes pupils far more likely to leave school early.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Damien, you have worked in schools.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: I taught in a comprehensive for twenty years. Theo is right, since a long-running study found held-back pupils were twice as likely to drop out.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Damien, is that holding pupils back pushes them out of education.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Put another way, a child who cannot do the work now will still not manage it next year, and that is my whole point.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Held-back pupils are separated from their friends and lose confidence, which is why they disengage.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: By the way, the inspectors' report is due in March.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take your calls after the break.

spec.topic: Should businesses disclose to customers when an automated system rather than a person drafts their replies?

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether businesses should tell customers when software, rather than a person, drafts a reply. Damien, you support disclosure?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Yes. Businesses should disclose that fact because disclosure lets customers decide how much to rely on a reply.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: But disclosure could slow customer service. For context, my customer-service team handled more than two thousand queries last week.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: A standard automation label could contain six words. More importantly, automated drafts can contain plausible errors.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Automated drafts can sound confident despite containing errors, which is why customers need to know whether software produced them.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: That problem is especially serious because automated systems often match patterns without understanding an individual customer's case.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Because automated drafts can contain plausible errors, customers should be warned that no person may have reviewed an automated reply.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: In other words, customers should be warned that an automated reply may not have received human review.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A clear disclosure prevents customers from assuming that a person wrote the reply; therefore, businesses should use a clear disclosure when software drafts a reply.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: So you are saying that businesses should use a clear disclosure when software drafts a reply.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Put another way, businesses should make the disclosure clear rather than obscure.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Clear, prominent notices are more likely to be seen by customers, which is why businesses should put the automation notice at the start of the reply.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: And that means businesses should place the automation notice at the beginning of the reply?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether supermarkets should remove sweets from checkout aisles. Jolene, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Children frequently ask their parents for sweets displayed at supermarket checkouts. That is why supermarkets should remove sweets from checkout aisles.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Checkout displays encourage unplanned purchases of confectionery, but I am not convinced that removing them is the right answer.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: For context, I usually buy my groceries on Saturday mornings.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Because children are pressured at the till and checkout displays encourage unplanned purchases, supermarkets should remove sweets from those aisles.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: However, removing sweets from checkout aisles would not eliminate children's access to confectionery. The debate should not pretend that it would.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Supermarkets can stock healthier snacks near the checkouts instead of sweets, because shoppers still want something convenient while they wait.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: So you are saying that supermarkets can stock healthier snacks near the checkouts instead of sweets.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Confectionery accounts for a substantial share of impulse purchases at supermarket checkouts, which is why supermarkets should remove it from those aisles.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Because the policy is limited to the checkout zone, removing sweets there would preserve shoppers' access to sweets elsewhere in supermarkets.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal concerns the checkout zone rather than every place where supermarkets sell sweets.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Since the proposal removes only checkout sweets, supermarkets could make the checkout area less tempting without banning confectionery.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal would reduce temptation at the checkout without banning sweets.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Because the change leaves sweets available elsewhere, removing sweets from checkout aisles would be a nudge rather than a ban.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Put another way, the suggested change would guide shoppers away from impulse purchases without forbidding sweets.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Because the proposal removes a prominent trigger, removing sweets from checkout aisles would make those displays less influential at the point of purchase.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: What Lorenzo means is that the change would reduce the influence of checkout displays on shoppers' decisions.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: A supermarket trial that removed checkout sweets recorded fewer confectionery purchases, which shows that supermarkets should remove sweets from checkout aisles.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: I have worked in supermarket management for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Jolene

utterances.speaker: Jolene

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Before we continue, Fiona's train was delayed this morning.

spec.topic: Should ministers be drawn partly from outside the elected legislature?

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Ministers should be drawn partly from outside the elected legislature, because governments need specialist expertise in areas like health, finance and engineering.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: But that would undermine democratic accountability, since voters cannot remove an unelected minister at the ballot box.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Outside ministers could still be questioned by the legislature and dismissed by the prime minister, which is why accountability would be preserved.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: I speak with some feeling, as I once worked as a hospital administrator.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Many elected legislators have no experience outside party politics, which shows the legislature lacks the knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: So you are saying that the legislature currently lacks specialist knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Yes, in other words, the legislature does not have enough specialist knowledge at present.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: My grandfather sat in parliament for thirty years, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Opening ministerial posts to outsiders would let the prime minister reward friends with jobs.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Put another way, appointing outsiders would give the prime minister too much patronage power.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether restaurant bills should always be divided equally. Sanna, make the case for equal splitting.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Equal splitting is fair when people dine together, because people who dine together share the table, service, and some communal dishes.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I disagree. Equal splitting is unfair when diners order very different amounts. The restaurant's printed receipts list every item separately.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: The difference between a tasting-menu order and a side-salad order can be enormous. That gap makes a single equal share difficult to justify.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: For tonight's group, the spending limit keeps each person's share affordable.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Everyone at this dinner agreed to share the appetisers and desserts.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Equal splitting is reasonable for this dinner because the spending limit keeps each share affordable; another reason is that everyone agreed to share the appetisers and desserts.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: So you are saying, Leopold, that equal splitting is unfair whenever diners order very different amounts?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: In other words, equal splitting is reasonable for this dinner.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: One small detail: the dining room has twelve windows.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Most of tonight's cost comes from dishes that everyone shared, which is another reason equal splitting is reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Because groups may have different expectations, groups should agree in advance on how to divide a restaurant bill.

utterances.text: I think sports clubs should be allowed to sell naming rights to their historic stadiums. The club's under-eighteen team also played its final match on Saturday.

utterances.text: In other words, you support permitting clubs to sell the names of historic grounds. I am not convinced that commercial branding belongs on places with such deep roots.

utterances.speaker: Olumide

utterances.speaker: Femi
