utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Historic stadium names carry memories that matter to local supporters, which is why clubs should preserve those names.

utterances.text: But unpaid volunteer roles give students valuable experience and a sense of community.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: In other words, predictable retirement rules help workers plan their finances. That is why I see some case for the proposal.

spec.topic: Should countries ban incineration of household waste in favour of recycling and composting?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether countries should ban the incineration of household waste in favour of recycling and composting. Dalia, you support a ban; Samir, you oppose it.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Household-waste incineration is more harmful to climate and public health than recycling and composting. That is the central reason I support a ban.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Most municipal compost bins are collected once a week.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Household-waste incinerators can generate electricity. Some cities use that power for nearby homes and public buildings.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: A landfill in Norland accepted 18,000 tonnes of household waste last year.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Dalia, explain what a ban would achieve beyond closing existing plants.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Because household-waste incineration is more harmful than recycling and composting, countries should ban it. If countries adopt that ban, municipalities will have to expand recycling and composting.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Because household-waste incinerators can generate electricity, incineration can be less harmful than recycling and composting when that electricity replaces fossil-fuel power. That challenges Dalia's claim that incineration is always more harmful.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: In other words, Dalia's position is that countries should ban the incineration of household waste.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Recycling and composting require separate collection systems and new processing capacity. Municipalities would face high transition costs if they replaced incineration with recycling and composting, because those systems must be built first.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: So you are saying that replacing incineration with recycling and composting would impose high transition costs on municipalities.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Since a ban would push municipalities to expand recycling and composting, expanding those systems would reduce countries' dependence on incinerators.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: That is why countries should fund the expansion of recycling and composting, even if the transition requires investment.

utterances.speaker: Clement

utterances.speaker: Clement

utterances.speaker: Clement

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: In other words, predictable access to land is essential to many family farms.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What alternative would you offer if compulsory changes are ruled out?

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Projects based on local consent are more likely to remain effective over time, because landowners are more willing to maintain arrangements they have accepted.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, you mean that rewilding projects last longer when local communities consent to them.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: A national power to override farmers would invite prolonged legal disputes.

utterances.speaker: Clement

spec.topic: Should local authorities hold council elections on weekends rather than weekdays?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether local authorities should hold council elections on weekends rather than weekdays. Anders, please begin with the participation case.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Weekday council elections require many voters to take leave from work. That requirement creates an avoidable barrier to participation.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Because of that weekday leave requirement, weekend council elections would reduce the number of voters who need to take leave from work.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Because many voters cannot take leave, weekend council elections would make voting possible for residents who cannot take leave from work.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: The weekday leave requirement suppresses participation; because of that requirement, weekend council elections would increase voter turnout.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Because weekday elections require time away from jobs, weekend council elections would include more shift workers in the electorate.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Because weekday voting requires employees to be absent during working hours, weekend council elections would reduce the disruption that voting causes employers.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Because weekday elections conflict with working and school schedules, weekend council elections would make it easier for families to arrange voting together.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Because the weekday leave requirement excludes some residents, local authorities should hold council elections on weekends rather than weekdays to improve participation.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The proposal under discussion is to hold council elections on weekends rather than weekdays. I want the cost issue recorded before we decide.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal under discussion is for weekend council elections instead of weekday council elections. Because this proposal changes the hours that election staff must work, weekend council elections would require higher staffing costs for local authorities.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: So you are saying that the meeting is considering a switch from weekday council elections to weekend council elections.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Separately, the council's electoral services office has three vacant administrative posts.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Put another way, the issue before the meeting is whether council elections should move from weekdays to weekends.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: The next committee meeting is scheduled for the first Tuesday of the month.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: To restate the proposal, the proposed change is to schedule council elections on weekends rather than weekdays.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: However, contrary to that weekend proposal, council elections should continue to be held on weekdays.

utterances.text: The agenda item is whether local authorities should hold council elections on weekends rather than weekdays. Anders, what is the main case for changing the schedule?

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Weekend elections would make voting easier for residents who work ordinary weekday hours. Because of that, shift workers would have more opportunity to vote.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Since the poll would not fall during the usual working day, residents would need to take less time off work in order to vote.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Because parents would face fewer weekday scheduling pressures, weekend elections would allow more parents to vote without arranging weekday childcare.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: The same practical advantage applies to election staff: weekend elections would make polling stations easier for volunteers to staff after their working week.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Because the election would be held at the weekend, local authorities would have more time to publicise the poll during the preceding week.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Weekend voting would also help community groups, because they could more easily organise transport to polling stations.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Because many younger residents have irregular weekday schedules, weekend elections would probably increase their participation.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: The broader result should be higher turnout, since removing weekday work barriers would probably increase overall turnout.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: In other words, I am saying that weekend elections would probably increase overall turnout.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: So you are saying that weekend elections would probably increase participation among younger residents.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The council chamber's heating system is due for inspection next month. Let us return to the objections.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: However, that benefit does not settle the question, because weekend elections would create additional staffing and security costs for local authorities.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Put another way, local authorities would have to spend more on staffing and security for weekend elections.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: A further concern is that weekend elections could clash with religious observances and customary weekend activities.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: In other words, weekend elections could conflict with residents' religious observances and regular weekend commitments.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: The committee will receive the revised accessibility report before its next meeting.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: We have heard the principal advantages and objections. I will record the item for a vote at the next meeting.

spec.topic: Should homeowners be required to trim hedges that overhang the pavement?

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether homeowners should be required to trim hedges that overhang the pavement. Giulia, you support the requirement?

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: I do. Homeowners should be required to trim hedges that overhang the pavement.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: What is the strongest practical reason for that position?

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: The studio windows are open tonight.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: I support that requirement because overhanging hedges narrow the usable pavement.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: The same rule is justified because overhanging hedges can force pedestrians into the road.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Another reason for requiring trimming is that it usually takes less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The proposal is also reasonable because a uniform trimming rule would give homeowners a clear standard.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Enforcement need not be excessive: the council could use complaints rather than frequent inspections, which supports the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: The rule is fair because hedge owners receive privacy benefits while the public bears the cost of an obstructed pavement.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: A warning followed by a deadline would make compliance manageable, so that is another reason to require trimming.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The requirement would also be worthwhile because trimmed hedges improve visibility at corners and crossings.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Full pavement width matters to wheelchair users, which is why homeowners should have this duty.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: The rule belongs with homeowners because the homeowner is the appropriate person to maintain a hedge growing from private property.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Requiring maintenance would save public resources, since councils currently spend time cutting back neglected private hedges.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Can the policy deal with unusual cases, such as protected vegetation?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes. The proposal remains workable because a trimming requirement could include exemptions for protected plants.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: But a blanket trimming requirement would impose unfair costs on homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Elodie, can you summarise the proposal as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: The proposal is to require homeowners to trim hedges that overhang the pavement.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: In other words, homeowners would be responsible for keeping their hedges off the pavement.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Put plainly, the suggested policy is a legal duty for homeowners to keep pavement edges clear of their hedges.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Thank you both. Giulia, any final comment?

utterances.speaker: Giulia

spec.topic: Should small firms offer profit-sharing to all staff rather than discretionary bonuses?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should small firms replace discretionary bonuses with profit-sharing for every member of staff?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Yes. Small firms should offer profit-sharing to all staff rather than discretionary bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest practical reason for that position?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Because small firms should offer profit-sharing to all staff, profit-sharing would give every employee a defined share of the firm's annual profit.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: The same policy would show employees how their work affects the firm's results, because the payout would be tied to the firm's performance.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say discretionary bonuses let owners respond to individual effort. What is wrong with keeping that flexibility?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Discretionary bonuses are unpredictable for employees.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Small firms should explain their reward policy clearly because discretionary bonuses are unpredictable.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Employees cannot plan around discretionary bonuses because those bonuses are unpredictable.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: To summarize your proposal, every employee would receive a reward calculated by a stated formula.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Exactly. In other words, the proposal would give every employee a reward calculated by a stated formula. Employees could discuss performance more constructively because that formula would be visible.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could a profit-sharing plan cope with a year in which the firm makes little money?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Discretionary bonuses can reward an exceptional individual even when the whole firm has a weak year.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What safeguard would your preferred system have?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: A written profit-sharing policy can pause payments when profits are absent.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: But that concern overlooks the safeguard: the profit-sharing plan can suspend payouts in a loss year; in other words, it can pause payments when profits are absent.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How would employees know that the calculation was fair?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Profit-sharing requires the firm to publish a calculation method before payments are made, and publishing the calculation method would let staff check whether their payments are accurate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: One final question: what personal experience informs your view?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: I joined the firm before it had a formal bonus scheme.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And what is the office schedule?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: The firm's office closes at six o'clock on Fridays.

spec.topic: Should schools teach philosophy as a standalone subject from primary age?

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: I think schools should teach philosophy as a standalone subject from primary age, because philosophy lessons teach children to reason carefully and to question their own assumptions.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: That fits, since children who can reason carefully are better at spotting weak arguments in the media they consume, which is the reason the first claim holds.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: But primary teachers have no training in this, so a standalone subject would be taught badly.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: My own primary school ran a weekly philosophy club, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Short training courses on running philosophy discussions already exist, which shows the lack of training can be fixed.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: The timetable is already overcrowded with core subjects. A new subject would squeeze out time for reading and maths.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: So you are saying philosophy can be taught within existing English lessons without a separate subject.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Exactly, in other words it can be folded into English lessons.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: I disagree with that, as philosophy needs its own protected lesson time to build the habit of sustained argument.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: I have two children in year four, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: I would suggest short weekly sessions of about forty minutes. Children enjoy them when they are built around stories and open questions.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Forty minutes a week is a small cost compared with the benefit of better reasoning, which is why I say go ahead. In other words, children enjoying it will keep questioning as they grow older.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether households should pay children for good school grades. Yusuf, you support the idea?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes, households should pay children for achieving good school grades because small payments give children an immediate reason to persist with schoolwork.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: I disagree. Paying children for grades can turn learning into a transaction, and that is an objection to Yusuf's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: School grades are an imperfect measure of what children have learned, since exam results can reflect test anxiety as well as academic understanding.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that Yusuf is proposing that households give children money for good grades?

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: A payment tied to grades gives children a concrete short-term goal.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Concrete short-term goals make children more likely to complete difficult assignments because they make the next step clear.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Completing difficult assignments can improve children's course performance; that is another reason to consider incentives.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Because grades are an imperfect measure, praise can focus children on effort rather than on imperfect grade labels; therefore parents should praise improvement rather than pay children for grades.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Does paying risk making children ignore learning for its own sake?

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: The local school district changed its report-card format last year.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: In other words, Orla's alternative is to reward academic progress with recognition rather than cash.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Clement, you are saying that grades do not perfectly measure children's learning?

spec.topic: Should firms replace annual pay rises with market-based salary adjustments for each role?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should firms replace annual pay rises with market-based salary adjustments for each role?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Yes, firms should replace annual pay rises with market-based salary adjustments for each role, because annual pay rises give the same increase to roles whose market values may have changed very differently.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest case for keeping an annual increase?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Annual pay rises provide employees with predictable salary progression. That predictability helps firms retain employees who value financial security.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How would the alternative identify the roles that need more money?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Market surveys reveal which roles are becoming harder for firms to fill, so market-based salary adjustments keep scarce roles competitive.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Keeping scarce roles competitive reduces the risk of losing critical staff. The compensation team publishes its market survey in October.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Does replacing annual rises create a risk for employees?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Annual pay rises give employees a visible yearly signal of recognition. Because of that, removing annual pay rises entirely could damage employee morale; that is an objection to replacing them completely.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Could a role-based system respond faster than the current cycle?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: A role-based system can adjust pay when the market value of a role changes. That is why firms can correct underpayment more quickly when they adjust salaries by role.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would make such a system credible to staff?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Publishing clear adjustment criteria would make a market-based salary system easier to understand. A salary system that employees understand is more likely to be trusted.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What problem does the fixed annual cycle create?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: A fixed annual pay cycle can encourage managers to postpone necessary salary changes, and postponed salary changes can leave important roles underpaid for months.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that firms should replace annual pay rises with role-specific market adjustments?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: In other words, firms would use market data to keep scarce roles competitive.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Finally, what experience informs your view?

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: I have worked in compensation for eleven years.

spec.topic: Should companies reveal individual salaries internally to all employees?

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether companies should reveal individual salaries internally to all employees. Daniela, why do you support that policy?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Companies should reveal each employee's individual salary internally to all employees. Internal salary disclosure would help employees identify unequal pay, because hidden differences are difficult to challenge.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: I oppose that proposal: revealing individual salaries internally would create resentment among employees. The reason is that employees would compare their own pay with their colleagues' pay.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Daniela, in other words, the proposal is for every employee to see the exact salaries of all colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Yes. Because employees would be able to compare pay openly, companies should make individual salaries visible internally. That would give staff a clearer basis for discussing fairness.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: For context, the debate has received more than three hundred viewer questions.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: The studio lights are unusually bright tonight.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to the question after the break.

spec.topic: Should drivers be required to use in-car systems that detect drowsiness and alert them?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether drivers should be required to use in-car systems that detect drowsiness and issue alerts. Renata, why should this become a legal requirement?

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Drowsy driving is involved in about one fifth of fatal crashes. That is why we should take early detection seriously.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Because an in-car system can give a warning before a driver loses control, drivers should be required to use one.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: The requirement is straightforward: every car should warn its driver when it detects dangerous drowsiness.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Current drowsiness-alert systems produce too many false alarms. For that reason, mandatory use may make roads less safe by causing drivers to ignore genuine warnings, which is an objection to Renata's requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: In other words, Sunita's objection is that mandatory use of drowsiness-alert systems could make roads less safe.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: But the latest systems have false-alarm rates below two percent, which supports requiring them. Manufacturers can also update drowsiness-detection software remotely, providing a further reason to require the systems.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Sunita, what other concern should drivers consider?

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Some proposed systems would record images inside the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Compulsory alerts could encourage drivers to rely on warnings instead of getting adequate rest, so that risk also argues against making the systems mandatory.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: In other words, my proposal is to require every driver to use a drowsiness-alert system, not to let the system take control of the car.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: So Renata is saying that drowsiness-alert systems can warn before a driver loses control.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: A national pilot found that twelve percent of drivers pulled over after receiving a drowsiness alert. That result supports requiring these systems.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: The debate will also affect the design of dashboard displays.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Drivers who pull over after an alert avoid continuing to drive while impaired. Because stopping interrupts the dangerous journey, some crashes caused by driver fatigue are prevented.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal is to make early drowsiness warnings compulsory for drivers. We will now hear brief closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: A warning cannot replace sleep, but it can give a dangerously tired driver one final chance to stop. That is a strong reason for requiring the technology.

spec.topic: Should governments tax sugary drinks to fund public health programmes?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether governments should tax sugary drinks to fund public health programmes. Kieran, why do you support the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: A tax on sugary drinks would raise substantial revenue.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: In other words, the revenue from a sugary-drink tax would be available for public health programmes. That revenue is one reason governments should adopt the tax.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: A sugary-drink tax would reduce consumption of sugary drinks.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: So you are saying that a sugary-drink tax would lower the amount of sugar people consume. That is another reason to support the tax.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: It would also encourage manufacturers to produce less sugary drinks.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: For all those reasons—the revenue, the health effect, and the incentive for manufacturers—governments should tax sugary drinks to fund public health programmes.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Dalia, do you think the policy would be fair?

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: The proposed sugary-drink tax would treat households fairly. But a sugary-drink tax would place a larger financial burden on low-income households, so I cannot accept that claim.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Before we move to closing statements, Kieran has worked in public policy for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Dalia's microphone is working properly, so we can hear her response.

spec.topic: Should the national government be required to publish the full legal advice behind major policy decisions?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should the national government be required to publish the full legal advice behind major policy decisions?

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Yes. The national government should be required to publish the full legal advice behind major policy decisions, because publishing the advice would let citizens assess the legal basis for major policies.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest objection to that requirement?

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: The strongest objection is that publishing full legal advice can expose confidential personal information. I read legal documents for pleasure, although that is not central to my argument.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So your proposal is that the government must publish the complete advice behind major policy decisions?

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Exactly. Another reason for requiring publication is that full legal advice makes responsibility for accepted legal risks traceable. I also spent several years as a junior barrister.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, you are saying that full legal advice makes responsibility for accepted legal risks traceable?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And the objection you acknowledge is that publication can expose confidential personal information?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How would publication affect parliamentary scrutiny?

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Because responsibility for legal risks becomes traceable, parliamentary scrutiny improves.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Since parliamentary scrutiny improves, legislators can test the government's legal reasoning.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: When legislators can test the government's legal reasoning, scrutiny can catch legal errors before a policy takes effect.

spec.topic: Should parents be fined when children miss school for term-time holidays?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: I think parents should be fined when their children miss school for term-time holidays.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Because term-time holidays make children miss lessons and learning activities, a fine is justified.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Regular attendance helps children keep up with their classmates. That is another reason to support a fine for avoidable term-time absences.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: The forum software will close for maintenance at midnight.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: But fining parents would unfairly punish families with limited incomes, especially when travel is cheaper during term time.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Most parents can arrange holidays during school breaks instead, which is why a fine would be reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: So you are saying that parents should face fines whenever their children miss school for a term-time holiday.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: In other words, Rashid's objection is that the fines would unfairly punish families with limited incomes.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Put another way, Rashid's concern is that term-time holiday fines would burden poorer families unfairly.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The proposed fines would be waived for illness or a family emergency, because those absences are not deliberate holidays.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Schools can already distinguish planned holidays from illness and emergencies through their absence codes, which supports that exemption.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A modest penalty would make parents less likely to book holidays during term time, so it would protect attendance without being excessive.

utterances.text: We should set aside fixed lane times exclusively for women. The reason is that many women avoid public sessions because they feel self-conscious around men.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind

utterances.speaker: Elif

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should assisted dying for terminally ill adults be legalised? Bernard, you start.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Assisted dying should be legalised for terminally ill adults.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Siobhan, you have a concern.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Legalisation would pressure vulnerable people into ending their lives, since elderly people already worry about being a burden.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Safe regulation is possible, and that is the reason I say it should pass, because where it is legal two independent doctors must sign off and abuse has stayed rare.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Damien, your view?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Legalisation is unnecessary, because palliative care can relieve almost all suffering.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that good hospice care makes an assisted dying law pointless.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Exactly. And it is very warm in this studio, I must say.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: But palliative care does not reach every dying patient, because hospice funding has been frozen for five years.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: So what you mean, Seamus, is that hospices cannot serve everyone who is dying.

utterances.speaker: Siobhan
utterances.text: Put another way on my own point, frail people would be nudged towards death, partly because families can lean on them to choose it.

spec.topic: Should councils charge extra parking fees for heavier vehicles such as large SUVs?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should councils charge extra to park large SUVs? Tariq, make your case.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Councils should charge extra for heavier vehicles, because they take up more space and wear the kerbside and road faster.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Esther, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: But extra fees would hit families who need large cars, since many big families have no alternative to a seven-seater.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Esther, you are saying the fee would land on families rather than on the drivers it is aimed at.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Yes, that is the risk. I drive a hatchback myself, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Heavier vehicles kill more pedestrians in collisions, since a tall bonnet strikes a person higher up on the body. That is another reason to charge them more than other cars.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Put another way, tall bonnets make a collision deadlier for anyone on foot.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Esther, would a fee even change what people buy?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Parking charges are a blunt tool for changing what people buy, since buyers choose a car once every several years, not according to the daily parking cost.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: In other words, parking charges barely influence which car people buy, and dealer surveys rarely list parking cost among buyers' reasons.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: The surcharge would raise enough revenue to cover its own running costs, because several thousand heavy vehicles park in our paid bays each day.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Tariq, you are saying the scheme would pay for itself.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Exactly, and since it pays for itself, there is every reason for councils to charge heavier vehicles more.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Several cities already price parking by vehicle emissions, so charging heavier vehicles more is nothing unusual.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: But emissions are not weight: an electric SUV is heavier than a petrol hatchback yet would pay less.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: For the record, the council votes on this next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, in short, heavier vehicles are deadlier for pedestrians. Thank you all.

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether managers should be barred from contacting staff on sick leave. Harriet, why do you support a complete ban?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Staff on sick leave need uninterrupted time to recover. Managers should be barred from contacting them because that boundary protects recovery.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Carmen, you oppose the proposal. What is your main concern?

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Sick-leave policies differ widely across industries. Small teams cannot always redistribute urgent work.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Because of that staffing problem, a blanket contact ban would delay essential decisions.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Because small teams cannot always redistribute urgent work, managers should be allowed to send one logistical message about return arrangements.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The studio lights were replaced this morning.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: A total contact ban would prevent managers from checking urgent safety information. That is a serious difficulty for workplaces handling hazardous equipment.

utterances.speaker: Harriet

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So you are saying managers may send one logistical message but may not start a wider conversation with staff on sick leave?

utterances.speaker: Chloe

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Councils should give long-term residents who are not citizens a vote in local elections, because they pay council tax and use local services just like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: But local voting should stay tied to citizenship, since voting belongs together with the duties of citizenship.

utterances.speaker: Enzo

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: For what it's worth, I moved here from Gdansk in 2012 myself.

utterances.speaker: Enzo

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Put another way, Enzo, voting by foreign residents has proved manageable in the Nordic countries, since Denmark and Sweden have done it for years.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, a vote is a citizen's privilege, because only citizens can be called to jury service.

spec.topic: Should failing to report a serious crime you witnessed be an offence?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Our question is whether failing to report a serious crime that someone witnessed should itself be an offence. Laleh, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Witnesses to serious crimes can provide investigators with timely, valuable information.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Because witnesses can hold that kind of information, failing to report a serious crime witnessed firsthand should be a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Because witnesses may possess timely evidence, a reporting offence would bring important information to investigators while that information is still useful.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Witnesses can provide investigators with timely information, so the law should impose a duty to report serious crimes rather than leave reporting entirely voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: The information witnesses hold may be valuable; because of that, the offence should carry modest penalties instead of severe prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Because witnesses can give investigators useful leads, a reporting requirement could help investigators identify repeat offenders sooner.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Witnesses' information can be valuable, which is why the offence should include protection for people who report through confidential channels.

utterances.speaker: Matteo

utterances.speaker: Kai

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Enforcing such an offence fairly would be difficult.

utterances.speaker: Gideon

utterances.speaker: Laleh

utterances.speaker: Matteo

utterances.speaker: Gideon

utterances.speaker: Kai

utterances.speaker: Laleh

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: I disagree with that exception because a claim of credible retaliation should not automatically excuse a witness from the reporting offence.

utterances.speaker: Kai

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: The proposed offence should apply only to serious crimes witnessed directly, not to every failure to help.

utterances.speaker: Kai

utterances.text: The agenda item is whether councils should charge more for floodlit pitches used late into the evening. Lars, would you make the case for the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: I propose that local councils charge more for floodlit pitches booked late into the evening. The reason is that late bookings increase councils' electricity and staffing costs.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: I worry that higher late-night pitch charges could push some youth teams out of evening sport.

utterances.speaker: Lars

utterances.speaker: Leilani

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Separately, the council's community-pitch booking system will be upgraded in July.

utterances.speaker: Leilani

spec.topic: Should university tuition debt be cancelled for graduates in nursing and teaching after ten years of service?

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether tuition debt should be cancelled for nursing and teaching graduates after ten years of service. Hiroshi, could you start with the case for the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Ten years of nursing or teaching service is a substantial contribution to the public.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Tuition-debt cancellation would help universities and public employers retain experienced nurses and teachers.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Nursing and teaching are demanding forms of public service with persistent staffing shortages.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Tuition debt can make experienced nurses and teachers leave public service for better-paid private jobs.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: The university could fund the debt cancellation through the savings from lower staff turnover.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Because ten years of service is a substantial public contribution, because cancellation would improve retention, because these professions face staffing shortages, because debt can drive experienced staff away, and because lower turnover could fund the policy, the university should cancel the tuition debt of nursing and teaching graduates after they complete ten years of service.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: In other words, Selin's proposal is to erase the tuition debt of qualifying nurses and teachers once they have served for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: So you are saying that the policy would reward nurses and teachers who complete a decade of service by cancelling their university tuition debt.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal means that ten years in nursing or teaching would lead to full tuition-debt cancellation.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: On the contrary, cancelling all tuition debt after ten years would be unfair to graduates in other essential professions.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Separately, the student union is holding its annual elections next month.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: I have submitted the revised meeting minutes.

spec.topic: Should businesses rotate team leaders every two years?

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether businesses should rotate team leaders every two years. Anika, make the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Businesses should rotate team leaders every two years. Fresh leadership exposes stagnant routines, which is why I support the policy.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: But I reject that schedule: rotating team leaders every two years can weaken trust before trust has developed. Separately, my team works across three remote offices.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: In other words, Anika's proposal is to replace each team leader after two years.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: A predictable two-year leadership cycle gives businesses regular succession practice. Since it provides that practice, it makes leadership gaps easier to cover.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: That easier coverage is why businesses should keep team leaders longer than two years; frequent planned transitions are not the only way to prepare successors.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Longer terms let team leaders finish complex projects. Because leaders can finish those projects, teams gain more continuity.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: That continuity helps businesses complete long-term plans, because long-term plans depend on sustained direction. I personally prefer clear reporting lines.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So you are saying, Amir, that a two-year term can end before team trust has developed. For that reason, businesses should keep team leaders longer than two years—in other words, that is the position Anika has now accepted.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Clement, your response?

utterances.speaker: Clement

utterances.text: Judges should be allowed to sentence offenders to community service instead of prison terms of six months or less. Short prison terms often make offenders lose stable jobs.

utterances.speaker: Anika

utterances.speaker: Alejandro

utterances.speaker: Astrid

utterances.speaker: Gwen

spec.topic: Should governments restore wetlands even when doing so removes land from potential housing development?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should governments restore wetlands even when doing so removes land that could otherwise be used for housing?

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Wetlands absorb and slow stormwater, which is why restored wetlands reduce flood peaks downstream.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say the housing shortage makes that trade-off unacceptable. How do you respond?

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: The region is expected to need about forty thousand additional homes within fifteen years. Still, restoration can be concentrated on degraded parcels that are poor candidates for housing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Restored wetlands also reduce the likelihood of expensive flood-insurance claims, so governments should not judge the land only by its potential sale value.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that restored wetlands lower flood risk for existing communities?

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Yes, and that is why governments should restore wetlands even when restoration removes some land from potential housing development.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, you recommend restoration despite its opportunity cost for housing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: I do. But the loss of potential housing land remains a serious objection to restoring wetlands.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: There are additional reasons for my recommendation: restored wetlands provide wildlife habitat and improve water quality, and restoration can give residents public benefits that a private housing project would not provide.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Put another way, the habitat and water-quality benefits are further reasons to restore wetlands?

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Exactly. Several restored wetlands in the region now attract migratory birds. More importantly, protecting existing homes from flooding is more urgent than maximizing every possible housing site.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So your priority is protecting existing homes rather than maximizing every possible housing site.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: That priority is also financially sensible, because restoration usually costs less than rebuilding roads, utilities, and homes after a major flood. I have worked on floodplain planning for more than a decade.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Wetland restoration can create seasonal public parks as well as flood protection. It can also be funded through climate-adaptation grants.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: That is to say, climate-adaptation grants can pay for wetland restoration.

utterances.speaker: Olumide

utterances.speaker: Renata

utterances.speaker: Olumide

spec.topic: Should stadiums reserve a fixed proportion of seats for standing spectators?

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Stadiums should reserve a fixed proportion of seats for standing spectators.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: A standing section can increase the atmosphere without making every spectator stand, which is why the policy is worth adopting.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: I can see the appeal. A fixed proportion gives clubs a predictable way to manage standing areas, so that is another reason to support it.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Standing sections can make tickets more affordable for supporters who do not need a seat; because of that saving, a reserved proportion would widen access.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Designated standing areas can be separated from family seating. That separation is a reason to reserve a defined proportion.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: A fixed proportion prevents standing spectators from spreading unpredictably through the stadium, which makes the proposal safer.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Many supporters prefer standing during parts of a match, and that preference supports reserving some standing places.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Reserved standing areas can preserve traditional match-day culture. Since that culture matters to many fans, the stadium should include such an area.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Clubs can inspect and regulate standing sections more easily when their size is fixed; this is why a fixed proportion is practical.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: A standing section can be closed temporarily if safety conditions deteriorate, which gives the policy an additional safeguard.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Reserving a fixed proportion allows clubs to test standing without converting the whole stadium. That limited trial is a further reason for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Still, a fixed standing proportion could reduce the usable capacity for spectators who require seats. I object to the proposal on that ground.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: In other words, I am proposing a limited, clearly defined part of the stadium for standing spectators.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal is for a controlled standing section rather than for standing throughout the stadium.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: Put another way, the policy would give standing spectators some places without requiring every spectator to give up a seat.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: That is to say, the suggested arrangement is a measured compromise between all-seated and unrestricted standing.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: In short, the question concerns a fixed standing allocation, not a general removal of seats.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The stadium's north stand was renovated last summer.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: I usually arrive at matches twenty minutes before kick-off.

spec.topic: Should large employers be required to publish their average pay by department?

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Large employers should be required to publish their average pay by department, since that exposes pay gaps that would otherwise stay hidden.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Why would hiding them matter that much? Surely people know roughly what colleagues earn.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: They do not, and workers who can see typical pay in their department negotiate with more confidence, which is another reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: But averages for small departments would effectively reveal individual salaries.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: I know how this works from the inside, because I spent six years in a hospital finance office.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: In other words, privacy concerns about small departments are a reason not to require publication.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Not quite, because small departments could be exempted or grouped together in the published figures.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Hm, okay.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: So what I am saying is that the privacy problem can be solved without dropping the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Fine. I think the reporting burden is overstated anyway, since employers already collect this payroll data for tax purposes.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Then publishing would add very little work for them.

spec.topic: Should landlords be required to accept rent payments through government-backed accounts?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should landlords be required to accept rent payments through government-backed accounts?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Yes. Landlords should be required to accept rent payments through government-backed accounts because those accounts would reduce missed rent payments by making transfers easier to track.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What practical benefit would the system provide beyond tracking payments?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Magnus has rented his current home for eight years. A standard government-backed payment portal would issue immediate receipts to both landlords and tenants.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why do those receipts matter?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Immediate payment receipts would reduce disputes about whether rent was paid on time, since both sides would have the same record.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Landlords often object that a mandatory system could cost them money. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Landlords should not have to pay transaction fees for accepting rent through the required accounts. The proposed accounts would impose transaction fees on landlords, and that cost must not be shifted onto them.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So the government would cover transaction fees through the government-backed accounts?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Exactly—in other words, the government will cover transaction fees through the government-backed accounts. That is why landlords should not have to pay the fees themselves, and it also makes the requirement more reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Are there any safeguards against someone sending rent under a false identity?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Government-backed accounts would verify the identity of the person making each rent payment. That identity verification would make fraudulent rent-payment instructions less likely.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Most tenants currently pay rent by bank transfer, so would this really change everyday practice?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: The proposed system should preserve familiar payment habits while adding a common record. It should be required because the tracking and verification benefits apply to every tenancy.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: To summarise your position, what condition would you attach to the requirement?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: In other words, landlords should not have to pay transaction fees for accepting rent through the required accounts. That directly challenges the objection that the proposal would impose transaction fees on landlords.

utterances.text: These facilities operate with trained staff, medical standards, and reporting rules. That matters because protection should be attached to a regulated health service, not to careless conduct.

spec.topic: Should adults be allowed to refuse life-saving treatment even when doctors believe the decision is irrational?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Competent adults should be allowed to refuse life-saving treatment even when doctors consider the refusal irrational.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason for that position is that respect for competent adults' bodily autonomy requires accepting their informed treatment refusals.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A further reason for allowing refusal is that a doctor's professional duty does not give the doctor ownership of a competent patient's body.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason is that allowing an exception whenever a doctor calls a refusal irrational would make personal liberty depend on a doctor's judgment. Compulsory treatment can also seriously damage a patient's trust in medical institutions, which is an additional reason to reject compulsion.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Medical consent forms often use technical language that patients may find difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The autonomy principle also supports this narrower claim: a competent adult's refusal can remain valid even when the refusal appears irrational to a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That conclusion is warranted because a competent adult can understand the relevant medical information and consequences without choosing what the doctor considers rationally.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That same fact supports a practical limit: doctors should not impose life-saving treatment solely because they judge a competent patient's refusal irrational.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a competent adult may reject life-saving treatment despite a doctor's contrary assessment of the decision's rationality; that position conflicts with treating the doctor's judgment as sufficient grounds for imposing treatment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the validity of a competent adult's refusal does not depend on the refusal appearing rational to the treating doctor.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To restate the practical limit, doctors should not override a competent refusal merely because they regard the refusal as irrational.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Family members may experience distress when a relative refuses life-saving treatment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Adults have a moral right to control what happens to their own bodies.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For that reason, competent adults should be allowed to refuse life-saving treatment even when doctors consider the refusal irrational.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, respecting an irrational refusal can still be respect for an adult's bodily autonomy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That principle matters because a person's right to make a medical decision should not depend on making a medically sensible choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A further reason is that respecting capable refusals prevents the state from treating adults as children whenever officials distrust their judgment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the law should protect medical self-determination rather than require every treatment decision to be reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This is why doctors should assess whether a patient has decision-making capacity, not whether the patient's reasons seem rational.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Compulsory treatment can also damage patients' trust in medical institutions.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, allowing capable refusals is a safeguard against excessive medical paternalism.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That safeguard has a limit, however: a capable refusal should not always settle the matter when carrying it out would create an immediate serious danger to other people.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because it guards against excessive paternalism, the general rule should therefore permit capable adults to refuse life-saving treatment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Hospitals need clear procedures for recording treatment refusals.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many families find treatment refusals emotionally difficult.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should people who live together keep one shared calendar for appointments and social plans? Olumide, you start.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Every household should keep one shared calendar, because double-booking is the commonest source of family arguments.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: A shared calendar also means nobody has to ask who is picking up the children, which is another reason to have one.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Anders, you look unconvinced.

utterances.text: But a shared calendar exposes private appointments, such as a doctor's visit, to the whole household. I keep my own diary on paper.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I back it, since most calendar apps let you mark an entry as busy without showing any details.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Leopold, in other words, the apps let people hide the details of an entry.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Anders, what you mean is that a shared calendar would put everyone's private business on show.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Yes, and young children would see appointments they cannot understand, which is a further reason privacy suffers.

utterances.speaker: Olumide

utterances.speaker: Jin

utterances.speaker: Leopold

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: So you are saying, Leopold, that syncing makes sharing take almost no effort.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Besides, the leading apps are free to use, which is another reason to adopt one.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Teenagers would feel watched, which is a further reason privacy suffers. Visitors would also glimpse entries on a kitchen display, which shows the exposure is real.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

spec.topic: Should horse-racing organisers prohibit whipping except when preventing an immediate accident?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Horse-racing organisers should prohibit whipping except when it is needed to prevent an immediate accident.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The first reason is that whipping hurts the horse, and the second is that hurting an animal for entertainment cannot be justified.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Nor does the whip buy anything in return, since it does not make horses run measurably faster.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is shown by studies of finishing times, in which jockeys who ride with hands and heels alone finish just as often in the places they were expected to.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public tolerance for visible harm to animals in sport is falling, and racing depends on public goodwill to survive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, racing's long-term survival is threatened if it keeps the whip.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some will object that a rule banning the whip would be impossible to police fairly.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But stewards already review race footage for every race and can spot whip use with ease.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I attended a race meeting last spring in the rain.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Others say jockeys need the whip to steer a tiring horse away from the rail.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the accident exception already covers the use of the whip to steer a horse away from danger.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many sports have already changed their rules to protect animals.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My neighbour keeps a retired racehorse.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That is to say, racing should end routine whipping now rather than wait for outside pressure to force it.

utterances.text: Many outdoor fixtures send light above the horizontal.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Towns should require shielded outdoor lighting, because many existing fixtures send light above the horizontal.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would that requirement help wildlife as well as the night sky?

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Yes. Because many fixtures send light above the horizontal, shielded outdoor lighting would protect nocturnal wildlife from unnecessary exposure.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: The proposal has a drawback, though: a shielded-lighting requirement would impose unacceptable costs on small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: How would you describe the policy you are proposing?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, your proposal is that towns should make shielded outdoor lighting a legal requirement.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: To state that objection plainly, the concern is that a shielded-lighting requirement would impose unacceptable costs on small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A wildlife survey found that moth activity fell near bright outdoor lamps.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Because of that finding, towns should use shielded fixtures beside wildlife reserves.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: The town council's next meeting is on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Finally, what experience do you bring to this issue?

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I have worked in environmental planning for six years.

spec.topic: Should schools prohibit parents from contacting teachers outside designated communication hours?

utterances.speaker: Jelena

spec.topic: Should hate-crime convictions carry enhanced sentences beyond punishment for the underlying offence?

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Our question is whether hate-crime convictions should carry an enhanced sentence beyond punishment for the underlying offence. Hector, you oppose that proposal.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: I do. Punishment for the underlying offence alone may leave the intimidation experienced by a targeted community unaddressed. For context, I have worked as a criminal-defence solicitor for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Hate crimes communicate a threat to people who share the victim's protected characteristic.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: That is why enhanced sentences are justified: hate crimes communicate a threat to people who share the victim's protected characteristic.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: I object that an enhanced sentence for a hate crime would punish the same criminal conduct twice.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: The law should add a sentence enhancement when a conviction proves a hate-motivated offence.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: That objection is mistaken: an enhancement is not double punishment, because it addresses the additional harm caused by the offender's discriminatory motive.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Because the enhancement addresses that additional harm, it can recognise the broader harm that a hate crime causes to a targeted community. It can also express society's condemnation of discriminatory violence for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Theo, what would supporters say the extra sentence achieves?

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal is that hate-crime convictions should receive an additional sentence beyond the punishment for the underlying offence.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Because hate-crime convictions should receive that additional sentence, a sentence enhancement can deter offenders who choose victims because of protected characteristics. It can also reassure members of targeted communities that the justice system takes their safety seriously.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Since the additional sentence makes discriminatory motive explicit, a sentence enhancement can improve public recognition of the distinctive harm caused by hate crimes.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: A separate point: a carefully defined enhancement could improve public confidence in the fairness of hate-crime sentencing.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Courts already consider an offender's motive when deciding the sentence for many offences. Prosecutors already have to prove evidence of discriminatory motive in a hate-crime case.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: In other words, the existing system already considers discriminatory motive when handling hate-crime cases.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Because the existing system already considers discriminatory motive, it should be strengthened with an additional sentence for proven hate motivation.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: That carefully defined enhancement could improve public confidence in hate-crime sentencing because it would make the response to discriminatory harm clearer.

utterances.text: Our question is whether a hate-crime conviction should bring a sentence beyond the punishment for the underlying offence. Hector, you support that approach.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: I do. Enhanced sentences for hate crimes recognize the additional harm caused by targeting people because of identity.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: I oppose the enhancement. Enhanced sentences can punish the same criminal conduct twice, and courts can punish the underlying assault or threat without adding a hate-crime enhancement.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: My concern is that enhanced sentences may make punishment depend too heavily on the offender's motive. Equal treatment requires sentencing offenders for their conduct rather than for their beliefs.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Yara, what harm do you think an enhancement addresses?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Identity-based attacks can make an entire community feel threatened. That is why enhanced sentences beyond the underlying offence are justified for hate crimes.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: A separate hate-crime enhancement may discourage defendants from challenging prosecutors' accounts of motive, because disputing motive can look like denying the victim's experience.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Sentencing guidelines can distinguish a genuine bias motive from protected unpopular opinion. Clear definitions can therefore limit hate-crime enhancements to intentional targeting of a protected group, which reduces the risk that hate-crime laws punish protected opinion.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: For context, the debate is being broadcast during the evening news. Theo, does that distinction solve your objection?

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: It helps, but it does not remove the proportionality problem.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: I have moderated criminal-justice debates for six years, and I want a direct answer from Hector.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: In other words, enhanced sentences for hate crimes recognize the additional harm caused by targeting people because of identity. That additional harm can make an entire community feel threatened, and it shows why an enhancement is justified.

utterances.speaker: Meera

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying that courts can punish the underlying assault or threat without adding a hate-crime enhancement. That concern matters because a separate enhancement may discourage defendants from challenging claims about motive.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: A bias motive is evidence that an offender deliberately selected a vulnerable target, and deliberately selecting a vulnerable target increases the offender's culpability.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: That is why enhanced sentences can acknowledge deliberate selection of a vulnerable target. But hate-crime enhancements should not be rejected merely because courts must distinguish motive from opinion.

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Some victims will distrust the justice system if hate crimes receive no distinct legal recognition.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: The victim's selection because of identity is an additional feature of the harm.

spec.topic: Should patients awaiting specialist treatment be allowed to transfer to any hospital with a shorter queue?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Patients awaiting specialist treatment should be allowed to transfer to any hospital with a shorter queue, since waiting times for the same operation vary enormously between hospitals in the same region.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That matters because long waits let treatable conditions worsen, and that is a further reason to allow transfers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But free transfer would overload the few hospitals with short queues and make their waits long.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, patients would move toward short-queue hospitals only until those queues grow, and the shortest queues would then be the new longest ones.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Still, hospitals that lose patients could be funded according to the number of patients they treat, which is why the policy would encourage them to improve and deserves support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My aunt waited fourteen months for a hip replacement.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In most regions a patient could reach a neighbouring hospital in under an hour.

spec.topic: Should international treaties require a parliamentary vote before ratification?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Item two: whether treaties should need a parliamentary vote before ratification. Wilhelmina will open.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: I say they should, because treaties bind the country for decades, far longer than any single government lasts.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: But a vote would slow down urgent negotiations.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: Parliament can already hold governments to account after the fact.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: So you are saying, Adrian, that a vote would make the government negotiate more slowly.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Yes, and I think delay is a price worth paying for democratic legitimacy... actually no, that was meant as your point, Wilhelmina, since you would want it.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: Noted. Separately, the committee room is booked until noon.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Public support for a treaty is stronger when elected representatives have debated it openly, which is another reason to require the vote.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: In other words, parliament would have the final say over commitments that bind the country.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Fair enough. A vote would also make the government negotiate more carefully, which is why delay is a price worth paying, since it would need to win the votes beforehand.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: Put another way, you think open debate gives treaties stronger public support.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Right. By the way, the treaty briefing was circulated on Monday.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: That is because foreign negotiators would trust a government more if it had secured a parliamentary mandate in advance, so careful negotiation follows.
